events.enhanced_description: In February 1616, King James I granted playwright Ben Jonson an annual pension of 100 marks, effectively making him the poet laureate of England. This recognition underscored Jonson's importance in the literary culture of the time.
events.name: James I grants Ben Jonson an annual pension

events.enhanced_description: On February 17, 1616, Nurhaci, the leader of the Manchus, declared himself khan and crowned himself as Emperor of China, founding the Later Jin dynasty. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics in East Asia.
events.name: Nurhaci declares himself khan and crowns himself as Emperor of China

events.enhanced_description: On February 19, 1616, the first recorded eruption of Mayon Volcano occurred, marking a significant geological event in the Philippines. Known for its perfect cone shape, Mayon is the most active volcano in the country.
events.name: The first recorded eruption of Mayon Volcano

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1616, a commission of Roman Catholic theologians known as the 'Qualifiers' declared the idea that the Sun is stationary to be 'foolish and absurd in philosophy' and heretical. This report reflected the Church's stance against heliocentrism during this period.
events.name: The Qualifiers report on the stationary Sun theory

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1616, astronomer Galileo Galilei appeared before Cardinal Roberto Bellarmino, who warned him against teaching or defending the Copernican theory that the Sun is stationary. This encounter marked a pivotal moment in the conflict between science and the Catholic Church.
events.name: Galileo Galilei warned by Cardinal Bellarmino

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1616, Vincenz Fettmilch, the leader of the anti-Jewish pogrom known as the Fettmilch uprising, was beheaded in Frankfurt. This uprising led to the expulsion of Jews from the city, and their return was only secured through the intervention of Holy Roman Emperor Matthias.
events.name: Vincenz Fettmilch beheaded after the Fettmilch uprising

events.enhanced_description: In March 1616, a Spanish squadron led by Francisco de Ribera engaged and defeated a Tunisian fleet in the Action of 1616 at La Goulette, showcasing the ongoing naval conflicts in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Action of 1616

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1616, Nicolaus Copernicus's seminal work 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium' was placed on the Index of Forbidden Books by the Roman Catholic Church. This action reflected the Church's opposition to heliocentric theories and its efforts to control scientific discourse.
events.name: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium placed on the Index of Forbidden Books

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1616, Galileo Galilei met with Pope Paul V to discuss his support for Copernican heliocentrism. The Pope assured Galileo of his safety from adversaries, but Galileo was subsequently instructed to refrain from teaching heliocentric theories for the next seven years.
events.name: Galileo Galilei meets Pope Paul V

events.enhanced_description: On March 19, 1616, Sir Walter Ralegh was released from the Tower of London, where he had been imprisoned for treason. This release was to allow him to lead a second expedition to South America in search of the legendary El Dorado, although the venture would ultimately end in failure.
events.name: Sir Walter Ralegh's release from prison

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1616, Mughal Emperor Jahangir conferred the title of Nur Jahan, meaning 'Light of the World', upon his 20th wife, marking her significant influence in the Mughal court and her role in governance.
events.name: Jahangir confers title of Nur Jahan

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1616, Sir John Coke ruled in the Court of King's Bench that the King's actions in a case of In commendam were illegal, highlighting the tensions between royal authority and legal principles in early 17th-century England.
events.name: Sir John Coke's ruling

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1616, the Treaty of Loudun was signed, effectively ending a series of rebellions in France, which were part of the broader conflicts of the French Wars of Religion.
events.name: Treaty of Loudun

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1616, the Earl of Somerset and his wife Frances were convicted of the murder of Thomas Overbury, a scandal that tarnished the reputation of King James I's court, leading to their imprisonment in the Tower of London.
events.name: Conviction of the Earl of Somerset

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1616, Pocahontas, now known as Rebecca, arrived in England with her husband John Rolfe and their son Thomas. This visit was part of a promotional effort by the Virginia Company to garner support for the colony, showcasing the cultural exchange between the New World and Europe.
events.name: Pocahontas arrives in England

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1616, the first recorded eruption of Manam Volcano occurred, resulting in the formation of a 10-km-wide island in the Bismarck Sea. This event marked the beginning of frequent eruptions that continue to this day.
events.name: First recorded eruption of Manam Volcano

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1616, Hugh O'Neill, the 2nd Earl of Tyrone, died in exile in Rome, marking the end of the Flight of the Earls, a significant event in Irish history that led to the decline of Gaelic nobility in Ireland.
events.name: Death of Hugh O'Neill

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1616, the Tokugawa shogunate enacted a decree forbidding foreigners, except for the Chinese, from traveling freely or trading outside the ports of Nagasaki and Hirado, solidifying Japan's isolationist policies.
events.name: Tokugawa shogunate forbids foreign travel

events.enhanced_description: On August 30, 1616, William Baffin, serving as pilot to Robert Bylot on the ship Discovery, conducted a detailed exploration of Baffin Bay while searching for the Northwest Passage. The expedition achieved significant discoveries, including Smith Sound and Lancaster Sound, and reached a record latitude of 77° 45' North.
events.name: William Baffin's exploration of Baffin Bay

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1616, the first non-aristocratic, free public school in Europe was opened in Frascati, Italy, marking a significant step towards accessible education for all social classes.
events.name: Opening of the first free public school in Europe

events.enhanced_description: In 1616, John Donne was appointed as Reader in Divinity at Lincoln's Inn, London, marking a significant moment in his career as a cleric and scholar. This position allowed him to influence the religious and intellectual landscape of the time.
events.name: John Donne appointed Reader in Divinity

events.enhanced_description: In October/November 1616, Ben Jonson's satirical five-act comedy, The Devil is an Ass, was produced at the Blackfriars Theatre in London, critiquing contemporary beliefs in witchcraft and the judicial system.
events.name: Ben Jonson's The Devil is an Ass produced

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1616, Sakazaki Naomori of Iwami Tsuwano han committed suicide after failing to kidnap Princess Sen, an event that reflects the tumultuous political landscape of feudal Japan.
events.name: Sakazaki Naomori's suicide

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1616, Dirk Hartog made the second recorded landfall by a European on Australian soil at Dirk Hartog Island, leaving behind the Hartog Plate to commemorate the event, which marked a significant moment in the European exploration of Australia.
events.name: Dirk Hartog's landfall in Australia

events.enhanced_description: In November 1616, Peter Paul Rubens signed a contract in Antwerp to begin work on classical tapestries, collaborating with local cloth dyers and a Genoese merchant. This project would further establish Rubens' reputation as a leading artist of the Baroque period.
events.name: Peter Paul Rubens begins tapestry work

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1616, Prince Charles, the 15-year-old son of James I of England, was formally invested as Prince of Wales at Whitehall, marking a significant moment in the royal lineage and the last such investiture until 1911.
events.name: Prince Charles invested as Prince of Wales

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1616, Bishop Lancelot Andrewes delivered the annual Gunpowder Treason sermon before King James I at Whitehall, both having been intended victims of the infamous plot.
events.name: Bishop Andrewes preaches Gunpowder Treason sermon

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1616, Ben Jonson's works were published in a collected folio edition, marking the first time any English playwright's works were compiled in such a manner, solidifying his legacy in English literature.
events.name: Publication of Ben Jonson's works

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1616, Captain William Murray was granted a royal patent, giving him the exclusive right to import tobacco to Scotland for 21 years, reflecting the growing economic importance of tobacco in early 17th-century Britain.
events.name: Captain William Murray granted tobacco patent

events.enhanced_description: On November 13, 1616, the renowned Italian artist Guido Reni's Pietà was placed on the greater altar of the church of Santa Maria della Pietà in Bologna. This masterpiece reflects Reni's Baroque style and deep religious sentiment, showcasing the emotional depth of the Virgin Mary mourning her son, Jesus.
events.name: Guido Reni's Pietà placed in Santa Maria della Pietà

events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1616, Sir Edward Coke was dismissed from his position as Chief Justice of the King's Bench by royal prerogative. This dismissal marked a significant moment in the struggle between the judiciary and the monarchy in early 17th century England.
events.name: Dismissal of Sir Edward Coke

events.enhanced_description: The Tepehuán Revolt began on November 16, 1616, in Nueva Vizcaya, Mexico, with an attack on a Spanish wagon train heading to Mexico City. This uprising challenged Spanish colonial authority and highlighted the tensions between indigenous peoples and colonial powers in the region.
events.name: Tepehuán Revolt begins

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1616, Cardinal Armand-Jean du Plessis de Richelieu was appointed French Secretary of State by the young King Louis XIII. This appointment would lead to Richelieu's pivotal role in transforming France into a centralized state capable of resisting external threats.
events.name: Cardinal Richelieu appointed Secretary of State

events.enhanced_description: In December 1616, the Italian traveler Pietro Della Valle married Jowaya, the daughter of a Nestorian Christian father and an Armenian mother, in Baghdad. This union symbolized the cultural exchanges occurring in the region during this period.
events.name: Pietro Della Valle marries in Baghdad

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1616, an ordinance was established in Scotland to create parish schools, aimed at improving education among the populace. This act also included a commendation for the abolition of the Gaelic language, reflecting the cultural shifts of the time.
events.name: Establishment of parish schools in Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1616, a widely reported earthquake struck Leipzig, Germany, causing significant alarm among the residents. This event was notable for its impact on the local community and was recorded in various historical accounts.
events.name: Earthquake in Leipzig

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1616, an Indian youth, referred to as one of 'the first fruits of India', was baptized as 'Peter' at St. Dionis Backchurch in London. This ceremony, attended by prominent officials, marked a significant moment in the Anglican Church's outreach to India.
events.name: Baptism of Indian youth in London

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1616, 'Father Christmas' was featured as a main character in 'Christmas, His Masque', written by Ben Jonson and presented at the court of King James I of England. This portrayal contributed to the evolving cultural representation of Christmas in England.
events.name: Father Christmas in Ben Jonson's Masque

events.enhanced_description: The Mad Lover, a play by John Fletcher, premiered in London, showcasing the rich theatrical tradition of the time. Fletcher's work contributed to the evolution of English drama in the early 17th century.
events.name: The Mad Lover first performance

events.enhanced_description: In 1617, at the Finspång witch trial, at least seven women were sentenced to death by burning for witchcraft. This event reflects the intense witch hunts occurring in Europe during this period, driven by superstition and fear.
events.name: Finspång witch trial

events.enhanced_description: In 1617, Giambattista Andreini's play The Penitent Magdalene was published in Mantua. This work is notable for its exploration of themes related to redemption and morality, characteristic of the Italian Renaissance theater.
events.name: Publication of The Penitent Magdalene

events.enhanced_description: The Book of Swindles, a collection of short stories detailing various forms of fraud during the late Ming dynasty, was published in 1617. This work provides insight into the social and economic conditions of the time, reflecting the complexities of human behavior.
events.name: Publication of The Book of Swindles

events.enhanced_description: Pocahontas and Tomocomo, representatives of the Powhatan tribe, were received as guests by King James I at the Banqueting House in Whitehall, London. This meeting symbolized the complex relations between Native Americans and English settlers during the early colonial period.
events.name: Pocahontas and Tomocomo meet King James I

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Stolbovo concluded the Ingrian War between Sweden and Russia, resulting in Sweden gaining control over Ingria and Kexholm. This treaty marked a significant shift in the balance of power in the Baltic region during the early 17th century.
events.name: The Treaty of Stolbovo ends the Ingrian War

events.enhanced_description: On Shrove Tuesday, a riot erupted in London leading to the burning of the Cockpit Theatre, fueled by public outrage over rising ticket prices. The incident resulted in the deaths of three rioters, illustrating the tensions between the public and theatrical establishments of the time.
events.name: Rioters burn down London's Cockpit Theatre

events.enhanced_description: Francis Bacon was appointed as Lord Keeper of the Great Seal of England, a pivotal role in the English government, and was designated by King James I to act as regent during the King's absence. This appointment underscored Bacon's influence in the political landscape of early 17th-century England.
events.name: Francis Bacon appointed Lord Keeper of the Great Seal

events.enhanced_description: Pocahontas, the daughter of the Powhatan chief and wife of English settler John Rolfe, tragically died of smallpox in Gravesend after a brief illness. Her death marked a significant loss for both her family and the colonial community, symbolizing the fraught relations between Native Americans and European settlers.
events.name: Pocahontas dies of smallpox

events.enhanced_description: The Second Battle of Playa Honda saw the Spanish navy achieve a decisive victory over a Dutch fleet in the Philippines. This battle was part of the larger conflict between Spain and the Dutch Republic during the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Second Battle of Playa Honda

events.enhanced_description: King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden founded the town of Uusikaupunki, known as Nystad in Swedish, as part of his efforts to expand Swedish influence in the region. This foundation marked an important development in the urban landscape of Finland.

image.caption: Aerial view of Uusikaupunki, Finland.
image.credit: kallerna — Own work
image.date_qualification: A modern aerial view of the town associated with the foundation event; the image date is 2020-05-22, not the event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Foundation of Uusikaupunki

events.enhanced_description: Seventeen-year-old Louis XIII, encouraged by Charles d'Albert, took decisive action against his mother, Marie de Medici, forcing her into retirement and orchestrating the assassination of her favorite, Concino Concini. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics within the French monarchy.
events.name: Louis XIII forces his mother into retirement

events.enhanced_description: King James I of England, also known as James VI of Scotland, returned to Scotland for the first time since the Union of the Crowns in 1603. His arrival at Dunglass Castle marked a significant moment in the history of the Scottish monarchy.
events.name: King James I returns to Scotland

events.enhanced_description: Portuguese Christian missionary João Baptista Machado de Távora was killed in Japan, becoming the first of the 205 Martyrs of Japan. His martyrdom reflects the intense persecution faced by Christians in Japan during this period.
events.name: João Baptista Machado de Távora killed

events.enhanced_description: King James VI of Scotland authorized the Scottish East India Company, led by Lord Glencairn, to engage in trade with the East Indies and other regions. This decision marked an important step in Scotland's economic expansion and overseas trade.
events.name: King James VI authorizes Scottish East India Company

events.enhanced_description: Eliya VIII was elected as the new Patriarch of the Church of the East, taking on the leadership role for Christians in Mesopotamia. His election was significant for the Christian community in the region during a time of political and religious upheaval.
events.name: Eliya VIII becomes Patriarch of the Church of the East

events.enhanced_description: In a significant political shift, the Prince-Bishops of Bamberg, Eichstätt, and Würzburg, along with the Prince-Provost of Ellwangen, withdrew their states from the Catholic League. This withdrawal indicated growing tensions within the Holy Roman Empire during the early stages of the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Prince-Bishops withdraw from the Catholic League

events.enhanced_description: Ferdinand II, Archduke of Inner Austria, was elected King of Bohemia, a pivotal moment that would lead to significant unrest due to his Catholic counter-reformation policies. His election set the stage for the conflicts that would escalate into the Thirty Years' War.

image.caption: G. Keller’s illustration depicting Ferdinand II’s coronation as King of Bohemia.
image.credit: G. Keller — Unknown source Unknown source
image.date_qualification: Depicted event dated 1617; the evidence does not establish when the artwork itself was created.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ferdinand II elected King of Bohemia

events.enhanced_description: Willem Schouten and the crew of the Dutch ship Eendracht completed a historic circumnavigation of the globe, returning to the Netherlands after two years and 17 days at sea. This expedition marked only the fourth successful circumnavigation and the first since 1588, significantly contributing to the age of exploration.
events.name: Willem Schouten returns from circumnavigation

events.enhanced_description: The secret Oñate treaty was signed in Vienna, establishing an agreement between King Philip III of Spain and the junior Habsburg branch led by Archduke Ferdinand II of Austria. This treaty reflected the intricate political alliances and negotiations of the Habsburg dynasty during this period.
events.name: The secret Oñate treaty signed

events.enhanced_description: The Sharp Resolution was passed in the States of Holland and West Friesland, allowing city governments to create their own mercenary armies, known as waardgelders. This resolution was a response to the need for maintaining public order amidst ongoing conflicts.
events.name: The Sharp Resolution passed

events.enhanced_description: King James I of England returned to England after spending three months in Scotland, arriving at Wharton, Cumbria. This return marked a significant moment in his reign as he navigated the complexities of governance across both kingdoms.
events.name: King James returns to England

events.enhanced_description: The 'Fruitbearing Society' (Die Fruchtbringende Gesellschaft) was founded in Weimar, bringing together German scholars and intellectuals. This society played a significant role in the cultural and literary development of the German language during the early 17th century.
events.name: The Fruitbearing Society founded

events.enhanced_description: The weighing ceremony of Jahangir, the Mughal Emperor, was documented by Sir Thomas Roe, the first English ambassador to the Mughal court. This ceremony was a grand display of the emperor's wealth and power, reflecting the opulence of the Mughal court.
events.name: Jahangir's weighing ceremony described

events.enhanced_description: The Peace of Busza was a treaty signed on September 23, 1617, between the Ottoman Empire and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, marking the end of hostilities between the two powers. This agreement solidified the territorial status quo and established a period of peace that lasted for several years.
events.name: The Peace of Busza is signed

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1617, the Treaty of Pavia was signed, resulting in the return of Monferrato to Mantua from Savoy. This treaty was significant in the context of the ongoing power struggles in Northern Italy during the early 17th century.
figures: Duke Charles Emmanuel I of Savoy
events.name: The Treaty of Pavia is signed

events.enhanced_description: The coronation ceremony of King Gustav Adolf of Sweden took place on October 12, 1617, in Stockholm, nearly six years after he ascended to the throne. This event was a significant moment in Swedish history, symbolizing the consolidation of his power and the continuation of the Vasa dynasty.
events.name: Coronation of King Gustav Adolf of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1617, a naval battle occurred between Sicilian forces and the Venetian fleet, ending inconclusively. This conflict was part of the broader struggles for control over trade routes and territorial dominance in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Naval battle between Sicilians and Venetians

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1617, Mustafa I ascended to the throne of the Ottoman Empire, succeeding his cousin Ahmed I. His reign was marked by instability and was characterized by the influence of court factions and the challenges of maintaining the empire's vast territories.
events.name: Mustafa I succeeds Ahmed I as Sultan of the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1617, Sir Thomas Roe, representing England's East India Company, arrived in Ahmedabad, seeking an audience with the Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan. This marked a significant moment in Anglo-Mughal relations and the expansion of British interests in India.
events.name: Sir Thomas Roe arrives in Ahmedabad

events.enhanced_description: An unexpected storm struck off the coast of Finnmark, Norway, on December 24, 1617, sinking ten ships and resulting in the drowning of at least 40 people. This disaster later contributed to witch trials in the region, as local beliefs attributed the storm to witchcraft.
events.name: Storm strikes off the coast of Finnmark

events.enhanced_description: On December 30, 1617, Lord Clifton was imprisoned in the Tower of London for threatening Francis Bacon, the Lord High Chancellor of England. His case was prosecuted by the Star Chamber, highlighting the political tensions of the time.
events.name: Lord Clifton imprisoned at the Tower of London

events.enhanced_description: Ben Jonson's play Pleasure Reconciled to Virtue premiered at the Palace of Whitehall in London in 1618. This performance highlighted the themes of morality and virtue, characteristic of Jonson's work during the English Renaissance.
events.name: Ben Jonson's play Pleasure Reconciled to Virtue premieres

events.enhanced_description: In 1618, the margraves of Brandenburg received Polish approval to inherit the Duchy of Prussia, leading to the establishment of the state of Brandenburg-Prussia. This political development set the stage for the rise of Prussia as a major European power.
events.name: Brandenburg-Prussia established

events.enhanced_description: The Teatro Farnese, the first permanent proscenium theatre, was constructed in 1618 in the Great Hall of the Palazzo della Pilotta in Parma, Italy. This architectural achievement marked a significant development in the history of theatre design.
events.name: Teatro Farnese built

events.enhanced_description: In 1618, the Ming Chinese embassy of the Wanli Emperor presented tea to the Russian tsar in Moscow. This event marked an important cultural exchange between China and Russia, highlighting the growing trade relations between the two nations.
events.name: Ming Chinese embassy presents tea to Russian tsar

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1618, Jahangir, the Mughal Emperor, granted an audience to Sir Thomas Roe, marking the first official engagement between the Mughal Empire and the British East India Company. This meeting was pivotal in establishing diplomatic relations and trade agreements.
events.name: Jahangir gives audience to Sir Thomas Roe

events.enhanced_description: On January 28, 1618, rules were established for the Ōoku, the section of Edo Castle that housed the Shōgun's consort and concubines. This regulation was significant in the context of the Tokugawa shogunate's governance and the role of women in the feudal system.
events.name: Rules established for the Ōoku

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1618, Jeong In-hong was appointed as the new Chief State Councillor of the Joseon Kingdom by Emperor Gwanghaegun. His appointment was crucial for the political landscape of Korea during a time of internal strife and external threats.
events.name: Jeong In-hong becomes Chief State Councillor

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1618, Osman II deposed his uncle Mustafa I, taking control as Sultan of the Ottoman Empire. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics within the empire, leading to a period of reform and conflict.
events.name: Osman II deposes Mustafa I

events.enhanced_description: On March 8, 1618, Johannes Kepler discovered the third law of planetary motion, which describes the relationship between the distance of planets from the sun and their orbital periods. This discovery was a significant advancement in the field of astronomy.
events.name: Kepler discovers third law of planetary motion

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1618, Spanish-born Jesuit missionary Pedro Páez became one of the first Europeans to see and describe the source of the Blue Nile in Ethiopia. His observations contributed to the European understanding of African geography.
events.name: Pedro Páez describes the source of the Blue Nile

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1618, the Second Defenestration of Prague occurred when Protestant noblemen threw two representatives of Ferdinand II out of a window, escalating tensions that led to the Bohemian Revolt and the Thirty Years' War. This act symbolized the deepening religious and political conflict in Europe.
events.name: The Second Defenestration of Prague

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1618, Joris Veseler printed the first Dutch newspaper, Courante uyt Italien, Duytslandt, &c., in Amsterdam. This publication marked a significant development in the history of journalism and the dissemination of news in Europe.
events.name: First Dutch newspaper printed

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1618, Ferdinand II was crowned King of Hungary at a meeting of the Bohemian diet in Pressburg. His coronation was significant as it solidified his power in Central Europe and was a key moment in the Counter-Reformation.
events.name: Ferdinand II crowned King of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1618, Alonso Fajardo de Entenza was appointed as the new Spanish Governor-General of the Philippines. His administration would oversee the continued Spanish colonial efforts in the archipelago during a period of significant change.

image.caption: Signature of Alonso Fajardo de Tenza.
image.credit: Alonso Fajardo de Tenza — Carta de la Audiencia de Manila sobre sentencia contra Riberos (Image 14)
image.date_qualification: The image_date is 1623-08-17, after the 1618 appointment; this is a later signature, not a contemporaneous depiction of the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Alonso Fajardo de Entenza becomes Governor-General of the Philippines

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1618, Pluto reached its second most recent aphelion, according to sophisticated mathematical calculations. This event is significant in the study of celestial mechanics and the understanding of the solar system.
events.name: Pluto reaches aphelion

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1618, Lenaert Jacobszoon and the crew of the Dutch East India Company ship Mauritius became the first Europeans to sight what is now the state of Western Australia, landing at North Cape. This event marked a significant moment in the European exploration of Australia.
events.name: First Europeans sight Western Australia

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1618, Johan van Oldenbarnevelt and Hugo Grotius were imprisoned by Maurice, Prince of Orange, marking a significant political conflict in the Dutch Republic. This event was part of the broader struggle between the States Party and the Orange faction, which had lasting implications for Dutch politics.
events.name: Johan van Oldenbarnevelt and Hugo Grotius are imprisoned by Maurice, Prince of Orange

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1618, a catastrophic avalanche struck the Alpine town of Piuro, burying the settlement and resulting in the tragic loss of 2,427 lives. This disaster highlighted the dangers of living in mountainous regions and had a profound impact on local communities.
events.name: Rodi avalanche

events.enhanced_description: The beginning of the 13th Baktun in the Mesoamerican Long Count calendar occurred on September 18, 1618, marking a significant point in the Maya calendar system. This event is often associated with various cultural and religious interpretations among Mesoamerican civilizations.
events.name: Beginning of the 13th Baktun

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Pilsen commenced on September 19, 1618, as Bohemian Protestant forces laid siege to the Catholic city during the Thirty Years' War. This marked the first major battle of the conflict, which would last for over two months and significantly impact the region.
events.name: Siege of Pilsen begins

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1618, the Battle of Orynin took place, where Polish and Lithuanian forces faced a devastating invasion by Crimean Tatars. The battle resulted in the Tatars burning villages and enslaving residents, highlighting the ongoing conflicts in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Battle of Orynin

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1618, residents of Mogilev revolted against Uniate bishop Josaphat Kuntsevych, reflecting the religious tensions of the time. This uprising was part of the broader conflict between Orthodox and Catholic factions in the region.
events.name: Residents of Mogilev revolt against Uniate bishop Josaphat Kuntsevych

events.enhanced_description: On October 29, 1618, Sir Walter Raleigh was executed at the Palace of Westminster after being convicted of treason. His execution was influenced by political pressures from Spain and marked the end of a controversial career as an explorer and courtier.
events.name: Execution of Sir Walter Raleigh

events.enhanced_description: The Synod of Dort held its first meeting on November 13, 1618, in Dordrecht, Netherlands. This assembly was convened to address theological disputes within the Reformed Church, particularly concerning Arminianism.
events.name: First meeting of the Synod of Dort

events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1618, Pilsen fell to Bohemian Protestant forces led by Ernst von Mansfeld after enduring more than two months of siege. This victory was significant in the context of the Thirty Years' War, as it bolstered the Protestant cause in Bohemia.
events.name: Pilsen falls to Bohemian Protestants

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1618, Russia and Poland signed the Truce of Deulino, which ended hostilities between the two nations. This truce was significant in shaping the political landscape of Eastern Europe during the early 17th century.
events.name: Truce of Deulino signed

events.enhanced_description: Anne of Denmark, queen consort of England, was buried at Westminster Abbey in 1619. Her burial marked the end of her significant role in the English court and her contributions to the cultural life of the period.
events.name: Burial of Anne of Denmark

events.enhanced_description: Jahangir, the Mughal Emperor, granted significant commercial concessions to a British mission in Surat, facilitating trade relations between England and India.
events.name: Jahangir grants commercial concessions at Surat

events.enhanced_description: The Salé Rovers declared the port of Salé an independent republic from the Sultan of Morocco, with Jan Janszoon as its president, marking a significant moment in the history of piracy and privateering.
events.name: Declaration of the Republic of Salé

events.enhanced_description: The Danish-Dutch whaling settlement of Smeerenburg was established in Svalbard, becoming a significant base for Arctic whaling during the 17th century.
events.name: Founding of Smeerenburg

events.enhanced_description: An expedition led by Filipe de Oliveira in Sri Lanka resulted in the deposition and execution of Cankili II, the last king of the Jaffna Kingdom, effectively ending its sovereignty.
events.name: End of the Jaffna Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: A Spanish expedition sailed around Tierra del Fuego, mapping the coastline and discovering the Diego Ramírez Islands, contributing to the European understanding of the southernmost regions of South America.
events.name: Spanish Expedition around Tierra del Fuego

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1619, James I of England's Banqueting House in Whitehall was destroyed by fire. Following this disaster, architect Inigo Jones was commissioned to design a new structure, which would become a significant example of Renaissance architecture in England.
events.name: James I's Banqueting House destroyed by fire

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1619, an earthquake devastated the town of Trujillo, Peru, resulting in hundreds of deaths and causing landslides in the surrounding areas. This natural disaster had a profound impact on the local population and infrastructure.
events.name: Earthquake in Trujillo, Peru

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1619, Matthias, Holy Roman Emperor, died, leaving the Holy Roman Empire without an official leader during a critical period marked by the Bohemian Revolt. His death created a power vacuum that would have significant ramifications for the empire's stability.
events.name: Death of Matthias, Holy Roman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On April 18, 1619, the Battle of Sarhu took place, where Manchu leader Nurhaci achieved a decisive victory over the Ming forces. This battle was pivotal in the rise of the Manchu and the eventual establishment of the Qing dynasty in China.
events.name: Battle of Sarhu

events.enhanced_description: The Synod of Dort held its final meeting on May 8, 1619, concluding a series of discussions that addressed key theological issues within the Reformed Church. The decisions made during this synod had lasting effects on Protestantism in Europe.
events.name: Final meeting of the Synod of Dort

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1619, Dutch statesman Johan van Oldenbarnevelt was executed in The Hague after being convicted of treason. His execution marked a significant turning point in Dutch politics, reflecting the intense factional struggles of the time.
events.name: Execution of Johan van Oldenbarnevelt

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1619, Jan Pieterszoon Coen, Governor-General of the Dutch East Indies, conquered Jayakarta and renamed it Batavia. This event marked a significant step in the Dutch colonization of Indonesia and the establishment of Dutch control in the region.
events.name: Conquest of Jayakarta

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1619, during the Thirty Years' War, the Battle of Sablat occurred, resulting in a defeat for Protestant forces. This battle was part of the ongoing conflict between Catholic and Protestant states in Europe.
events.name: Battle of Sablat

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1619, Dulwich College was founded by Edward Alleyn in Dulwich, London. This institution became one of the oldest independent schools in England, emphasizing the importance of education in the early modern period.

image.caption: Illustrated London News illustration of the new buildings at Dulwich College.
image.credit: Illustrated London News — from the Illustrated London News (1869).
image.date_qualification: The illustration depicts the college’s new buildings, not its 1619 founding; it is dated c. 1869.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Dulwich College founded

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1619, the Virginia General Assembly, the first English-speaking representative assembly in the Americas, convened in Jamestown, Virginia. This assembly marked a significant step towards self-governance in the American colonies.
events.name: First English-speaking representative assembly convenes in Jamestown

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Vítkovice was a significant conflict during the Thirty Years' War, where Bohemian forces achieved a notable victory against the Austrians, marking a pivotal moment in the early stages of the war.
events.name: Thirty Years' War: Battle of Vítkovice

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Angoulême concluded the civil war between Louis XIII and his mother, Marie de' Medici, restoring stability to France and reaffirming Louis's authority as king.
events.name: Treaty of Angoulême

events.enhanced_description: In a landmark event, a group of enslaved Africans were brought to Point Comfort, Virginia, marking the beginning of a tragic chapter in American history and the establishment of slavery in the English colonies.
events.name: Landing of Enslaved Africans at Point Comfort

events.enhanced_description: Frederick V of the Palatinate was elected King of Bohemia by the states of the Bohemian Confederacy, a significant event that contributed to the tensions leading to the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Election of Frederick V as King of Bohemia

events.enhanced_description: Ferdinand II was unanimously elected as Holy Roman Emperor by the prince-electors, solidifying his power and influence during a tumultuous period in European history.
events.name: Election of Ferdinand II as Holy Roman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: During a revolt against the Habsburg Empire, Prince Gabriel Bethlen of Transylvania, aided by George I Rákóczi, successfully conquered Kassa, furthering his campaign against Habsburg rule.
events.name: Conquest of Kassa by Gabriel Bethlen

events.enhanced_description: Gaj Singh Rathore ascended to the throne as the new Raja of Marwar in Jodhpur, succeeding his father Sur Singh, continuing the lineage of Rajput leadership in the region.
events.name: Gaj Singh Rathore becomes Raja of Marwar

events.enhanced_description: Ferdinand II's coronation took place in Vienna, marking the formal recognition of his authority as Holy Roman Emperor and his commitment to the Habsburg dynasty's interests.
events.name: Coronation of Ferdinand II

events.enhanced_description: Abba Yoannis El-Mallawany was elected as the new head of the Coptic Christian Church, taking the name Pope John XV of Alexandria, succeeding Pope Mark V.
events.name: Election of Pope John XV of Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Munich was signed between Ferdinand II and Maximilian I of Bavaria, solidifying alliances during the Thirty Years' War and shaping the political landscape of Central Europe.
events.name: Treaty of Munich

events.enhanced_description: While stationed along the Danube River, René Descartes experienced a series of dreams that inspired him to apply mathematical methods to philosophy, laying the groundwork for modern philosophical thought.
events.name: Descartes' Dreams

events.enhanced_description: William Parker School was founded in Hastings, England, by the will of Reverend William Parker, contributing to the educational landscape of the region.
events.name: Founding of William Parker School

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Humenné, Polish Lisowczycy troops aided the Holy Roman Emperor by defeating a Transylvanian force, compelling Gabor Bethlen to abandon his siege of Vienna.
events.name: Battle of Humenné

events.enhanced_description: Thirty-eight colonists from England celebrated what is considered by some historians to be the first Thanksgiving in the Americas at Berkeley Hundred, Virginia, marking a moment of gratitude and community.
events.name: First Thanksgiving in the Americas

events.enhanced_description: In 1620, a Dutch ship sold 20 enslaved Africans to the Virginia Colony, marking the beginning of a tragic chapter in American history regarding slavery. This event laid the groundwork for the institutionalization of slavery in the English colonies.
events.name: First African Slaves Sold to Virginia Colony

events.enhanced_description: In early 1620, a severe frost caused the River Thames to freeze, while Scotland experienced 13 continuous days of snow. This harsh winter had significant impacts on agriculture and livestock, with many sheep perishing in the cold.
events.name: Severe Frost in England and Scotland

events.enhanced_description: The early 1620s marked the beginning of witch-hunts in Scotland, a period characterized by paranoia and persecution of those accused of witchcraft. This movement reflected broader European trends of witch trials and the societal fears of the time.
events.name: Witch-hunts begin in Scotland

events.enhanced_description: In 1620, Cornelis Drebbel successfully demonstrated the first navigable submarine on the River Thames in London. This innovative vessel marked a significant advancement in underwater exploration technology.
events.name: Cornelis Drebbel Demonstrates First Navigable Submarine

events.enhanced_description: The early 1620s saw the development of the modern violin, an instrument that would go on to play a pivotal role in Western classical music. This period marked the refinement of violin-making techniques that are still in use today.
events.name: Development of the Modern Violin

events.enhanced_description: In 1620, Juan Pablo Bonet, a teacher of deaf children in the Spanish court, created a sign alphabet that significantly contributed to the education of the deaf community. His work laid the foundation for modern sign language systems.
events.name: Juan Pablo Bonet Creates Sign Alphabet

events.enhanced_description: In 1620, Francis Bacon published 'Novum Organum', a foundational text in the philosophy of science that advocated for empirical methods and inductive reasoning. This work significantly influenced the development of modern scientific thought.
events.name: Francis Bacon Publishes Novum Organum

events.enhanced_description: In 1620, Bartolomé de las Casas' 'A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies' and Johannes Gysius' works were re-published in the Netherlands, highlighting the atrocities committed against indigenous peoples in the Americas. This re-publication played a role in shaping public opinion on colonialism.
events.name: Re-publication of Bartolomé de las Casas' Works

events.enhanced_description: In 1620, Shōgun Tokugawa Hidetada began the restoration of Osaka Castle, which would later become a symbol of the Tokugawa shogunate. This restoration was part of broader efforts to consolidate power and establish stability in Japan.
events.name: Tokugawa Hidetada Begins Restoring Osaka Castle

events.enhanced_description: The Thirty Years' War, which began in 1618, continued into 1620, primarily affecting the territories of modern-day Germany. This conflict involved numerous European powers and was marked by widespread devastation and significant political changes.
events.name: The Thirty Years' War Continues

events.enhanced_description: Ben Jonson's play, News from the New World Discovered in the Moon, was first performed in London as a presentation to King James I, blending scientific observations with imaginative storytelling.
events.name: First Performance of News from the New World Discovered in the Moon

events.enhanced_description: In France, Charles d'Albert, duc de Luynes, and his wife signed a marriage contract for their daughter, establishing a political alliance with the House of Guise.
events.name: Marriage Contract in France

events.enhanced_description: Karan Singh II ascended to the throne of the Kingdom of Mewar in Udaipur following the death of his father, Maharana Amar Singh I, continuing the legacy of Rajput leadership.
events.name: Karan Singh II becomes ruler of Mewar

events.enhanced_description: Prince Bethlen Gabor secured a peace treaty with Ferdinand II, Holy Roman Emperor, which helped to stabilize the region amidst the ongoing conflicts of the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Peace Treaty between Bethlen Gabor and Ferdinand II

events.enhanced_description: King Karma Phuntsok Namgyal of Tibet died of smallpox after a brief reign, following a purported tantric spell cast by Ngawang Namgyal of Bhutan, highlighting the intertwining of politics and spirituality in the region.
events.name: Death of King Karma Phuntsok Namgyal

events.enhanced_description: English sailor Owen Fitzpen was captured by Turkish pirates during a trading voyage in the Mediterranean Sea, leading to a seven-year ordeal of slavery in North Africa before his eventual escape.
events.name: Capture of Owen Fitzpen by Turkish Pirates

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1620, Ferdinand II, Holy Roman Emperor, issued a two-month ultimatum to Frederick V of Bohemia, demanding his departure from Prague. Frederick's refusal to comply escalated tensions leading to the outbreak of the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Ferdinand II sends ultimatum to Frederick of Bohemia

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1620, the earliest recorded earthquake in South Africa was documented at Robben Island. This seismic event marked a significant moment in the geological history of the region.

locations.name: Robben Island, Western Cape, South Africa

events.name: Earliest recorded earthquake in South Africa

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1620, Mian Shahul Mouhammed Kalhoro ascended to the throne as the king of Sindh, ruling from Karachi until 1657. His reign was marked by significant developments in the region's governance and culture.
events.name: Mian Shahul Mouhammed Kalhoro begins reign

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1620, the first recorded merry-go-round was observed at a fair in Philippapolis, Turkey. This event marked a significant development in recreational activities during the early modern period.
events.name: First merry-go-round seen at fair

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1620, the construction of Notre-Dame-des-Anges, the oldest stone church in French North America, commenced in Quebec City. This church became a significant landmark in the history of the region.
events.name: Construction of Notre-Dame-des-Anges begins

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1620, under the terms of the Treaty of Ulm, the Protestant Union officially declared neutrality, ceasing support for Frederick V of Bohemia. This decision had significant implications for the ongoing Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Protestant Union declares neutrality

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1620, the armed merchant ship Mayflower embarked from Rotherhithe, London, carrying approximately 65 emigrants bound for New England. This journey would lead to the establishment of one of the first permanent European settlements in North America.
events.name: Mayflower embarks for New England

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1620, the ship Speedwell departed from Delfshaven, carrying English separatist Puritans from Leiden to rendezvous with the Mayflower. This journey was part of the larger migration to the New World.
events.name: Speedwell departs with Puritans

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1620, the mother of renowned astronomer Johannes Kepler was arrested on charges of witchcraft. This incident reflects the superstitions and societal tensions of the time, impacting Kepler's life and work.
events.name: Johannes Kepler's mother arrested for witchcraft

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1620, the Mayflower and Speedwell departed together from Southampton, but were forced to return to Dartmouth for repairs due to a leak in the Speedwell. This delay impacted the timeline of the Pilgrims' journey to America.
events.name: Mayflower and Speedwell depart together

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1620, the Mayflower and Speedwell departed from Dartmouth, but encountered further issues with the Speedwell leaking. This led to significant changes in the plans for the voyage to America.
events.name: Mayflower and Speedwell depart from Dartmouth

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1620, the Mayflower finally departed from Plymouth, England, on its third attempt to cross the Atlantic. This voyage would lead to the establishment of the Plymouth Colony in New England.
events.name: Mayflower departs from Plymouth

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1620, the Battle of Cecora took place, where the Ottoman Empire defeated the combined forces of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and Moldavian troops. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Battle of Cecora

events.enhanced_description: On October 6, 1620, the Battle of Amedamit occurred in Gojjam, Ethiopia, where Ras Sela Kristos, half-brother of Emperor Susenyos, defeated rebels opposed to Susenyos' pro-Catholic policies. This battle was significant in consolidating Catholic influence in Ethiopia.
events.name: Battle of Amedamit

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1620, the Great Patent was granted to Plymouth Colony, formalizing its governance and land rights. This document was crucial for the establishment of the colony's legal framework.
events.name: The Great Patent granted to Plymouth Colony

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1620, the Battle of White Mountain occurred near Prague, where Catholic Habsburg forces achieved a decisive victory over Bohemian rebels. This battle marked a turning point in the Thirty Years' War.

locations.name: White Mountain, near Prague, Czech Republic

events.name: Battle of White Mountain

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1620, the Mayflower arrived at what is now known as Provincetown Harbor, Massachusetts. Here, 41 settlers signed the Mayflower Compact, establishing a foundational governing document for the Plymouth Colony.
events.name: Mayflower arrives at Cape Cod

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1620, the wedding of Gustav II Adolf and Maria Eleonora took place in Sweden. This union was significant for the political alliances in Northern Europe during the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Wedding of Gustav II Adolf and Maria Eleonora

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1620, William Bradford and the Pilgrims aboard the Mayflower landed near Plymouth Rock, marking the establishment of Plymouth Colony. This event is significant as it represents one of the earliest successful English settlements in North America and the beginning of a new chapter in American history.
events.name: Plymouth Colony: William Bradford and the Mayflower Pilgrims land near what becomes known as Plymouth Rock

events.enhanced_description: In 1621, Spanish conquistadors founded the city of Petare in Venezuela, originally named San Jose de Guanarito. This settlement marked the expansion of Spanish influence in the region.
events.name: Foundation of Petare

events.enhanced_description: In 1621, King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden founded the city of Gothenburg, which became a significant port and trade center. The establishment of Gothenburg was part of Sweden's efforts to strengthen its presence in the region.
events.name: Foundation of Gothenburg

events.enhanced_description: In 1621, Tamblot led a large-scale revolt against the Spanish Empire in Bohol, Philippines. This uprising was part of a broader resistance against colonial rule in the region.
events.name: Tamblot's revolt in Bohol

events.enhanced_description: In 1621, the Dutch East India Company dispatched 2,000 soldiers under Jan Pieterszoon Coen to the Banda Islands to enforce a trade monopoly on nutmeg. This military action resulted in the massacre of most of the indigenous population.
events.name: Dutch East India Company military action

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1621, Şehzade Mehmed, the 15-year-old half-brother of Ottoman Sultan Osman II, was executed on Osman's orders. This act of fratricide was a reflection of the brutal power struggles within the Ottoman dynasty.
events.name: Execution of Şehzade Mehmed

events.enhanced_description: On January 18, 1621, the Dutch East India Company formally named its fortress at Jayakarta as Batavia. This city would later become the capital of the Dutch East Indies and is known today as Jakarta.
events.name: Dutch East India Company Names Fortress Batavia

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1621, the Tianqi era began in Ming Dynasty China, following the ascension of Zhu Changluo as the Taichang Emperor. This period was marked by political instability and the eventual decline of the Ming dynasty.
events.name: Tianqi Era Begins in Ming Dynasty China

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1621, following the execution of Prince Mehmed, Constantinople experienced riots as citizens believed that the harsh winter was divine punishment for Sultan Osman II. This unrest highlighted the political tensions and public sentiment towards the Sultan.
events.name: Riots in Constantinople After Prince Mehmed's Murder

events.enhanced_description: On January 28, 1621, Pope Paul V died at the age of 70 after serving as Pontiff for 15 years. His papacy was marked by significant political and religious challenges, including the Counter-Reformation.
events.name: Death of Pope Paul V

events.enhanced_description: On January 29, 1621, Ferdinand II, Holy Roman Emperor, declared Frederick V, Elector of the Palatinate, a traitor to the Empire. This declaration intensified the conflicts of the Thirty Years' War and underscored the political divisions within the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Ferdinand II Declares Frederick V a Traitor

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1621, the Papal Conclave convened to elect Pope Gregory XV, who succeeded Pope Paul V as the 234th pope. His papacy would be noted for its efforts in the Counter-Reformation and the establishment of the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith.
events.name: Papal Conclave of 1621

events.enhanced_description: On February 17, 1621, Myles Standish was appointed as the first commander of Plymouth Colony. His leadership was crucial in the early years of the settlement, particularly in defense and relations with Native American tribes.
events.name: Myles Standish Appointed Commander of Plymouth Colony

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1621, Samoset, a Mohegan, visited the settlers of Plymouth Colony and greeted them with the words, "Welcome, Englishmen! My name is Samoset." This encounter marked the beginning of diplomatic relations between the Pilgrims and Native Americans.
events.name: Samoset Visits Plymouth Colony

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1621, the Pilgrims of Plymouth Colony signed a peace treaty with Massasoit, the leader of the Wampanoag tribe. This treaty established a crucial alliance that would help ensure the survival of the colony in its early years.
events.name: Pilgrims Sign Peace Treaty with Massasoit

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1621, King Philip IV of Spain ascended to the throne, beginning a 44-year reign marked by military conflicts and economic challenges. His rule would see Spain's influence wane in Europe and the Americas.
events.name: King Philip IV of Spain Begins His Rule

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1621, the colonists of Plymouth, Massachusetts, created the first treaty with Native Americans, establishing formal relations and mutual agreements for coexistence. This treaty was pivotal in the early interactions between European settlers and indigenous peoples.
events.name: Plymouth Colonists Create First Treaty with Native Americans

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1621, the Mayflower set sail from Plymouth, Massachusetts, on its return trip to England. This marked the end of the ship's historic journey that brought the Pilgrims to the New World.
events.name: Mayflower Sets Sail for Return Trip to England

events.enhanced_description: On April 9, 1621, the Twelve Years' Truce between the Dutch Republic and the Spanish Empire expired, leading both sides to prepare for renewed conflict in the Eighty Years' War. This event marked a significant escalation in the ongoing struggle for control in the region.
events.name: Expiration of the Twelve Years' Truce

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1621, a significant earthquake struck the Isthmus of Panama, registering an estimated magnitude of 6.9. The quake caused considerable damage and was felt across the region, marking a notable geological event in the area.
events.name: The Panama earthquake affects the Isthmus of Panama

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1621, King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden founded the city of Tornio in Lapland, establishing it as the northernmost city in the world at that time. This act was part of Sweden's broader territorial ambitions in the region.

image.caption: Hallituskatu street in central Tornio, Finland.
image.credit: BishkekRocks — Own work
image.date_qualification: A 2007 photograph of a street in Tornio; it shows the city, not its 1621 foundation.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Foundation of Tornio

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1621, the Protestant Union, a coalition of Protestant states in the Holy Roman Empire, was formally dissolved. This event marked a significant shift in the political landscape of Europe during the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Dissolution of the Protestant Union

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1621, the Dutch West India Company was founded, aimed at expanding Dutch trade and colonial interests in the Americas and West Africa. This company played a crucial role in the Dutch Golden Age and the Atlantic slave trade.
events.name: Foundation of the Dutch West India Company

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1621, during the Thirty Years' War, twenty-seven Czech lords were executed in the Old Town Square of Prague as a consequence of their defeat in the Battle of White Mountain. This event symbolized the harsh reprisals against the Bohemian rebels.
events.name: Execution of Czech Lords in Prague

events.enhanced_description: On December 2, 1569, the Catholic army led by the Duc d'Anjou successfully besieged Saint-Jean-d'Angély, dealing another blow to the Huguenots during the French Wars of Religion. This victory further solidified Catholic dominance in the region.
events.name: Siege of Saint-Jean-d'Angély

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1621, remnants of the Bohemian army engaged Imperial forces in the Battle of Neu Titschein, temporarily holding off their advance in Silesia. This battle was part of the ongoing conflict of the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Neu Titschein

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1621, the French Protestant city of La Rochelle joined the Huguenot revolt led by Benjamin, Duke of Soubise. This marked a significant escalation in the conflict between Huguenots and the French crown.
events.name: La Rochelle joins Huguenot rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1621, Louis XIII of France besieged the Huguenot city of Montauban but was forced to abandon the siege by November 9 due to strong resistance. This event highlighted the ongoing tensions during the Huguenot rebellions.
events.name: Siege of Montauban

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1621, the Battle of Khotyn commenced as over 120,000 Ottoman troops attacked the Moldavian city of Khotyn. Despite being outnumbered, the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth forces achieved victory, leading to a surrender five weeks later.
events.name: Battle of Khotyn begins

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1621, the Treaty of Khotyn was signed, concluding the First Polish-Ottoman War between the Ottoman Empire and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. This treaty established peace and defined territorial boundaries.

image.caption: Marcello Bacciarelli’s painting, “Treaty of Khotyn (1621).”
image.credit: Marcello Bacciarelli — http://www.i-mnk.pl/gallerybox.php?dir=SU116
image.date_qualification: Painted in 1796, 175 years after the treaty was signed in 1621.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Treaty of Khotyn signed

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1777, the United States celebrated its first Thanksgiving, commemorating the victory of American rebels over British General John Burgoyne at Saratoga in October. This event marked a significant moment of gratitude and unity among the colonies during the Revolutionary War.
events.name: First Thanksgiving celebration

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1621, the ship Fortune arrived at Plymouth Colony, bringing 35 additional settlers. This influx of people contributed to the growing community in the early years of the colony.
events.name: Arrival of the ship Fortune

events.enhanced_description: In December 1621, the Dutch mathematician and astronomer Willebrord Snel van Royen revealed his rediscovery of the law of refraction, known as Snell's Law. This discovery was pivotal in the field of optics and laid the groundwork for future scientific advancements.
events.name: Rediscovery of the law of refraction

events.enhanced_description: On December 31, 1621, the Peace of Nikolsburg was signed between Ferdinand II, Holy Roman Emperor, and Gabor Bethlen, Prince of Transylvania. This treaty marked a significant resolution in the Thirty Years' War, granting religious freedom in Moravia.
events.name: Peace of Nikolsburg signed

events.enhanced_description: The Huguenot city of Royan was captured by royal forces after a brief siege, illustrating the ongoing conflicts between Huguenots and the French crown during the Huguenot rebellions. This event further solidified royal control in the region.
events.name: Siege of Royan

events.enhanced_description: Dutch ships under the command of Jochem Swartenhont successfully repelled a Spanish squadron near Gibraltar while escorting a convoy. This engagement highlighted the ongoing naval conflicts between the Dutch and Spanish during this period.
events.name: Dutch Repulsion of Spanish Squadron

events.enhanced_description: After 107 years of Portuguese control, the island of Ormus was lost, marking a significant shift in power in the Persian Gulf. This event was part of the larger struggle for dominance in trade routes between European powers and local empires.

image.caption: Map of Hormuz (Ormus).
image.credit: Georg Braun; Frans Hogenberg — Georg Braun; Frans Hogenberg: Civitates Orbis Terrarum, Band 1, 1572 (Ausgabe Beschreibung vnd Contrafactur der vornembster Stät der Welt , Köln 1582; [VD16-B7188) Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg http://diglit.ub.uni-heidelberg.de/diglit/braun1582bd1
image.date_qualification: Depicts Hormuz in 1572, 50 years before the loss of Portuguese control in 1622.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Portugal loses control of the island of Ormus, after 107 years

events.enhanced_description: In a significant religious event, Albertus Magnus was beatified and Teresa of Ávila was canonized by the Roman Catholic Church, recognizing their contributions to theology and spirituality. This event highlighted the Church's role in promoting saints who influenced Christian thought.
events.name: Albertus Magnus is beatified, and Teresa of Ávila is canonized, by the Roman Catholic Church

events.enhanced_description: The Rosicrucian movement, which combined mysticism and esoteric knowledge, sparked significant interest and controversy in Paris during this period. This cultural phenomenon reflected the broader European fascination with secret societies and spiritual enlightenment.
events.name: Rosicrucianism furor breaks out in Paris

events.enhanced_description: The conflict between the Netherlands and Spain reignited in 1622, following the end of the Twelve Years' Truce. This resumption of hostilities marked a critical phase in the Eighty Years' War, as both sides sought to assert their dominance in the region.

image.caption: Map of military movements during the Eighty Years’ War.
image.credit: Nederlandse Leeuw, rowanwindwhistler — File:Nederlanden_1621-1628.PNG , https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Nederlanden_vooravond_1629-es.svg
image.date_qualification: The depicted period is 1621–1628, as stated in the image description; no more specific depicted date is supplied.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: War between the Netherlands and Spain recommences, after the Twelve Years' Truce (1609–1621)

events.enhanced_description: In an unusual meteorological event, the Golden Horn in Istanbul froze, which was a rare occurrence in the region's history. This phenomenon captured the attention of locals and historians alike, reflecting the harsh winter conditions of the time.
events.name: The Golden Horn freezes

events.enhanced_description: The first documented instance of bottled spring water in England occurred at Holy Well in Malvern, marking the beginning of a trend that would grow in popularity. This event reflects the early commercialization of natural resources for health and wellness.
events.name: First record of bottled spring water in England at Holy Well, Malvern

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1626, King Charles I of England dissolved the English Parliament, a move that would have significant implications for the governance of England and the relationship between the monarchy and Parliament. This act was part of the king's broader strategy to consolidate power.
events.name: Dissolution of the English Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1622, Pope Gregory XV canonized several prominent figures, including Ignatius of Loyola and Francis Xavier, marking a significant moment in the Catholic Church's history and its efforts in the Counter-Reformation.
events.name: Canonization of Saints

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1622, the Jamestown massacre occurred when Algonquian natives killed 347 English settlers outside Jamestown, Virginia, significantly impacting the colony's population and escalating the American Indian Wars.
events.name: Jamestown massacre

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1622, Hormuz was captured from the Portuguese by an Anglo-Persian force, marking a significant shift in control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz during the early 17th century.
events.name: Capture of Hormuz

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1622, during the Thirty Years' War, Protestant forces under Mansfeld and Georg Friedrich of Baden-Durlach defeated Imperial forces at the Skirmish at Mingolsheim. This victory was significant, although it led to further conflict as Tilly regrouped with Spanish forces.
events.name: Skirmish at Mingolsheim

events.enhanced_description: During the Thirty Years' War, the Battle of Wimpfen took place as Protestant forces led by Georg Friedrich of Baden-Durlach were ambushed by the Imperial army under Count Tilly. The battle resulted in a devastating defeat for the Protestant forces, significantly impacting the war's dynamics.
events.name: Battle of Wimpfen

events.enhanced_description: The Eendracht, a ship of the Dutch East India Company (VOC), wrecked off the western coast of Ambon Island, marking a significant event in the early European exploration of Australia. This incident highlights the challenges faced by early maritime explorers in the region.
events.name: Wreck of the Eendracht

events.enhanced_description: Ottoman Sultan Osman II was assassinated by rebelling Janissaries who feared his plans to reform the military and curb their power. This event marked a significant turning point in the Ottoman Empire's political landscape.
events.name: Assassination of Osman II

events.enhanced_description: The English ship Tryall, en route from Plymouth to Batavia (now Jakarta), wrecked on the Tryal Rocks, marking a notable maritime disaster in the early 17th century. The ship's fate remained unknown until its wreck was discovered in 1969.
events.name: Wreck of the Tryall

events.enhanced_description: The royal forces captured the Huguenot city of Nègrepelisse after a short siege, leading to the massacre of its entire population and the city's destruction. This brutal event exemplified the violent nature of the Huguenot rebellions.
events.name: Siege of Nègrepelisse

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Höchst, Imperial forces under Count Tilly engaged Protestant troops led by Christian the Younger of Brunswick, inflicting significant casualties and capturing valuable supplies. This battle was a key moment in the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Höchst

events.enhanced_description: During the Dutch–Portuguese War, the Battle of Macau saw outnumbered Portuguese forces successfully defend their territory against a Dutch fleet, ensuring the continuation of Portuguese influence in the Far East.
events.name: Battle of Macau

events.enhanced_description: After failing to relieve the siege of Heidelberg, Frederick V of the Palatinate disbanded Ernst von Mansfeld's army, which had been a key player in the Protestant efforts during the Thirty Years' War. This decision led to the re-employment of the troops by the Dutch.
events.name: Disbandment of Mansfeld's Army

events.enhanced_description: In a naval engagement near Portuguese East Africa, English and Dutch ships united to defeat the Portuguese, showcasing the shifting power dynamics in maritime trade and colonial ambitions during the early 17th century.
events.name: Naval Battle near Portuguese East Africa

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Bergen op Zoom was a critical event during the Eighty Years' War, where Spanish forces under Ambrogio Spinola besieged the city. The siege lasted for 86 days before a Dutch army led by Maurice of Nassau and Ernst von Mansfeld successfully relieved it.

locations.name: Bergen op Zoom, North Brabant, Netherlands

events.name: Siege of Bergen op Zoom

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Fleurus was a significant confrontation during the Thirty Years' War, where Spanish forces led by Gonzalo de Córdoba successfully repelled the Protestant army of Mansfeld and Brunswick. This battle underscored the ongoing struggle for control in the region.
events.name: Battle of Fleurus

events.enhanced_description: Armand Jean du Plessis was appointed Cardinal Richelieu, a pivotal figure in French politics who would later become the chief minister to King Louis XIII. His tenure marked the rise of royal power and the centralization of the French state.
figures: Armand Jean du Plessis, Cardinal Richelieu

image.caption: Engraved portrait of Cardinal Richelieu by Robert Nanteuil.
image.credit: Robert Nanteuil — Bibliothèque nationale de France
image.date_qualification: 1657; 35 years after the appointment in 1622.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Cardinal Richelieu's Appointment

events.enhanced_description: The Spanish treasure fleet sank off the Marquesas Keys in the Straits of Florida, resulting in the loss of valuable cargo. The wrecks of ships like the Atocha and Margarita would later become significant archaeological sites.
events.name: Sinking of the Spanish Treasure Fleet

events.enhanced_description: During the Great Genna Martyrdom, 55 Christians were executed in Nagasaki, reflecting the intense persecution of Christians in Japan during this period. This event is a stark reminder of the religious conflicts of the time.
events.name: Great Genna Martyrdom

events.enhanced_description: The Imperial army under Count Tilly captured Heidelberg after a three-month siege, marking a significant victory in the Thirty Years' War. This event had lasting implications for the Protestant cause in the region.
events.name: Fall of Heidelberg

events.enhanced_description: After enduring a siege of 86 days, Bergen op Zoom was finally relieved by a Dutch army led by Maurice of Nassau and Ernst von Mansfeld. This victory was crucial in maintaining Dutch resistance against Spanish forces during the Eighty Years' War.

image.caption: Map of Bergen op Zoom by Blaeu.
image.credit: Blaeu — Atlas van Loon. S.1034_(15). Map 094
image.date_qualification: The map is dated 1649, after the 1622 siege; it depicts the city, not the siege in progress.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: Bergen op Zoom, North Brabant, Netherlands

events.name: Relief of Bergen op Zoom

events.enhanced_description: The signing of the Treaty of Montpellier marked the end of the first Huguenot rebellion, establishing terms that would temporarily ease tensions between the Huguenots and the French crown. This treaty was a significant step towards religious coexistence.
events.name: Treaty of Montpellier

events.enhanced_description: The inconclusive Naval Battle of Saint-Martin-de-Ré was fought between the Huguenot fleet of La Rochelle, commanded by Jean Guiton, and a royal fleet under Charles of Guise. This battle exemplified the ongoing naval conflicts during the Huguenot rebellions.
events.name: Naval Battle of Saint-Martin-de-Ré

events.enhanced_description: After a siege lasting 13 days, the city of Mannheim was captured from English forces by Spanish and Imperial troops led by Count Tilly. This event underscored the ongoing military struggles during the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Capture of Mannheim

events.enhanced_description: King Christian IV of Denmark invited Sephardic Jews from Amsterdam to settle in the newly-built town of Lykstad, promising them religious freedom. This invitation marked an important moment in the history of Jewish communities in Northern Europe.
events.name: Invitation to Sephardic Jews

events.enhanced_description: A fleet of 43 Dutch ships from Suriname launched an attack on the Araya Peninsula in Venezuela, aiming to disrupt Spanish fortification efforts. The Spanish successfully repelled the Dutch after six weeks of conflict.
events.name: Dutch Attack on Araya Peninsula

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Mbumbi, Portuguese forces allied with Imbangala warriors achieved a military victory over the Kingdom of Kongo during the First Kongo-Portuguese War. This battle exemplified the complex interactions between European powers and African kingdoms.
events.name: Battle of Mbumbi

events.enhanced_description: The Spanish colonial city of Bucaramanga was founded in the colony of Nueva Granada, now known as Colombia. This establishment marked the expansion of Spanish influence in the region during the early colonial period.
events.name: Foundation of Bucaramanga

events.enhanced_description: In January 1623, forces from the Kingdom of Kongo achieved a significant victory over the Portuguese at the Battle of Mbanda Kasi. This battle underscored the resistance of African kingdoms against European colonial powers during this period.
events.name: Battle of Mbanda Kasi: Forces from the Kingdom of Kongo defeat the Portuguese

events.enhanced_description: In 1623, the imprisoned Italian Dominican philosopher Tommaso Campanella's utopian work, 'The City of the Sun' (Civitas Solis), was published in Latin in Frankfurt. This influential text envisioned a society governed by reason and communal living, reflecting the philosophical and political ideas of the time.
events.name: Publication of The City of the Sun

events.enhanced_description: In 1623, Wilhelm Schickard, a German polymath, invented the Calculating Clock, one of the earliest mechanical calculators. This innovative device was designed to perform arithmetic calculations automatically, laying the groundwork for future developments in computing technology.
events.name: Invention of the Calculating Clock

events.enhanced_description: In 1623, the Zildjian family began the commercial manufacture of cymbals in Istanbul, Turkey. This company would go on to become one of the most renowned cymbal manufacturers in the world, influencing music across cultures and generations.
events.name: Commercial Manufacture of Cymbals by Zildjian

events.enhanced_description: In 1623, men from Dorchester, Dorset, England, first inhabited the area that would become Gloucester, Massachusetts. This settlement marked an important step in the English colonization of New England and the development of fishing and maritime industries.

image.caption: Map showing Gloucester’s location within Essex County, Massachusetts, based on 2010 U.S. Census data.
image.credit: Rcsprinter123 — Own work
image.date_qualification: Map published in 2017; depicts geographic context based on 2010 U.S. Census data, not the 1623 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Settlement of Gloucester, Massachusetts

events.enhanced_description: In 1623, the settlement of Hilton's Point, which would later become Dover, New Hampshire, was established by men from London, England. This event marked the arrival of the first European settlers in New Hampshire, contributing to the expansion of English colonies in North America.
