events.name: Establishment of Hilton's Point

events.enhanced_description: Viscount Falkland, as Lord Deputy of Ireland, issued a proclamation mandating the expulsion of all Roman Catholic priests from Ireland. This action had significant implications for religious tensions and negotiations regarding the Spanish match.
events.name: Viscount Falkland issues proclamation against Roman Catholic priests in Ireland

events.enhanced_description: On February 7, 1623, France, Savoy, and Venice signed the Treaty of Paris, agreeing to collaborate in the removal of Spanish forces from the strategic Valtelline pass. This treaty was pivotal in the context of the Thirty Years' War and European alliances.
events.name: Treaty of Paris signed by France, Savoy, and Venice

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1623, Duke Maximilian I of Bavaria was appointed Elector of the Palatinate, a significant political maneuver during the Thirty Years' War. This appointment strengthened Bavaria's influence in German politics and the Catholic League.
events.name: Duke Maximilian I of Bavaria becomes Elector of the Palatinate

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1623, Virginia enacted its first temperance law, reflecting early colonial attitudes towards alcohol consumption. This law marked a significant step in the regulation of social behavior in the New World.
events.name: First American temperance law enacted in Virginia

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1623, Charles, Prince of Wales, arrived incognito in Madrid alongside his favorite, George Villiers, to negotiate a marriage alliance with the Catholic Habsburg Infanta Maria Anna of Spain. This visit was pivotal in shaping Anglo-Spanish relations.
events.name: Charles, Prince of Wales, arrives in Madrid for negotiations

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1623, the Amboyna massacre occurred when ten English merchants and others were executed by agents of the Dutch East India Company. This incident escalated tensions between the English and Dutch in the East Indies.
events.name: Amboyna massacre

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1623, Crown Prince Yi Ji of the Korean kingdom of Joseon was deposed and exiled to Ganghwa Island, where he died shortly after. This event marked a significant shift in the Joseon dynasty's power dynamics.
events.name: Crown Prince Yi Ji is deposed in Joseon

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1623, Richard Frethorne began writing a poignant letter to his parents from Jamestown, Virginia, detailing the hardships faced by settlers. His correspondence provides valuable insight into early colonial life.
events.name: Richard Frethorne begins writing a letter from Jamestown

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1623, King Gwanghaegun of Joseon was deposed in a coup led by supporters of King Injo. This political upheaval had lasting effects on the governance of the Joseon dynasty.
events.name: Injo coup in Joseon

events.enhanced_description: On April 29, 1623, a fleet of 11 Dutch ships set sail for the coast of Peru, aiming to seize Spanish treasure. This expedition was part of the broader conflict between Dutch and Spanish colonial interests in the Americas.
events.name: Dutch fleet departs for Peru

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1623, Mughal Emperor Jahangir appointed Raja Gaj Singh of Marwar to hunt down his rebel son, Shihab-ud-Din Muhammad Khurram. This event highlights the internal conflicts within the Mughal Empire during Jahangir's reign.
events.name: Mughal Emperor Jahangir deputizes Raja Gaj Singh

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1623, a Dutch East India Company party led by explorer Jan Carstenszoon engaged in a skirmish with 200 indigenous Wik peoples in Australia. This encounter marked one of the early interactions between European explorers and Indigenous Australians.
events.name: Skirmish between Dutch East India Company and Indigenous Australians

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1623, negotiations between Captain William Tucker of the English settlers and Chief Opchanacanough of the Powhatan Confederacy culminated in a banquet that turned deadly. The poisoned wine led to the deaths of many Powhatan, escalating tensions following previous conflicts.
events.name: Negotiations with Powhatan Confederacy

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1623, Rev. Gerville Pooley filed the first breach-of-promise lawsuit in Virginia against Cicely Jordan, although he ultimately lost the case. This event is notable for its implications on social contracts and legal proceedings in the early American colonies.
events.name: First breach-of-promise lawsuit in Virginia

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1623, the première of Pedro Calderón de la Barca's first play, 'Amor, honor y poder' (Love, Honor and Power), took place at the Court of Habsburg Spain. This event marked a significant moment in Spanish Golden Age literature.
events.name: Première of Calderón's play at the Court of Habsburg Spain

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1623, Pope Gregory XV died from a kidney ailment after a brief reign of just over two years. His death marked a transition in the papacy during a tumultuous period in European history.
events.name: Death of Pope Gregory XV

events.enhanced_description: The English ship Anne arrived at Plymouth Colony, becoming the third vessel to bring settlers to this Puritan settlement in modern-day Massachusetts. This event followed the arrivals of the Mayflower in 1620 and the Fortune in 1621, contributing to the establishment of one of the earliest successful colonies in New England.

image.caption: Map of Plymouth Colony.

image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Arrival of the English ship Anne at Plymouth Colony

events.enhanced_description: Trịnh Tùng was deposed as the ruler of the kingdom of Đại Việt after more than 50 years of rule. Following his deposition, his son Trịnh Xuân burned the palace, and Trịnh Tùng was abandoned by his servants, leading to his demise, while Trịnh Tráng succeeded him.
events.name: Deposition of Trịnh Tùng

events.enhanced_description: A significant astronomical event occurred with a great conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn, where the two planets were only 5 arc minutes apart, marking the closest conjunction between 1226 and 2874. This conjunction likely went unobserved due to its proximity to the Sun and the recent invention of the telescope.
events.name: Great conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn

events.enhanced_description: The second Thanksgiving was celebrated in Plymouth Colony, marking a continuation of the Pilgrims' tradition of giving thanks for a successful harvest. This event is part of the early history of Thanksgiving in America.
events.name: Second Thanksgiving in Plymouth Colony

events.enhanced_description: The English ship Little James arrived at Plymouth Colony, 26 days after the Anne, bringing additional settlers to the Puritan settlement. This continued the influx of new inhabitants to the colony, which was crucial for its growth and sustainability.
events.name: Arrival of the English ship Little James at Plymouth Colony

events.enhanced_description: Pope Urban VIII, born Maffeo Barberini, was elected as the 235th pope during the 1623 papal conclave, succeeding Pope Gregory XV. His papacy would be marked by significant political and cultural developments within the Catholic Church.
events.name: Election of Pope Urban VIII

events.enhanced_description: Negotiations for the planned 'Spanish match' between Prince Charles of England and a Spanish princess broke down, culminating in Charles's return to England without a bride. This event reflected the ongoing tensions between England and Spain during this period.
events.name: Breakdown of the Spanish Match negotiations

events.enhanced_description: At the age of 11, Murat IV succeeded his deposed uncle Mustafa I as the Ottoman Emperor. Due to his minority, his mother, Kösem Sultan, acted as regent until he came of age in 1632, navigating the complexities of the empire's politics during this time.

image.caption: Ottoman miniature of Sultan Murad IV on his way to the Baghdad campaign, dressed in Arab-style armor.
image.credit: Ottoman miniature painting — Badisches Landesmuseum
image.date_qualification: The source dates the depicted work to between 1623 and 1640; the upload date is not the depicted date. The image is not identified as depicting the accession itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Murat IV becomes Ottoman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: The 'Fatal Vespers' incident occurred when an upper floor of the French ambassador's house in London collapsed under the weight of a congregation attending a mass, resulting in the tragic deaths of 95 people. This event highlighted the dangers of overcrowding in public spaces.
events.name: Fatal Vespers incident in London

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Anjar was fought in modern-day Lebanon, where the Druze emir Fakhr al-Din II successfully defeated an invasion led by Mustafa Pasha al-Hannaq, the Ottoman Governor of Damascus, capturing him in the process. This victory solidified Fakhr al-Din's power in the region.
events.name: Battle of Anjar

events.enhanced_description: The 'First Folio' of William Shakespeare, a collection of 36 plays, was published in London. This landmark publication included many works that had not been printed before, significantly influencing English literature and drama.
events.name: Publication of Shakespeare's First Folio

events.enhanced_description: During the Great Martyrdom of Edo, 50 Christians were executed in Edo, Japan, reflecting the intense persecution of Christians during this period. This event is part of the broader context of religious conflict in Japan.
events.name: Great Martyrdom of Edo

events.enhanced_description: In May 1624, the first Dutch settlers disembarked at Governors Island, marking the establishment of New Netherland, a significant Dutch colonial venture in North America. This event laid the groundwork for the future development of New York City.
events.name: First Dutch settlers arrive in New Netherland

events.enhanced_description: In 1624, after years of unprofitable operation, the charter of Virginia was revoked, and it was transformed into a royal colony. This change marked a significant shift in governance and control over the colony, leading to increased royal oversight.
events.name: Virginia becomes a royal colony

events.enhanced_description: In 1624, the Japanese shōgun expelled the Spanish from Japan, severing trade ties with the Philippines. This event was part of Japan's broader policy of isolation and control over foreign influence.
events.name: Expulsion of the Spanish from Japan

events.enhanced_description: In 1624, Henry Briggs published 'Arithmetica Logarithmica,' a groundbreaking work that introduced logarithms to a wider audience and significantly advanced mathematical calculations. This publication had a lasting impact on the field of mathematics.
events.name: Publication of Arithmetica Logarithmica

events.enhanced_description: In 1624, Jakob Bartsch published a chart depicting the constellation Camelopardalis surrounding the North Star. This work contributed to the field of astronomy and the understanding of celestial navigation.
events.name: Chart of Camelopardalis published

events.enhanced_description: In 1624, Queen Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba began her rule, becoming a prominent figure in the resistance against Portuguese colonialism in Angola. Her leadership and diplomatic skills would later become legendary.
events.name: Queen Nzinga starts to rule

events.enhanced_description: In 1624, Dutch painter Frans Hals created the famous portrait known as the 'Laughing Cavalier.' This work is celebrated for its vibrant colors and lively expression, exemplifying the Baroque style.
events.name: Frans Hals produces the Laughing Cavalier

events.enhanced_description: In 1624, the German-language Luther Bible was publicly burned by order of the Pope, symbolizing the ongoing religious conflicts and tensions of the Reformation period. This act was part of the Catholic Church's efforts to suppress Protestantism.
events.name: Burning of the Luther Bible

events.enhanced_description: In 1624, a confrontation between Swedish and Danish councillors concluded with a Swedish diplomatic victory, showcasing Sweden's ability to mobilize quickly and effectively in the face of regional tensions. This event reflected the shifting balance of power in Northern Europe.
events.name: Swedish diplomatic victory over Denmark

events.enhanced_description: On January 14, 1624, after 90 years of Ottoman occupation, Baghdad was recaptured by the Safavid Empire under the leadership of Shah Abbas I. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics in the region and reinforced Safavid control over Persia.
events.name: Recapture of Baghdad by the Safavid Empire

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1624, General Yi Gwal led an uprising of 12,000 soldiers against King Injo in the Joseon Kingdom, occupying Hanseong (modern-day Seoul). This rebellion was part of the larger context of internal strife and power struggles within the kingdom.
events.name: Yi Gwal's Uprising in Joseon Korea

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1624, Afonso Mendes, appointed by Pope Gregory XV as Prelate of Ethiopia, arrived at Massawa from Goa. His mission was to strengthen the Catholic Church's influence in Ethiopia and to address the challenges faced by Christians in the region.
events.name: Arrival of Afonso Mendes in Massawa

events.enhanced_description: On January 28, 1624, England first colonized the islands of Saint Kitts and Nevis. This event marked the beginning of English colonial expansion in the Caribbean, which would have lasting impacts on the region's demographics and economy.
events.name: Colonization of Saint Kitts and Nevis

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1624, General Yi Gwal installed Prince Heungan, son of the late King Seongjo, to the Korean throne during a tumultuous period in the Joseon Kingdom. This act was part of Yi Gwal's rebellion against King Injo, reflecting the intense political struggles of the time.
events.name: Installation of Prince Heungan on the Korean Throne

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1624, Yi Gwal's Rebellion came to an end when the rebels murdered Yi Gwal at Mukbang-ri. This marked a significant turning point in the conflict, leading to the restoration of royal authority in the Joseon Kingdom.
events.name: End of Yi Gwal's Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On February 16, 1624, Kara Mustafa Pasha was appointed as the Ottoman Governor of Egypt for the second time. His governance would play a crucial role in the administration and military strategies of the Ottoman Empire in North Africa.
events.name: Kara Mustafa Pasha becomes Governor of Egypt

events.enhanced_description: On February 19, 1624, King Filipe III of Portugal issued a decree prohibiting the enslavement of Chinese people in Portugal and its colonies. This decree reflected the growing awareness of human rights issues and the complexities of colonial rule during this period.
events.name: Decree Prohibiting Enslavement of Chinese People

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1624, a decree was issued in Norway making it illegal for Jesuits or Roman Catholic monks to be harbored in the country. This reflected the Protestant Reformation's impact on religious policies in Scandinavia.
events.name: Decree Against Jesuits in Norway

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1624, the English House of Commons passed a resolution making it illegal for a Member of Parliament (MP) to quit or willfully give up his seat. This resolution aimed to stabilize parliamentary representation and prevent political instability.
events.name: Resolution of the English House of Commons

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1624, Ferdinand II, Holy Roman Emperor, renewed his oath to restore Catholicism in Germany, Bohemia, Hungary, and Croatia during a ceremonial event. This reaffirmation was part of his broader efforts to consolidate Catholic power during the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Ferdinand II Renews Oath to Restore Catholicism

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1624, Garcia Mvemba a Nkanga was enthroned as King Garcia I of the Kongo, following the death of his father, King Pedro II. His reign would be marked by significant interactions with European powers and the complexities of colonial influence in Africa.
events.name: Enthronement of King Garcia I of Kongo

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1624, the University of Saint Francis Xavier was founded in Cochabamba, Bolivia. This institution played a crucial role in the education and cultural development of the region during the colonial period.
events.name: Foundation of the University of Saint Francis Xavier

events.enhanced_description: On April 29, 1624, Louis XIII of France appointed Cardinal Richelieu to the Conseil du Roi (Royal Council). This appointment marked the beginning of Richelieu's significant influence on French politics and his role in strengthening the monarchy.
events.name: Cardinal Richelieu Appointed to Royal Council

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1624, a fleet from the Dutch West India Company captured the Brazilian city of Salvador, Bahia, from the Portuguese Empire. This event was part of the broader conflict between the Dutch and Portuguese for control of trade routes and colonies in the Americas.
events.name: Capture of Bahia by Dutch West India Company

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1624, a major earthquake struck Fez, Morocco, estimated at a magnitude of 6.0 Mw. The quake caused severe damage and resulted in thousands of casualties, highlighting the region's vulnerability to seismic activity.
events.name: Major Earthquake in Fez, Morocco

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1624, the city of Oslo was destroyed by fire for the fourteenth time. Following this disaster, King Christian IV decreed its rebuilding on a new site, which would be renamed Christiania, reflecting the city's resilience and the king's commitment to urban development.
events.name: Destruction of Oslo by Fire

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1624, the Scottish city of Dunfermline was devastated by fire. Despite the destruction, significant structures such as The Abbey, The Palace, and the Abbot House survived, showcasing the city's historical resilience.
events.name: Fire in Dunfermline, Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1624, a contingent of 5,000 Chinese troops led by Admiral Yu Zigao and General Wang Mengxiong attacked the Dutch fortress at Magong. The Dutch, commanded by Martinus Sonck, were outnumbered and surrendered after five days of siege.
events.name: Attack on Dutch fortress at Magong

events.enhanced_description: In August 1624, Portuguese Jesuit priest António de Andrade became the first European to enter Tibet, arriving at Tsaparang. His journey marked a significant moment in the history of European exploration in Asia.
events.name: António de Andrade enters Tibet

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1624, the Dutch East India Company agreed to Chinese demands to withdraw from the Penghu islands, relocating its trading post to Fort Zeelandia in Tainan, Taiwan. This decision reflected the shifting power dynamics in the region.
events.name: Dutch East India Company withdraws from Penghu

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1624, The King's Men performed Thomas Middleton's satire 'A Game at Chess' at the Globe Theatre in London. The play was later suppressed due to its political allusions, reflecting the tense atmosphere of the time.
events.name: A Game at Chess performed

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1624, Cardinal Richelieu was appointed chief minister by King Louis XIII of France, following the arrest of Charles de La Vieuville for corruption. Richelieu's leadership would significantly shape French politics and foreign policy.
events.name: Cardinal Richelieu appointed chief minister

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1624, Jasper Vinall became the first recorded person to die while playing cricket, struck on the head by a bat during a game in Horsted Keynes, England. This incident highlighted the growing popularity and risks associated with the sport.
events.name: Jasper Vinall dies playing cricket

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Breda commenced on August 28, 1624, marking the beginning of a protracted military engagement that would last until June 5, 1625. This siege was a pivotal moment in the Eighty Years' War between the Dutch Republic and Spain.
events.name: Siege of Breda begins

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1624, the Parlement of Paris registered a decree forbidding the publication of criticism of 'anciently approved authors' without prior approval from the Faculty of Theology of the University of Paris, imposing severe penalties for violations. This decree reflected the tensions between censorship and intellectual freedom in early modern France.
events.name: Decree by the Parlement of Paris

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1624, Ketevan, the former queen consort of Kakheti, was tortured and killed in Shiraz after refusing to renounce her Christian faith. Her martyrdom became a symbol of resistance against religious persecution.
events.name: Ketevan's martyrdom

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1624, Michael I of Russia married Maria Dolgorukova in Moscow, making her the Tsaritsa. Unfortunately, Maria fell ill shortly after their marriage and died five months later, which had significant implications for the royal lineage.
events.name: Marriage of Michael I of Russia

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1624, the Roman Catholic church's Dicastery for the Clergy issued a decree stating that no monk could be expelled from his order unless he was deemed 'truly incorrigible.' This decree aimed to protect the rights of monks within the church.
events.name: Decree on monks by the Roman Catholic Church

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1624, a combined squadron of fifteen Neapolitan, Tuscan, and Papal galleys defeated a squadron of six Algerian ships near San Pietro, Sardinia. This naval engagement was part of the ongoing conflicts in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Naval battle near Sardinia

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1624, Rodrigo Pacheco arrived in Mexico City to assume the role of Viceroy of New Spain. His administration would oversee significant developments in the colony during a period of economic and social change.
events.name: Rodrigo Pacheco becomes Viceroy of New Spain

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1624, King Christian IV of Denmark-Norway ordered the establishment of Denmark's first postal service. This initiative marked a significant advancement in communication and administration within the kingdom.
events.name: Denmark's first postal service launched

events.enhanced_description: In 1625, Dutch settlers established the town of New Amsterdam on the southern tip of Manhattan Island, which would later evolve into modern-day New York City. This settlement was part of the Dutch efforts to expand their colonial presence in North America.
events.name: Founding of New Amsterdam

events.enhanced_description: In 1625, King Andrianjaka founded Antananarivo, which would become the capital of Madagascar. This establishment marked a significant development in the political landscape of the island.
events.name: Founding of Antananarivo

events.enhanced_description: In 1625, an unprecedented high tide struck the Thames River in England, causing significant damage to sea walls in Kent, Essex, and Lincolnshire. This event resulted in widespread desolation in coastal areas, highlighting the vulnerability of these regions to natural disasters.
events.name: High Tide in England

events.enhanced_description: In 1625, the English established a colony in Barbados, marking a significant step in the expansion of English colonial interests in the Caribbean. This colony would become a key player in the sugar trade.
events.name: Establishment of English Colony in Barbados

events.enhanced_description: In 1625, the first members of the Society of Jesus (Jesuits) arrived in Quebec, Canada, to establish missions and spread Catholicism among Indigenous peoples. This marked the beginning of a significant religious presence in New France.
events.name: Arrival of Jesuits in Quebec

events.enhanced_description: Around 1625, Shyaam a-Mbul began the process of unifying the Kuba Kingdom in Central Africa, a significant political development that would shape the region's history. His leadership was pivotal in consolidating power and establishing a centralized authority.
events.name: Unification of the Kuba Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1625, the Huguenots, led by the Duke of Soubise, launched a surprise naval assault against a French fleet in Blavet, marking a significant moment in their ongoing rebellion against King Louis XIII's authority. This event underscored the tensions between the Huguenots and the French crown during the early 17th century.
events.name: Huguenots' Second Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: In February 1625, Huguenot forces under the command of the Duke of Soubise successfully captured the strategically important Island of Ré. This event was part of the larger conflict between the Huguenots and the French crown, showcasing the ongoing struggle for religious and political autonomy.
events.name: Capture of the Island of Ré

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1625, Francesca Caccini's opera 'La liberazione di Ruggiero' premiered in Florence, Italy. This opera is notable for being one of the earliest operas composed by a woman and has continued to be performed for nearly 400 years.
events.name: Premiere of La liberazione di Ruggiero

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1625, Bogislaw XIV was recognized as the final Duke of Pomerania, a title that would become extinct upon his death in 1637. His reign marked the end of the ducal line in Pomerania, which had significant implications for the region's political landscape.
events.name: Bogislaw XIV becomes Duke of Pomerania

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1625, Hafız Ahmed Pasha was appointed as the Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire by Sultan Murad IV, just 11 days after the death of his predecessor, Çerkes Mehmed Pasha. This appointment was part of a broader effort to stabilize the empire during a tumultuous period.
events.name: Hafız Ahmed Pasha appointed Grand Vizier

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1625, one of the largest naval battles in the Persian Gulf occurred in the Straits of Hormuz, where the fleets of the Dutch East India Company and the English East India Company defended Persia against an attack from the Portuguese. This battle was a significant event in the Dutch-Portuguese War.
events.name: Battle in the Straits of Hormuz

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, 1625, James Ussher was appointed as the Archbishop of Armagh and Primate of All Ireland. Ussher was a prominent theologian and scholar, known for his works on biblical chronology.
events.name: James Ussher appointed Archbishop

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1625, the Battle of Martqopi took place, where the Safavid forces were defeated in Georgia. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts between the Safavid Empire and various regional powers.
events.name: Battle of Martqopi

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1625, Charles I ascended to the throne of England, Scotland, and Ireland following the death of his father, King James VI and I. His reign would be marked by significant political and religious conflicts, leading to the English Civil War.
events.name: Charles I succeeds to the throne

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1625, Frederick Henry of Nassau married Amalia, Countess von Solms-Braunfels. This marriage was significant in strengthening political alliances within the Dutch Republic.
events.name: Marriage of Frederick Henry of Nassau

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1625, Albrecht von Wallenstein was appointed as the German supreme commander. His leadership would play a crucial role in the Thirty Years' War, influencing the course of the conflict.
events.name: Albrecht von Wallenstein appointed

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1625, Stadtholder Maurice of Nassau of the Dutch Republic died, and his younger brother, Frederick Henry, succeeded him. Maurice's death marked a significant transition in the leadership of the Dutch Republic during a critical period of the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Death of Maurice of Nassau

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1625, during the First Savoine War, the Spanish fleet successfully relieved the Republic of Genoa by overcoming the Franco-Savoyard occupation of the city. This event was crucial in maintaining Spanish influence in the region.
events.name: Relief of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1625, a Portuguese-Spanish expedition successfully recaptured Salvador, Bahia from the Dutch. This event was part of the larger struggle for control over Brazil during the colonial period.
events.name: Recapture of Salvador, Bahia

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1625, 16 rebellious farmers were hanged in Vocklamarkt, Upper Austria, as a response to their uprising against the authorities. This event reflects the tensions and struggles faced by rural populations during this period.
events.name: Execution of rebellious farmers

events.enhanced_description: On June 2, 1625, Prince Frederick Henry was sworn in as the stadtholder of Holland and Zeeland. His leadership would be pivotal in the ongoing conflicts of the Dutch Republic during the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Frederick Henry sworn in as Stadtholder

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1625, during the Eighty Years' War, Spanish troops under Ambrogio Spinola conquered the city of Breda after a nine-month siege. This victory was a significant strategic gain for Spain in the ongoing conflict.
events.name: Conquest of Breda

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1625, King Charles I of England married Henrietta Maria of France and Navarre in Canterbury. This marriage was significant as it united the English crown with a Catholic princess, which would have lasting implications for religious tensions in England.
events.name: Marriage of Charles I and Henrietta Maria

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1625, the English Parliament refused to grant King Charles I the right to collect customs duties for his entire reign, limiting him to one year instead. This decision reflected the growing tensions between the monarchy and Parliament that would culminate in the English Civil War.
events.name: Parliament restricts Charles I's customs duties

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1625, the Safavid Empire in Iran defeated an invasion from the Kingdom of Georgia in the Battle of Marabda, resulting in heavy losses on both sides, including the Georgian commander, Teimuraz I. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts between the Safavid Empire and its neighbors.
events.name: Battle of Marabda

events.enhanced_description: In July 1625, Barbary pirates launched their first attack on south-western England, specifically targeting Mount's Bay in Cornwall. This marked the beginning of a series of raids that would lead to the enslavement of approximately 60 people from the area.
events.name: Barbary pirates attack England

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1625, Ernest Casimir of Nassau-Dietz was appointed as the stadtholder of Groningen. His appointment was part of the ongoing political restructuring within the Dutch Republic during the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Ernest Casimir appointed Stadtholder of Groningen

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1625, Ernest Casimir of Nassau-Dietz was appointed as the stadtholder of Drenthe. This role was part of his broader influence in the governance of the Dutch Republic during a time of conflict.
events.name: Ernest Casimir appointed Stadtholder of Drenthe

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1625, the Treaty of Southampton was signed, establishing an alliance between England and the Dutch Republic against Spain. This treaty was significant in the context of the ongoing conflicts of the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Treaty of Southampton

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1625, a total of 16 rabbis, including the notable Isaiah Horowitz, were imprisoned in Jerusalem. This event highlights the religious tensions and conflicts within the region during this period.
events.name: Imprisonment of Rabbis in Jerusalem

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1625, troops under the command of the Marquis de Toiras successfully recaptured the strategically important Île de Ré from Huguenot forces, leading to the flight of the Duke of Soubise to England. This event marked a significant turning point in the second Huguenot rebellion against the French crown.
events.name: Recapture of the island of Ré

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1625, a Dutch fleet launched an attack on San Juan, Puerto Rico, as part of their broader efforts to disrupt Spanish colonial holdings in the Caribbean. This assault was part of the larger context of the Dutch-Portuguese War.
events.name: Dutch attack on San Juan

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1625, a Dutch fleet attacked the Portuguese garrison at Elmina Castle in present-day Ghana but suffered a significant defeat, resulting in heavy casualties. This loss, along with other defeats in Bahia and Puerto Rico, led to a five-year hiatus in Dutch assaults on Spanish and Portuguese territories.
events.name: Battle of Elmina

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1625, during the Cádiz Expedition, English forces led by Admiral George Villiers faced a decisive defeat against the Spanish fleet in Cádiz. This battle underscored the ongoing naval conflicts between England and Spain during this period.
events.name: Cádiz Expedition

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1625, the Netherlands and England signed the Treaty of The Hague, which aimed to provide military and economic support to King Christian IV of Denmark-Norway during his campaigns in the Thirty Years' War. This treaty reflected the complex alliances and conflicts of the period.
events.name: Treaty of The Hague

events.enhanced_description: In 1626, a pandemic began in Asia, eventually spreading to Europe, Africa, North America, and South America. This outbreak had significant impacts on populations and societies across multiple continents.
events.name: Pandemic outbreak

events.enhanced_description: The Würzburg and Bamberg witch trials began in 1626, leading to the mass executions of hundreds of people accused of witchcraft until 1630/31. These trials were among the largest witch hunts in history, reflecting the intense social and religious turmoil of the time.
events.name: Würzburg and Bamberg witch trials begin

events.enhanced_description: In 1626, Samuel de Champlain decided to establish Cap Tourmente Farm near Quebec City to raise livestock, aiming to provide food for settlers and reduce reliance on supplies from France. This initiative was crucial for the sustainability of the French colony in North America.
events.name: Samuel de Champlain's decision for Cap Tourmente Farm

events.enhanced_description: In 1626, the coastal settlement of Salem was established in Massachusetts, becoming one of the earliest Puritan settlements in New England. Salem would later gain notoriety for the witch trials that occurred in the late 17th century.

image.caption: Aerial view of Salem, Massachusetts.
image.credit: Pi.1415926535 — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 20 March 2022; contemporary view of the city, not an image from 1626.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Establishment of Salem, Massachusetts

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1626, during the Polish-Swedish War, King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden achieved a decisive victory over a Polish army at the Battle of Wallhof in Latvia. This battle was part of the larger conflict that shaped the balance of power in Northern Europe.
events.name: Battle of Wallhof

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1626, Peter Minuit set sail from Texel Island, Netherlands, with two ships carrying Dutch emigrants to establish the New Netherland colony in North America. His leadership would be crucial in the development of this colony.
events.name: Peter Minuit sails for New Netherland

events.enhanced_description: On February 2, 1626, King Charles I of England was crowned at Westminster Abbey, but his wife, Henrietta Maria, chose not to participate in the non-Catholic ceremony. This event highlighted the tensions between the monarchy and religious factions in England.
events.name: Coronation of King Charles I

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1626, the Battle of Ningyuan took place in Xingcheng, China, where Ming dynasty commander Yuan Chonghuan achieved a remarkable victory against a much larger Manchu force led by Nurhaci. This battle was pivotal in the ongoing conflicts between the Ming dynasty and the rising Manchu power.
events.name: Battle of Ningyuan

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1626, Emperor Susenyos of Ethiopia and Patriarch Afonso Mendes declared the primacy of the Roman See over the Ethiopian Church, establishing Roman Catholicism as the state religion. This marked a significant shift in the religious landscape of Ethiopia.
events.name: Primacy of the Roman See in Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1626, the Treaty of Monzón was signed between France and Spain, effectively ending the Valtellina War and the First Genoese-Savoyard War. This treaty was significant in reshaping the political landscape of Southern Europe.
events.name: Treaty of Monzón

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1626, Ambrósio I Nimi a Nkanga ascended to the throne as the new monarch of Kongo, following the overthrow of Garcia I Mvemba a Nkanga. His reign marked the restoration of the Kwilu dynasty and was significant for the political dynamics in the region.
events.name: Ambrósio I Nimi a Nkanga becomes monarch of Kongo

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1626, Portugal declared war on Queen Nzinga of the Kingdom of Ndongo, located in present-day Angola. This conflict was part of the broader struggle for control over the region and marked a significant moment in the history of colonial resistance.
events.name: Portugal declares war on Queen Nzinga

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1626, during the Thirty Years' War, the Battle of Dessau Bridge saw Albrecht von Wallenstein defeat the army of Ernst von Mansfeld. This battle was crucial in the ongoing conflict between Catholic and Protestant forces in Europe.
events.name: Battle of Dessau Bridge

events.enhanced_description: On May 4, 1626, Peter Minuit was appointed as the director-general of New Netherland for the Dutch West India Company. His leadership was instrumental in the development and governance of this crucial colonial territory.
events.name: Peter Minuit becomes director-general of New Netherland

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1626, the Dutch ship Arms of Amsterdam arrived in Europe from New Netherland, reporting the purchase of Manhattan Island from the indigenous people for the value of 60 guilders. This transaction marked a significant moment in the colonial history of North America.
events.name: Purchase of Manhattan

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1626, the Wanggongchang Explosion occurred in Beijing, China, when a gunpowder factory exploded, resulting in the destruction of a significant part of the city and the deaths of approximately 20,000 people. This disaster highlighted the dangers of industrial activities in densely populated areas.
events.name: Wanggongchang Explosion

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1626, a devastating 7.0 magnitude earthquake struck Lingqiu County in Shanxi Province, China, resulting in the deaths of approximately 5,200 residents. This earthquake is one of the deadliest recorded in Chinese history.
events.name: Lingqiu County Earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1626, the Ottoman Army halted its campaign to retake Baghdad from Persian control after losing the city in 1624. This marked a significant moment in the ongoing conflict between the Ottoman Empire and the Safavid Empire over territorial dominance in the region.
events.name: Ottoman attempt to retake Baghdad

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1626, nine Jesuit missionaries, including six Japanese and three Spanish, were executed in Nagasaki, Japan, as part of the Tokugawa shogunate's crackdown on Christianity. This event highlighted the tensions between the shogunate and Christian converts, leading to further persecution of Christians in Japan.
events.name: Execution of Jesuit missionaries in Japan

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1626, George II ascended to the title of Landgrave of Hesse-Darmstadt following the death of his father, Louis V. His reign would be marked by efforts to stabilize the region amidst the ongoing Thirty Years' War.
events.name: George II becomes Landgrave of Hesse-Darmstadt

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1626, Ernst Casimir of Nassau-Dietz successfully retook Oldenzaal from Spanish control during the Eighty Years' War, forcing Spain to withdraw from the Overijssel region. This victory was significant in the ongoing struggle for Dutch independence.
events.name: Retaking of Oldenzaal during the Eighty Years' War

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1626, during the Thirty Years' War, the Battle of Lutter took place where the forces of Count Tilly defeated the army of King Christian IV of Denmark. This battle was pivotal in the Danish phase of the war, showcasing the strength of the Catholic League.

image.caption: Michael Caspar Lundorp’s printed depiction of the Battle of Lutter.
image.credit: Michael Caspar Lundorp — Lundorp, Michael Caspar (1628) [1625] (in German) Östreichischer Lorberkrantz ("Continuatio" / part 3) , Frankfurt : Schönwetter, Kempfer OCLC : 312044264 .
image.date_qualification: Retrospective printed depiction of the 1626 battle; the saved image date is 1627.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Lutter

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1626, Nurhaci, the chief of the Jurchens and founder of the Qing dynasty, died and was succeeded by his son, Hong Taiji. Nurhaci's death marked a significant transition in the leadership of the Jurchen people and the consolidation of power that led to the establishment of the Qing dynasty.

image.caption: Anonymous Qing dynasty portrait painting of Nurhaci in court dress.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Palace Museum, Beijing （故宫博物院）
image.date_qualification: Portrait of Nurhaci, not a depiction of his death; the supplied image date is a 17th-century date, while supported_display_date is null.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Death of Nurhaci

events.enhanced_description: On November 18, 1626, the new St Peter's Basilica in Vatican City was consecrated, coinciding with the 1,300th anniversary of the original church established in 326 AD. This event marked a significant milestone in the history of the Catholic Church and its architectural legacy.
events.name: Consecration of St Peter's Basilica

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1626, Pasha Muhammad ibn Farukh, the tyrannical Governor of Jerusalem, was forced out of his position. His removal was part of the broader political struggles within the Ottoman Empire during this period.
events.name: Removal of Pasha Muhammad ibn Farukh

events.enhanced_description: In March 1627, the Trịnh–Nguyễn War began in Vietnam, as Trịnh Tráng led an army of 200,000 troops southward to attack the Đàng Trong governed by Lord Nguyễn Phúc Nguyên. This conflict marked a significant chapter in the history of Vietnam's feudal wars.
events.name: Start of Trịnh–Nguyễn War

events.enhanced_description: Barbary corsairs from Salé raided the fishing village of Grindavík, capturing inhabitants and taking them into slavery. This event marked the beginning of a series of raids that would terrorize Icelandic coastal communities.
events.name: Turkish Abductions: Barbary corsairs raid Grindavík

events.enhanced_description: In 1627, Habsburg Spain faced a significant economic collapse, primarily due to the depletion of resources from its overseas colonies and the burdens of continuous warfare in Europe. This collapse marked a turning point in Spanish history, leading to a decline in its power and influence.
events.name: Habsburg Spain suffers an economic collapse

events.enhanced_description: The last recorded aurochs, a wild ancestor of domestic cattle, died in the Jaktorów Forest in 1627. This event marked the extinction of the species in the wild, highlighting the impact of human activity on biodiversity.
events.name: The last recorded aurochs die in the Jaktorów Forest of Poland

events.enhanced_description: In 1627, the innovative use of black gunpowder for rock blasting was first implemented in the mining operations beneath Banská Štiavnica. This technique revolutionized mining practices and significantly increased efficiency in extracting valuable minerals.

locations.name: Banská Štiavnica, Banská Bystrica Region, Slovakia

events.name: Rock blasting is invented: Black gunpowder is first used in mining, in a mineshaft under Banská Štiavnica, Slovakia

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1627, the Dutch ship 't Gulden Zeepaert, captained by François Thijssen, made the first recorded sighting of the coast of South Australia. This event marked an important moment in the European exploration of Australia.
events.name: First recorded sighting of South Australia

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1627, the administrative rural parish of Iisalmi was established in Savonia by order of King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden. This decision was part of broader administrative reforms during his reign.
events.name: Establishment of Iisalmi parish

events.enhanced_description: On February 17, 1627, England landed the first European settlers on Barbados, marking the beginning of English colonization in the Caribbean. This event would lead to significant changes in the island's demographics and economy.
events.name: First European settlers land on Barbados

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1627, following the First Manchu invasion, the Joseon dynasty of Korea became a tributary state of the Manchus while still paying respects to the Ming dynasty of China. This marked a significant shift in the power dynamics in East Asia.

image.caption: A Korean painting depicting two Jurchen warriors and their horses, by Kim Yun-gyeom.
image.credit: Kim Yun-gyeom (1711 ~ 1775) — http://www.seoul.co.kr/news/newsView.php?id=20070912026002&spage=4
image.date_qualification: 18th century; image metadata gives an approximate date of 1750, not the event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Joseon dynasty becomes tributary to Manchus

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1627, Maurice, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel, was forced to abdicate due to financial mismanagement that led the landgraviate to bankruptcy. His son, William V, succeeded him and took steps to stabilize the region.
events.name: Maurice of Hesse-Kassel forced to abdicate

events.enhanced_description: On April 10, 1627, the Dutch ship 't Gulden Zeepaert reached Batavia in the Dutch East Indies, marking an important moment in the Dutch colonial expansion in Southeast Asia.
events.name: Arrival of 't Gulden Zeepaert in Batavia

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1627, the States of Friesland agreed on a 28-point Appeal about Abuses, allowing citizens to voice their complaints. This agreement was part of the broader movement towards greater civic engagement and governance in the Dutch Republic.
events.name: Friesland's 28-point Appeal about Abuses

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1627, the Kingdom of England reached an agreement with Sidi Al-Ayyashi, a Moroccan Mujahidin leader, to assist in the release of English captives seized by Barbary corsairs. This agreement highlighted the complex diplomatic relationships of the time.
events.name: Agreement with Sidi Al-Ayyashi

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1627, France and England signed an agreement to divide the island of Saint Kitts, establishing colonial claims that would shape the Caribbean's geopolitical landscape for years to come.
events.name: Division of Saint Kitts

events.enhanced_description: Ngarolamo ascended to the throne as the Sultan of Tidore, a significant sultanate in the Maluku Islands, known for its spice trade. His reign marked a continuation of the political dynamics in the region, particularly in relation to European colonial interests.
events.name: Ngarolamo becomes the new Sultan of Tidore

events.enhanced_description: The States of Friesland promulgated a resolution addressing grievances related to abuses, reflecting the political tensions and governance issues of the time. This event highlights the role of regional governance in the broader context of Dutch politics.
events.name: Resolution on the April 17 appeal about abuses

events.enhanced_description: Sir Oliver Cromwell sold Hinchingbrooke House to Sidney Montagu, marking a significant transaction in the context of English land ownership and political alliances during the turbulent times of the English Civil War.
events.name: Sale of Hinchingbrooke House

events.enhanced_description: Barbary corsairs from Algiers conducted a raid on the East Fjords of Iceland, capturing locals and taking them into slavery. This raid was part of a broader pattern of maritime piracy that affected Iceland during this period.
events.name: Turkish Abductions: Barbary corsairs raid East Fjords

events.enhanced_description: The Barbary corsairs from Algiers raided the island of Heimaey, capturing residents and killing others. This event was part of a series of violent incursions that devastated Icelandic communities.
events.name: Turkish Abductions: Barbary corsairs raid Heimaey

events.enhanced_description: Frederick Henry, Prince of Orange, initiated the Siege of Grol, targeting the last Spanish stronghold in the eastern Netherlands. The siege concluded successfully after 30 days, marking a significant victory in the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Siege of Grol

events.enhanced_description: The English forces, led by the Duke of Buckingham, launched an invasion of Île de Ré in support of the Huguenots in La Rochelle. The invasion ultimately failed, highlighting the complexities of religious and political conflicts in France.
events.name: Invasion of Île de Ré

events.enhanced_description: An earthquake devastated the cities of San Severo and Torremaggiore in southern Italy, causing significant destruction and loss of life. This event underscored the vulnerability of the region to seismic activity.
events.name: Earthquake in San Severo and Torremaggiore

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1628, 21 Christian converts were executed in Nagasaki, Japan, as part of the ongoing persecution of Christians in the country. This event highlighted the severe repression faced by Christians during this period.
events.name: Persecution of Christians in Japan

events.enhanced_description: Following the siege that began on July 20, Grol was captured by Frederick Henry, Prince of Orange. This victory was pivotal in the ongoing Eighty Years' War, contributing to the decline of Spanish power in the region.
events.name: Capture of Grol

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of La Rochelle commenced as Catholic France, supported by Spain, sought to suppress the Protestant Huguenots' revolt in the city. This event marked a significant escalation in the religious conflicts of the time.
events.name: Siege of La Rochelle begins

events.enhanced_description: Mohammed Adil Shah ascended to the throne as the Sultan of Bijapur following the death of his father, Ibrahim Adil Shah II. His reign would be marked by significant cultural and political developments in the Deccan region.
events.name: Mohammed Adil Shah begins reign as Sultan of Bijapur

events.enhanced_description: William V, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel, signed the Hauptakkord with George II of Hesse-Darmstadt, which resulted in significant territorial cessions. This agreement was pivotal in the political landscape of the German states during the 17th century.
events.name: Hauptakkord signed by William V and George II

events.enhanced_description: The reign of the Tianqi Emperor, Zhu Youjiao, came to an end after seven years, marking a tumultuous period in the Ming dynasty characterized by political instability and internal strife.
events.name: End of Tianqi Emperor's reign

events.enhanced_description: Zhu Youjian, the younger brother of the deceased Tianqi Emperor, was enthroned as the Chongzhen Emperor. His ascension marked the beginning of a reign that would face significant challenges, ultimately leading to the fall of the Ming dynasty.
events.name: Zhu Youjian enthroned as Chongzhen Emperor

events.enhanced_description: Mughal Emperor Jahangir died of a respiratory illness near Bhimber while attempting to return to his palace in Lahore. His death marked a significant turning point in Mughal history, leading to a succession struggle.
events.name: Death of Mughal Emperor Jahangir

events.enhanced_description: Shahryar Mirza, the son of the late Emperor Jahangir, was installed as the new Mughal Emperor in Lahore. His reign was short-lived and marked by political instability and challenges from rival factions.
events.name: Shahryar Mirza installed as Mughal Emperor

events.enhanced_description: Bogislaw XIV, Duke of Pomerania, signed the Capitulation of Franzburg, which required Pomerania to pay for the Imperial army occupying it. This event exemplified the harsh realities of the Thirty Years' War and its impact on regional governance.
events.name: Capitulation of Franzburg signed

events.enhanced_description: During the Polish-Swedish War, a Polish-Lithuanian fleet achieved a decisive victory over a Swedish fleet at the Battle of Oliwa. This battle was significant in asserting Polish naval power during the conflict.

image.caption: Anonymous retrospective illustration of the Battle of Oliwa, from Heinrich Böhme’s album.
image.credit: Anonymous, 1638. — https://www.wbc.poznan.pl/dlibra/show-content/publication/edition/470943?id=470943
image.date_qualification: Image is attributed to 1638; 2020-09-07 is the recorded digital image date, not the depicted event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Oliwa

events.enhanced_description: La selva sin amor, written by Lope de Vega with music by Alessandro Piccinini, premiered as the first Spanish opera. This event marked a significant milestone in the development of Spanish musical and theatrical traditions.
events.name: Premiere of La selva sin amor

events.enhanced_description: Vincenzo II Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua, died at the age of 33 due to poor health. His death led to a succession crisis, as Charles I Gonzaga took over the duchy, igniting the War of the Mantuan Succession.
events.name: Death of Vincenzo II Gonzaga

events.enhanced_description: In Madrid, ministers of King Philip IV of Spain drafted proposals for a 'Kingdom and Republic of Ireland' aimed at breaking with England. This initiative reflected the complex political landscape of the time and Spain's interest in Irish affairs.
events.name: Proposals for a Kingdom and Republic of Ireland

events.enhanced_description: Shihab-ud-Din Muhammad Khurram, later known as Shah Jahan, entered Lahore after defeating his brother Shahryar Mirza. His ascension marked the beginning of a new era in Mughal history, culminating in the construction of the Taj Mahal.
events.name: Shihab-ud-Din Muhammad Khurram enters Lahore

events.enhanced_description: In 1628, the siege of Stralsund was initiated by Field Marshals Hans Georg von Arnim-Boitzenburg and Wallenstein's forces of the Holy Roman Imperial Army. This siege was part of the larger conflict of the Thirty Years' War and would last until August 4.
events.name: Thirty Years' War: Siege of Stralsund begins

events.enhanced_description: The War of the Mantuan Succession erupted in 1628 over the territories of Mantua and Montferrat, pitting the Duke of Savoy, backed by Spain, against the Duke of Nevers, supported by France. This conflict was part of the larger power struggles in Europe during this period.
events.name: War of the Mantuan Succession

events.enhanced_description: In 1628, William Harvey published 'Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus' in Frankfurt, presenting his groundbreaking discoveries on blood circulation. This work laid the foundation for modern physiology and transformed medical understanding.
events.name: William Harvey publishes findings on blood circulation

events.enhanced_description: In 1628, the publication of Sir Edward Coke's 'Institutes of the Lawes of England' began with 'A Commentary upon Littleton'. This influential legal text would shape legal thought and practice in England and America for centuries.
events.name: Publication of Sir Edward Coke's Institutes

events.enhanced_description: In 1628, the Collegiate School was established in New York City, becoming the oldest surviving educational institution in the United States. It played a crucial role in the development of education in the New World.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Establishment of the Collegiate School

events.enhanced_description: In 1628, the first black slaves arrived in Dutch Manhattan, marking the beginning of a tragic chapter in American history. This event set the stage for the development of slavery in the New World.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Arrival of the first black slaves in Dutch Manhattan

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1628, the reign of Shahryar Mirza, the Mughal Emperor, came to a violent end when he was defeated by his brother Shihab-ud-Din Muhammad Khurram, who subsequently ascended the throne as Shah Jahan. This power struggle marked a significant shift in the Mughal dynasty.
events.name: The reign of Salef-ud-din Muhammad Shahryar as the Mughal Emperor ends

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1628, following his defeat, Shahryar Mirza was executed on the orders of his brother Shah Jahan, along with several members of the court. This brutal act solidified Shah Jahan's claim to the Mughal throne and marked a violent chapter in the dynasty's history.
events.name: Shahryar Mirza is put to death

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1628, the indigenous Mapuche people laid siege to the Spanish colonial settlement of Nacimiento in present-day Chile. Despite the Spanish captain and his small force holding out for two days, the siege exemplified the ongoing resistance against colonial rule.
events.name: Mapuche lay siege to Nacimiento

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1628, Zhu Youjian ascended the throne as the Chongzhen Emperor, marking the beginning of the Chongzhen Era in the Ming dynasty. His reign would be characterized by attempts to reform the government amidst growing internal strife and external threats.
events.name: Chongzhen Era begins in Ming dynasty China

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1628, King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden issued an order to prohibit the public from making pilgrimages to see the religious visionary Margareta i Kumla, whom he deemed a source of 'foolishness and insanity.' This action reflected the tensions between state authority and religious movements.
events.name: Gustavus Adolphus issues order against Margareta i Kumla

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1628, Shah Jahan was formally crowned as the ruler of the Mughal Empire in Agra. His reign would be marked by significant architectural achievements, including the construction of the Taj Mahal.
events.name: Coronation of Shah Jahan

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1628, King Charles I issued writs requiring every county in England to pay ship tax, expanding the tax beyond traditional seaport towns. This move was met with resistance and contributed to the growing tensions between the monarchy and Parliament.
events.name: Writs issued by King Charles I for ship tax

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1628, Oliver Cromwell made his first appearance in the English Parliament as a Member for Huntingdon. His political career would later play a pivotal role in the English Civil War and the establishment of the Commonwealth.
events.name: Oliver Cromwell's first appearance in Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1628, Damat Halil Pasha was dismissed from his position as Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire by Sultan Murad IV due to his failure to suppress a rebellion and win the ongoing war against Persia. His dismissal reflected the challenges faced by the Ottoman leadership during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Damat Halil Pasha is fired as Grand Vizier

events.enhanced_description: On April 8, 1628, the Sacred Congregation of Rites of the Roman Catholic Church issued a decree prohibiting the veneration of saints whose sanctity had not been officially declared by the Holy See. This decree aimed to standardize practices within the Church and curb unauthorized veneration.
events.name: Decree prohibiting veneration of uncanonized saints

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1628, Generalissimo Albrecht von Wallenstein was appointed Admiral of the Baltic Sea by Emperor Ferdinand II. This appointment was part of Wallenstein's broader military and political maneuvers during the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Albrecht von Wallenstein made Admiral of the Baltic Sea

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1628, Cardinal Girolamo Grimaldi-Cavalleroni was appointed as the Governor of Rome by Pope Urban VIII. This position placed him at the center of political and religious power in the Papal States during a critical period.
events.name: Cardinal Girolamo Grimaldi-Cavalleroni appointed Governor of Rome

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1628, Count Johann Tserclaes, a Field Marshal of the Catholic League, successfully captured the German city of Stade after a prolonged siege. This victory was part of the larger conflict of the Thirty Years' War, significantly impacting the balance of power in the region.
events.name: Count of Tilly captures Stade

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1628, Matthew Cradock was elected as the first Governor of the Massachusetts Bay Company, marking a significant step in the establishment of the colony. His leadership would influence the early governance and development of New England.
events.name: Matthew Cradock elected Governor of the Massachusetts Bay Company

events.enhanced_description: On May 21, 1628, Muhsin ibn Husayn, the Emir of Mecca, surrendered control to Ahmad ibn Abd al-Muttalib. This transfer of power was significant in the context of the shifting political landscape in the Hejaz region.
events.name: Muhsin ibn Husayn surrenders control of Mecca

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1628, Mehmed III Giray, the Khan of Crimea, was forced to flee Bakhchysarai after a siege by 4,000 Cossacks led by Mykhailo Doroshenko. This event underscored the instability in the region and the challenges faced by the Crimean Khanate.
events.name: Mehmed III Giray forced to leave Bakhchysarai

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1628, King Charles I reconvened the English Parliament and accepted the Petition of Right, a crucial document that limited the king's power and affirmed certain rights of the subjects. This act was a significant step in the conflict between the monarchy and Parliament.
events.name: King Charles I reconvenes the English Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1628, Prince Minyedeippa assassinated his father, King Anaukpetlun, to seize the throne of the Kingdom of Ava. This act of regicide led to a power struggle and instability within the kingdom.
events.name: Prince Minyedeippa assassinates his father, King Anaukpetlun

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1628, with the assistance of Danish and Swedish reinforcements, Stralsund successfully resisted Wallenstein's siege. The arrival of a Danish army led by Christian IV forced Wallenstein to abandon the siege and confront the new threat.
events.name: Thirty Years' War: Stralsund resists Wallenstein's siege

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1628, the Swedish warship Vasa sank just 20 minutes into her maiden voyage in Stockholm Harbor. The sinking was due to design flaws and has since become a symbol of the challenges faced by naval engineering during the period.
events.name: Vasa sinks in Stockholm Harbor

events.enhanced_description: In 1628, Sultan Agung of Mataram launched a naval campaign against the Dutch fort at Batavia, aiming to expel the Dutch East India Company from Java. The siege lasted four months but ultimately failed, marking a significant moment in the struggle for control over the region.
events.name: Siege of Batavia

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1628, George Villiers, the first Duke of Buckingham and a prominent courtier, was assassinated by John Felton in London. This event had significant political ramifications, as Villiers was a key favorite of King James I.
events.name: Assassination of George Villiers

events.enhanced_description: During the Thirty Years' War, the Battle of Wolgast occurred on September 2, 1628, where Wallenstein's forces decisively defeated the army of Christian IV of Denmark. This victory solidified Wallenstein's reputation as a formidable military leader.
events.name: Battle of Wolgast

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1628, a group of Puritans settled in Salem, which would later become part of the Massachusetts Bay Colony. This settlement marked a significant moment in the establishment of Puritan communities in New England.
events.name: Settlement of Salem

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1628, during the Eighty Years' War, Dutch admiral Piet Hein captured 16 ships of the Spanish treasure fleet in the Bay of Matanzas. This victory provided a significant financial boost to the Dutch Republic, allowing them to fund their military efforts.
events.name: Battle in the Bay of Matanzas

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1628, Abaza Mehmed Pasha surrendered to Ottoman forces, effectively ending the Abaza rebellion. This event marked a consolidation of power for the Ottoman Empire during a period of internal strife.
events.name: Surrender of Abaza Mehmed Pasha

events.enhanced_description: The siege of La Rochelle concluded on October 28, 1628, with the surrender of the Huguenots to royal forces. This event was a pivotal moment in the French Wars of Religion, leading to the decline of Huguenot power in France.
events.name: Siege of La Rochelle

events.enhanced_description: On November 29, 1628, John Felton, the man who assassinated the Duke of Buckingham, was executed by hanging at Tyburn prison in London. His execution was a significant event in the political landscape of England at the time.
events.name: Execution of John Felton

events.enhanced_description: The Mataram Sultanate's attempt to expel the Dutch East India Company from western Java concluded on December 3, 1628, after 103 days of siege. This failure underscored the challenges faced by local powers against European colonial forces.
events.name: Failure of Mataram Sultanate's Campaign

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1628, Muhammad Imaduddin I ascended to the throne as the Sultan of the Maldives, beginning a reign that would last for 29 years. His rule was marked by significant developments in the archipelago.
events.name: Muhammad Imaduddin I becomes Sultan

events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1628, Chetthathirat was crowned as the new King of Thailand at the young age of 15, taking the regnal name Borommaracha II. His reign was short-lived, as he was killed less than a year later.
events.name: Chetthathirat crowned King of Thailand

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1628, O Yun-gyeom was appointed as the new Yeonguijeong (Chief of the State Council) in the Joseon Kingdom of Korea during the reign of King Injo. His appointment was significant in the political landscape of Korea at the time.
events.name: O Yun-gyeom becomes Yeonguijeong

events.enhanced_description: During the Anglo-Spanish War, a Spanish expedition led by Fadrique de Toledo successfully wiped out the English colony on Nevis. This event underscored the ongoing conflict between Spain and England in the Caribbean.
events.name: Anglo-Spanish War: Destruction of the English colony on Nevis

events.enhanced_description: In 1629, the Spanish East Indies constructed Fort Santo Domingo in Tamsui, Taiwan, as part of their efforts to secure trade routes and establish a foothold in East Asia during the Age of Exploration.
events.name: Fort Santo Domingo is built

events.enhanced_description: In 1629, the Chongzhen Emperor of the Ming dynasty reiterated the prohibition against female infanticide as the empire faced severe economic decline and social unrest, highlighting the struggles of the dynasty during its final years.
events.name: Chongzhen emperor's prohibition against female infanticide

events.enhanced_description: The rule of Nzinga, the influential queen of Ndongo and Matamba in present-day Angola, came to an end in 1629, marking a significant shift in the region's resistance against Portuguese colonial expansion.
events.name: End of Nzinga's rule

events.enhanced_description: In 1629, a ban was imposed on actresses in Japan, reflecting the societal attitudes towards women in the performing arts during the Edo period, which sought to control and regulate public entertainment.
events.name: Actresses are banned in Japan

events.enhanced_description: In 1629, William Alexander, 1st Earl of Stirling, briefly established a Scottish colony at Port Royal, Nova Scotia, as part of efforts to expand Scottish influence in North America during the early colonial period.
events.name: Scottish colony at Port Royal

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1629, Henry Frederick, the 15-year-old Hereditary Prince of the Palatinate, tragically drowned while sailing to Amsterdam. His untimely death had significant implications for the succession in the Palatinate.
events.name: Death of Henry Frederick, Hereditary Prince of the Palatinate

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1629, Abbas the Great, one of the most powerful rulers of the Safavid dynasty in Iran, passed away after a reign of over 40 years. His leadership significantly shaped the political and cultural landscape of Persia.
events.name: Death of Abbas the Great

events.enhanced_description: On January 28, 1629, Sam Mirza was crowned as the new Shah of Persia, taking the regnal name Safi. His ascension marked a new chapter in the Safavid dynasty following the death of his grandfather, Abbas the Great.
events.name: Crowning of Sam Mirza as Shah of Persia

events.enhanced_description: Led by Francis Higginson aboard the Lyon's Whelp, six ships of Puritans arrived in Salem, Massachusetts, marking a significant moment in the Puritan migration to New England. This migration was driven by the desire for religious freedom and the establishment of a new society.
events.name: Puritan migration to New England

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1629, the Massachusetts Bay Colony was granted a royal charter, establishing it as one of the first colonies in what would later become the United States. This charter laid the foundation for self-governance in the colony.
events.name: Royal charter granted to Massachusetts Bay Colony

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1629, Ferdinand II, Holy Roman Emperor, issued the Edict of Restitution, which mandated the restoration of Catholic properties lost to Protestantism since 1552. This edict intensified the religious conflicts of the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Ferdinand II issues the Edict of Restitution

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1629, Charles I of England dissolved Parliament, initiating a period known as the Eleven Years' Tyranny. This action marked a significant escalation in tensions between the monarchy and Parliament, leading to future conflicts.
events.name: Charles I dissolves Parliament

events.enhanced_description: In the context of the Eighty Years' War, Frederick Henry, Prince of Orange, laid siege to 's-Hertogenbosch, a key fortress for Spain along the Spanish-Dutch border. The successful siege marked a significant turning point in the conflict, weakening Spanish control in the region.
events.name: Eighty Years' War: Siege of 's-Hertogenbosch

events.enhanced_description: During the Huguenot rebellions, Louis XIII of France successfully captured Privas after a 15-day siege. This victory was part of the broader effort to suppress Huguenot resistance in France.
events.name: Huguenot rebellions: Capture of Privas

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Lübeck was signed by Christian IV of Denmark and Albrecht von Wallenstein, effectively ending Denmark's involvement in the Thirty Years' War. This treaty marked a significant shift in the balance of power in Northern Europe.
events.name: Thirty Years' War: Treaty of Lübeck

events.enhanced_description: As a consequence of the Edict of Restitution during the Thirty Years' War, Prince Frederick of Denmark was expelled from the Prince-Bishopric of Verden by the Catholic League. He was replaced by the staunch Catholic Francis of Wartenberg, further intensifying the religious conflict.
events.name: Thirty Years' War: Expulsion of Prince Frederick of Denmark

events.enhanced_description: The Dutch East India Company ship Batavia was wrecked on a reef near Beacon Island during its maiden voyage to the Indies. The aftermath of the wreck led to a mutiny among the survivors, marking a dark chapter in early Australian history.
events.name: Wreck of the Batavia

events.enhanced_description: The Dutch States-General ratified the Charter of Freedoms and Exemptions for the Dutch West India Company, making investments in the colony of New Netherland more attractive. This charter aimed to stimulate economic growth and settlement in the region.

locations.name: New Netherland, New York, United States

events.name: Dutch West India Company's Charter of Freedoms and Exemptions

events.enhanced_description: The Huguenot stronghold of Alès surrendered after a prolonged siege, leading to the capitulation of the Duke of Rohan, a key figure in the Huguenot Rebellions. This event marked a significant decline in Huguenot power in France.
events.name: Huguenot rebellions: Surrender of Alès

events.enhanced_description: Louis XIII of France signed the Peace of Alès in Lédignan, effectively ending the Huguenot rebellions. While the Huguenots retained some religious freedoms, they lost significant political and military rights, marking a pivotal moment in the French Wars of Religion.
events.name: Huguenot rebellions: Peace of Alès

events.enhanced_description: In the context of the Anglo-French War, Samuel de Champlain surrendered the city of Quebec to an English force led by David Kirke. This event marked a significant loss for the French in North America.
events.name: Anglo-French War: Surrender of Quebec

events.enhanced_description: French Admiral Isaac de Razilly bombarded the city of Salé with a fleet composed of several ships, successfully destroying three corsair vessels. This military action was part of France's efforts to assert its power in the region.
events.name: Bombardment of Salé

events.enhanced_description: In the Kingdom of Joseon, Mao Wenlong was executed after being captured by Ming Chinese general Yuan Chonghuan. His execution was part of the Later Jin invasion, which significantly impacted the region's stability.
events.name: Later Jin invasion of Joseon: Execution of Mao Wenlong

events.enhanced_description: A small Dutch army surprised the Spanish garrison of Wesel, capturing the city during the Eighty Years' War. This loss forced Hendrik van den Bergh's army to retreat, impacting the ongoing siege of 's-Hertogenbosch.
events.name: Eighty Years' War: Capture of Wesel

events.enhanced_description: Montauban, one of the last Huguenot strongholds, surrendered without a fight to the troops of Cardinal Richelieu. This event marked a significant decline in Huguenot resistance in France.
events.name: Huguenot rebellions: Surrender of Montauban

events.enhanced_description: The Cambridge Agreement was signed in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, establishing control of the colony under stockholders who would emigrate to New England. This agreement laid the groundwork for the self-governance of the colony.
events.name: Cambridge Agreement

events.enhanced_description: As a result of the Cambridge Agreement, the Massachusetts Bay Colony transitioned into a self-governing entity. This development was crucial for the political evolution of the colony and its future governance.
events.name: Massachusetts Bay Colony becomes self-governing

events.enhanced_description: In the ongoing Anglo-Spanish War, a Spanish expedition led by Fadrique de Toledo destroyed the English colony on St. Kitts. This event highlighted the fierce competition for colonial dominance in the Caribbean.

locations.name: Saint Kitts, Saint Kitts and Nevis

events.name: Anglo-Spanish War: Destruction of the English colony on St. Kitts

events.enhanced_description: After a five-month siege, 's-Hertogenbosch surrendered to Frederick Henry, Prince of Orange. This capture was a critical blow to Spanish defenses in the region and significantly altered the course of the Eighty Years' War.
events.name: Eighty Years' War: Surrender of 's-Hertogenbosch

events.enhanced_description: The Italian plague arrived in Milan, marking the beginning of a devastating outbreak that would affect the region for years. The arrival of the plague was exacerbated by the presence of German soldiers at the Forte di Fuentes.
events.name: 1629–1631 Italian plague: Arrival in Milan

events.enhanced_description: Ahmad ibn Abd al-Muttalib, who had forcefully taken power as Emir of Mecca, was assassinated by order of Kansuh Pasha, the Governor of Yemen. This event reflected the turbulent political landscape of the region during this period.
events.name: Assassination of Ahmad ibn Abd al-Muttalib
