events.enhanced_description: The Truce of Altmark was signed between Sweden and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, effectively ending the Polish-Swedish War on favorable terms for Sweden. This agreement solidified Sweden's position as a major power in Northern Europe.

image.caption: Memorial commemorating the Polish-Swedish truce.
image.credit: Pawmak — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph of a memorial at Stary Targ, not a contemporary photograph of the 1629 signing; image date: 2009-06-21.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Polish–Swedish War: Truce of Altmark

events.enhanced_description: In what is now Western Australia, seven crew members of the Batavia were hanged on the Abrolhos Islands for their involvement in the massacre of 125 passengers and crew. This event highlighted the brutal consequences of mutiny and lawlessness during early European exploration.
events.name: Execution of crew members of the Batavia

events.enhanced_description: Portuguese Navy Captain Pedro Teixeira led a force of 2,000 men in the successful capture of Fort Taurege from the English in Brazil. This event was part of the broader struggle for control over territories in South America.
events.name: Capture of Fort Taurege

events.enhanced_description: The St Etienne baronets title was created in England as part of the British nobility system, reflecting the social hierarchy and the importance of land ownership during the early 17th century.
events.name: The St Etienne baronets British nobility title is created

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1629, Emperor Go-Mizunoo of Japan abdicated in favor of his daughter, Princess Okiko, marking a significant moment in the Japanese imperial lineage as she became Empress Meishō.
events.name: Emperor Go-Mizunoo abdicates the throne

events.enhanced_description: Giovanni I Cornaro, who served as the Doge of Venice since 1625, passed away on December 23, 1629, leading to the election of Nicolò Contarini as his successor during a tumultuous period for the Republic.
events.name: Death of Giovanni I Cornaro

events.enhanced_description: In March 1630, the Zaporozhian Cossacks, led by Taras Triasylo, rebelled against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, occupying parts of modern-day Ukraine, culminating in the Treaty of Pereyaslav.
events.name: Fedorovych Uprising

events.enhanced_description: In 1630, Milan reported its first case of plague, which would lead to a devastating outbreak that claimed approximately 186,000 lives by the end of 1631, decimating the city's population.
events.name: The first case of plague is reported in Milan

events.enhanced_description: In 1630, Italian astronomers Niccolò Zucchi and Daniello Bartoli became the first scientists to observe the belts on Jupiter, contributing to the early understanding of the planet's atmospheric phenomena.
events.name: Italian astronomers observe the belts on Jupiter

events.enhanced_description: In July 1630, the Italian plague of 1629–31 reached Venice, exacerbating the already dire situation in the city and leading to significant mortality.
events.name: The Italian plague of 1629–31 reaches Venice

events.enhanced_description: In 1630, Swedish King Gustav Adolf made landfall at Peenemünde, marking the beginning of Sweden's intervention in the Thirty Years' War on the Protestant side, which would significantly alter the course of the conflict.
events.name: Swedish intervention in the Thirty Years' War begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1630, the English first settled Paramaribo, which would later become the capital of Suriname, marking an important step in colonial expansion in South America.
events.name: Paramaribo is first settled by the English

events.enhanced_description: The Deccan Famine began in 1630 and lasted until 1632, resulting in the deaths of approximately two million people in India due to severe drought and mismanagement, marking one of the deadliest famines in Indian history.
events.name: The Deccan Famine of 1630–32 begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1630, the central square of Covent Garden in London was laid out, marking the beginning of its transformation into a vibrant market area. This development played a significant role in the economic and social life of London, eventually becoming a renowned hub for trade and entertainment.
events.name: Development of Covent Garden Market

events.enhanced_description: Johann Heinrich Alsted's 'Encyclopaedia septem tomis distincta' was published in 1630, contributing significantly to the field of encyclopedic knowledge during the early modern period. This work aimed to compile and categorize knowledge across various disciplines, reflecting the intellectual currents of the time.
events.name: Publication of Encyclopaedia septem tomis distincta

events.enhanced_description: In 1630, settlers departed from Pannaway Plantation to establish a new settlement at Strawbery Banke, which would later be renamed Portsmouth in 1653. This movement marked an important step in the expansion of English settlements in New England.
events.name: Settlement of Strawbery Banke

events.enhanced_description: On January 2, 1630, the first case of bubonic plague was reported in Turin, marking the beginning of a devastating outbreak that would sweep through Italy, leading to widespread mortality and social disruption.
events.name: First case of bubonic plague in Turin

events.enhanced_description: On January 5, 1630, a team of Portuguese military advisers, led by Gonçalo Teixeira Corrêa, arrived in Zhuozhou, China, to assist the Ming dynasty in modernizing its military tactics and artillery.
events.name: Portuguese military advisers arrive in China

events.enhanced_description: On January 11, 1630, Otto III and his brother William Augustus, Dukes of Brunswick-Harburg, sold their rights to inherit the rule of Brunswick-Lüneburg to Prince Christian in exchange for the payment of their substantial debts.
events.name: Sale of rights to inherit Brunswick-Lüneburg

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1630, General Yuan Chonghuan was arrested in Beijing after being invited to meet the Chongzhen Emperor, accused of collusion with the enemy, leading to his execution later that year.
events.name: General Yuan Chonghuan arrested

events.enhanced_description: On January 18, 1630, Nicolò Contarini was elected as the new Doge of Venice, a position he held during a critical time as the city faced a bubonic plague epidemic.
events.name: Nicolò Contarini elected Doge of Venice

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1630, Native American Quadequine introduced popcorn to English colonists, showcasing the agricultural knowledge and culinary traditions of Indigenous peoples in North America.
events.name: Quadequine introduces popcorn

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1630, a fleet sent by the Dutch West India Company captured Recife from the Portuguese, marking the establishment of Dutch Brazil and a significant shift in colonial power in the region.
events.name: Capture of Recife by Dutch West India Company

events.enhanced_description: The 1630 Crete earthquake occurred on March 9, 1630, causing significant destruction and loss of life on the island, which was part of the Venetian Republic at the time.
events.name: The 1630 Crete earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On May 4, 1630, during an invasion of Persia, Grand Vizier Gazi Hüsrev Pasha led Ottoman forces to a decisive victory against the Persians at Mahidasht, furthering Ottoman expansion in the region.
events.name: Ottoman invasion of Persia

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1630, the first case of plague was reported in Milan, which would lead to a catastrophic epidemic resulting in the deaths of nearly three-quarters of the city's population by the end of 1631.
events.name: First case of plague in Milan

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1630, the Swedish National Heritage Board was established in Stockholm, with Johannes Bureus as its first director, aimed at preserving Sweden's cultural heritage and history.
events.name: Swedish National Heritage Board created

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1630, during the Fedorovych uprising, the Zaporozhian Cossacks, led by Taras Triasylo, achieved a significant victory against Polish and Lithuanian troops near Pereiaslav.
events.name: Fedorovych uprising victory

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1630, the Battle of Villabuona was fought in Lombardy, resulting in the deaths of over 4,000 French and Venetian troops due to an attack led by Matthias Gallas of the Holy Roman Empire's army.
events.name: Battle of Villabuona

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1630, Alexander Leighton, a Scottish-born Presbyterian, was brought before Archbishop William Laud's Star Chamber court in London for publishing a seditious pamphlet, resulting in severe punishment.
events.name: Alexander Leighton trial

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1630, Swedish warships departed from Stockholm for Central Europe, marking Sweden's active involvement in the Thirty Years' War and its expansionist ambitions.
events.name: Swedish warships depart for Central Europe

events.enhanced_description: The Massachusetts Bay Colony was established in 1630, led by John Winthrop, who served as its first governor. This colony became a significant Puritan settlement in New England, shaping the region's early political and social landscape.
events.name: Massachusetts Bay Colony is founded, with John Winthrop as governor

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1630, the passengers of the Arbella, including Anne Bradstreet, disembarked in Salem, Massachusetts. Bradstreet would go on to become the first published American poet, marking a significant moment in American literary history.
events.name: Passengers of the Arbella, including Anne Bradstreet, arrive in the New World

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1630, the Success, the last ship of the Winthrop Fleet, arrived safely at Salem harbor, completing a significant migration of Puritan settlers to the New World.
events.name: The Success lands safely at Salem harbor

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1630, during the Thirty Years' War, Swedish forces captured Stettin, a strategic port city, marking a significant advance in Sweden's military campaign in the region.
events.name: Thirty Years' War: Stettin is taken by Swedish forces

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1630, during the War of the Mantuan Succession, Mantua was sacked by an army of the Holy Roman Empire led by Count Johann von Aldringen, resulting in widespread destruction and loss.
events.name: War of the Mantuan Succession: Mantua is sacked

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1630, the title of Sibbald baronets was created in England, reflecting the ongoing evolution of the British nobility during this period.
events.name: The Sibbald baronets British nobility title is created

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1630, John Winthrop played a crucial role in founding a church in Massachusetts, which would later be known as the First Church in Boston, establishing a significant religious institution in the colony.
events.name: John Winthrop helps in founding a church in Massachusetts

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1630, under pressure from the Prince-electors, Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand II dismissed General Albrecht von Wallenstein from command of the Imperial Army, a pivotal moment in the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Thirty Years' War: Ferdinand II dismisses Albrecht von Wallenstein

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1630, during the Sinhalese–Portuguese War, King Senarat of Kandy led over 35,000 troops in a decisive battle against the Portuguese, resulting in a significant victory for the Sinhalese forces.
events.name: Sinhalese–Portuguese War: Battle of Randeniwela

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1630, the Treaty of Stettin was signed, solidifying an alliance between Sweden and the Duchy of Pomerania and granting Sweden military control over the region, significantly impacting the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Thirty Years' War: Treaty of Stettin signed

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1630, Governor John Winthrop passed a resolution to officially rename Trimontaine on Shawmut peninsula to Boston, establishing the name that would become synonymous with the city.
events.name: Governor John Winthrop declares Trimontaine as Boston

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1630, the settlement of Boston was officially founded as part of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, becoming a central hub for Puritan settlers and a key location in early American history.
events.name: Settlement of Boston, Massachusetts Bay Colony is founded

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1630, the first ship of de Sauce's emigrants arrived at Southampton Hundred on the James River in Virginia, marking another chapter in the colonization of North America.
events.name: The first ship of de Sauce's emigrants arrive at Southampton Hundred

events.enhanced_description: On October 13, 1630, the Peace of Regensburg was signed, confirming Charles Gonzaga as Duke of Mantua and bringing a temporary resolution to the War of the Mantuan Succession.
events.name: War of the Mantuan Succession: Peace of Regensburg is signed

events.enhanced_description: On October 17, 1630, Empress Meishō was officially crowned in Kyoto, marking a significant event in Japanese history as she became one of the few female emperors in Japan.
events.name: Empress Meishō's Coronation takes place

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1630, Frendraught Castle, the home of James Crichton of Frendraught, was destroyed by fire, an event that marked a significant loss of heritage in Scotland.
events.name: Frendraught Castle burns down

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1630, the Day of the Dupes occurred when Marie de' Medici attempted to remove Cardinal Richelieu from power in the French Court, but her efforts ultimately failed after two days of political maneuvering.

image.caption: Maurice Leloir’s retrospective illustration depicts Louis XIII, Marie de’ Medici, and Cardinal Richelieu during the Day of the Dupes.
image.credit: Maurice Leloir — Cahu, Théodore ; Leloir, Maurice (1910) Richelieu , Collection d'albums historiques, Paris : Boivin & Cie., p. 55 OCLC : 1012269 .
image.date_qualification: Illustration published in 1901, depicting the 1630 event; it is not a contemporary event photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Day of the Dupes: Marie de' Medici attempts to oust Cardinal Richelieu

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1630, Abd Allah ibn Hasan was selected as the new Emir of Mecca following the death of Mas'ud ibn Idris from tuberculosis, marking a transition in leadership in this key Islamic city.
events.name: Abd Allah ibn Hasan is selected as the new Emir of Mecca

events.enhanced_description: In 1631, Moses Amyraut published 'Traite des Religions,' a significant work that contributed to theological discourse during the Reformation. This publication reflected the era's intellectual currents and debates surrounding religion.
events.name: Publication of Traite des Religions

events.enhanced_description: In 1631, Antonio Colmenero de Ledesma published 'Chocolate: or, An Indian Drinke,' introducing European audiences to the cultural significance and preparation of chocolate. This work played a role in the growing popularity of chocolate in Europe.
events.name: Publication of Chocolate: or, An Indian Drinke

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1631, Sweden and France signed the Treaty of Bärwalde, establishing a military alliance during the Thirty Years' War. This treaty marked a significant collaboration against the Habsburgs, with France providing financial support to the Swedish army as it invaded northern Germany.

image.caption: Portrait of Gustav II Adolf of Sweden, attributed to Jacob Hoefnagel.
image.credit: Attributed to Jacob Hoefnagel — Unknown source Unknown source
image.date_qualification: Circa 1624; the portrait predates the treaty of 23 January 1631.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Treaty of Bärwalde

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1631, Puritan leader Roger Williams arrived in Boston, Massachusetts. His arrival was significant as he later became a prominent advocate for religious freedom and the separation of church and state, ultimately founding the colony of Rhode Island.
events.name: Roger Williams arrives in Boston

events.enhanced_description: The Reval Gymnasium was founded on February 16, 1631, in Tallinn, Estonia, by Swedish King Gustavus II Adolphus. This institution played a crucial role in the educational landscape of the region, promoting learning and scholarship during a time of significant political change.
events.name: Foundation of Reval Gymnasium

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1631, a fire broke out in Westminster Hall, one of the oldest parts of the Palace of Westminster. Fortunately, the fire was extinguished before it could cause significant damage, preserving this historic site that has been central to British governance for centuries.
events.name: Fire in Westminster Hall

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1631, Ambrósio I Nimi a Nkanga, the ruler of the Kingdom of Kongo, died after a five-year reign. His death marked a significant moment in the history of the Kongo Kingdom, which was experiencing internal strife and external pressures during this period.
events.name: Death of Ambrósio I Nimi a Nkanga

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1631, Al Walid ben Zidan ascended to the throne as the new Sultan of Morocco following the death of Abu Marwan Abd al-Malik II. His reign would be marked by efforts to stabilize the kingdom amidst internal conflicts and external threats.
events.name: Al Walid ben Zidan becomes Sultan of Morocco

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1631, the siege of the Protestant city of Magdeburg by the Catholic League commenced. This brutal siege would last for over two months, culminating in the city's fall and a tragic massacre of its inhabitants, highlighting the intense religious conflicts of the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Siege of Magdeburg begins

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1631, during the Thirty Years' War, Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden achieved a significant victory against an imperial garrison at Frankfurt an der Oder. This battle underscored Sweden's military prowess and its role in the conflict against the Habsburgs.
events.name: Gustavus Adolphus defeats imperial garrison

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1631, John Winthrop took the oath of office in Dorchester, Boston, becoming the first Governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony. His leadership was pivotal in shaping the early governance and social structure of the colony.
events.name: John Winthrop becomes Governor of Massachusetts

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1631, after a two-month siege, the Imperial Army, commanded by Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly, sacked the Protestant city of Magdeburg, resulting in the massacre of over 20,000 inhabitants. This event shocked many Protestant states, prompting them to ally with Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden.
events.name: Sack of Magdeburg

events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1631, William Claiborne sailed from England to establish a trading post on Kent Island, marking the first English settlement in Maryland. This settlement played a crucial role in the early colonial economy and interactions with Indigenous peoples.
events.name: William Claiborne establishes trading post

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Fontainebleau was signed on April 11, 1814, marking the end of the War of the Sixth Coalition. Under this treaty, Napoleon Bonaparte was forced to abdicate unconditionally as Emperor of the French, leading to significant political changes in Europe.
events.name: Treaty of Fontainebleau

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1631, Mumtaz Mahal died during childbirth in Burhanpur, prompting her husband, Shah Jahan, to commission the Taj Mahal as her mausoleum. This iconic structure, completed in 1653, is celebrated as a masterpiece of Mughal architecture and a symbol of eternal love.
events.name: Death of Mumtaz Mahal

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1631, the Treaty of Cherasco was signed, officially ending the War of the Mantuan Succession. This treaty marked a significant moment in Italian politics, reshaping alliances and territorial claims in the region.
events.name: Treaty of Cherasco

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1631, Algerian pirates sacked the town of Baltimore in County Cork, Ireland. This raid resulted in the capture of many locals and highlighted the ongoing threat of piracy along the coasts of Europe during this period.
events.name: Sack of Baltimore by Algerian pirates

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1631, Koca Musa Pasha, the Ottoman Governor of Egypt, orchestrated the murder of Emir Kitas Bey, who was set to lead an invasion of Persia. This act of political intrigue reflects the tumultuous power dynamics within the Ottoman Empire during this era.
events.name: Koca Musa Pasha arranges murder

events.enhanced_description: On July 16, 1631, the city of Würzburg was taken by Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden, effectively ending the notorious Würzburg witch trials. These trials had resulted in the execution of approximately 900 individuals accused of witchcraft, marking a dark chapter in the region's history.
events.name: Würzburg witch trials end

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1631, during the Thirty Years' War, the Battle of Werben took place, where Tilly's forces defeated Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden, albeit not decisively. This battle exemplified the ongoing struggle for dominance in the conflict between Protestant and Catholic states.
events.name: Battle of Werben

events.enhanced_description: In August 1631, during the Thirty Years' War, Count Tilly's forces were compelled to enter the Electorate of Saxony due to supply shortages. This maneuver aimed to secure resources and provoke a response from the Saxon and Swedish leaders.
events.name: Tilly's Army Moves into Saxony

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1631, the Treaty of Werben was signed, establishing an alliance between Hesse-Cassel and Sweden during the Thirty Years' War. This treaty was part of the broader realignment of alliances as various states sought to navigate the complexities of the ongoing conflict.
events.name: Treaty of Werben

events.enhanced_description: On 1 Safar 1041 A.H. (August 29, 1631), Abd Allah ibn Hasan, the Emir of Mecca, abdicated his position, passing the leadership to his son Muhammad and his great-nephew Zayd. This transition marked a significant moment in the governance of Mecca during a period of political instability.
events.name: Abdication of Abd Allah ibn Hasan

events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1631, following Tilly's invasion, John George of Saxony allied with Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden. This alliance aimed to repel the Imperial forces from Saxony, marking a pivotal shift in the conflict.
events.name: Saxon Alliance with Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On September 12, 1631, during the Eighty Years' War, a Spanish fleet commanded by Admiral Antonio de Oquendo achieved a decisive victory over a Dutch fleet off the coast of Brazil. This battle underscored the ongoing naval conflicts between Spain and the Dutch Republic.
events.name: Battle of Albrolhos

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1631, during the Eighty Years' War, a Spanish fleet of 95 ships carrying 5,500 soldiers was nearly annihilated by a Dutch fleet off the coast of the Netherlands. This battle was a significant blow to Spanish naval power.

locations.name: Off the coast of the Netherlands

events.name: Battle of the Slaak

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1631, the Battle of Breitenfeld marked a turning point in the Thirty Years' War as Gustavus II Adolphus of Sweden decisively defeated Tilly's Imperial army. This victory was the first significant win for Protestant forces in the conflict.
events.name: Battle of Breitenfeld

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1631, a Saxon army successfully captured Prague, a key city in the ongoing Thirty Years' War. This takeover was part of the broader conflict between Protestant and Catholic forces in Central Europe.
events.name: Saxon Army Takes Over Prague

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1631, King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden took possession of Prague, the capital of Bohemia, further solidifying his influence in the region during the Thirty Years' War. This event was crucial in the Protestant campaign against the Catholic Habsburgs.
events.name: Gustavus Adolphus Takes Prague

events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1631, a special mass was held in Venice to celebrate the end of a devastating two-year bubonic plague that had claimed thousands of lives. This event marked a significant moment of relief and gratitude for the city's inhabitants.
events.name: Mass in Venice Celebrating End of Plague

events.enhanced_description: On November 29, 1631, the Treaty of Höchst was signed between King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden and George II of Hesse-Darmstadt. The treaty involved the surrender of the fortress of Rüsselsheim in exchange for Sweden's recognition of Hesse-Darmstadt's neutrality in the ongoing Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Treaty of Höchst Signed

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1631, Gustavus II Adolphus of Sweden captured the city of Mainz without facing any resistance. This strategic acquisition was part of his campaign during the Thirty Years' War to strengthen Protestant positions in the region.
events.name: Gustavus II Adolphus Takes Mainz

events.enhanced_description: On January 8, 1632, the University of Amsterdam was established, evolving from the Athenaeum Illustre. This institution became a significant center of learning and scholarship in the Netherlands, contributing to the intellectual life of Europe.
events.name: Establishment of the University of Amsterdam

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1632, Dr. Nicolaes Tulp conducted a public dissection for medical students in Amsterdam, an event famously captured in Rembrandt's painting 'The Anatomy Lesson.' This moment highlighted the intersection of art and science in the 17th century.
events.name: Dissection by Dr. Nicolaes Tulp

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1632, Galileo's 'Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems' was published in Florence. This work presented arguments for heliocentrism and sparked significant controversy with the Catholic Church.
events.name: Publication of Galileo's Dialogue

events.enhanced_description: In March 1632, Gustavus Adolphus invaded Bavaria with his army, marking a significant escalation in the Thirty Years' War. This invasion aimed to strengthen Protestant positions against the Catholic League.
events.name: Gustavus Adolphus Invades Bavaria

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1632, during the Thirty Years' War, Count Tilly's forces defeated the Swedish army under Gustav Horn at the Battle of Bamberg. This victory allowed the Catholic League to regain control over the town.
events.name: Battle of Bamberg

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, 1632, King Gustavus Adolphus made a triumphant entry into Nuremberg, where he was warmly welcomed by the populace. He pledged to protect the Protestant cause, reinforcing his commitment to the war against Catholic forces.
events.name: Gustavus Adolphus Enters Nuremberg

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1632, the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye was signed, returning Quebec to French control after it had been seized by the English in 1629. This treaty was significant in the context of colonial power struggles in North America.
events.name: Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1632, during the Thirty Years' War, Gustavus Adolphus defeated Tilly's Catholic League forces at the Battle of Rain. Tilly was severely wounded in this encounter and would die shortly thereafter.
events.name: Battle of Rain

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1632, the Swedish army captured Munich, the capital of Bavaria, during the Thirty Years' War. This victory was a significant achievement for Gustavus Adolphus and bolstered the Protestant cause in the region.
events.name: Capture of Munich

events.enhanced_description: In June 1632, during the Eighty Years' War, Frederick Henry, Prince of Orange, leads a Dutch army to capture the cities of Venlo, Roermond, and Sittard in quick succession before laying siege to Maastricht, a strategic stronghold.
events.name: Frederick Henry captures cities

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1632, Sir Francis Windebank was appointed as chief Secretary of State in England. His role was crucial in the administration of King Charles I's government during a tumultuous period leading up to the English Civil War.
events.name: Appointment of Sir Francis Windebank

events.enhanced_description: Mumtaz Mahal, the beloved wife of Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan, dies on June 17, 1632, after giving birth to their 14th child. Her death prompts Shah Jahan to begin the construction of the Taj Mahal, a mausoleum that would become a symbol of love and architectural brilliance.
events.name: Mumtaz Mahal dies

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1632, Charles I of England issues a charter for the colony of Maryland, named in honor of his wife Henrietta Maria. The charter grants control of the colony to Lord Baltimore, establishing a haven for English Catholics.
events.name: Charter for Maryland

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1632, Fasilides, the Emperor of Ethiopia, re-establishes Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity as the state religion, reversing the policies of his father, Susenyos. He also confiscates lands from Jesuit missionaries, limiting their influence in the region.
events.name: Fasilides declares Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity

events.enhanced_description: The University of Tartu is founded on June 30, 1632, marking a significant development in higher education in the region. It becomes one of the oldest universities in Northern Europe, contributing to the cultural and intellectual life of Estonia.
events.name: University of Tartu founded

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1632, three hundred colonists depart from Dieppe, France, bound for New France. This migration reflects the ongoing European interest in colonization and the establishment of settlements in North America.
events.name: Colonists depart Dieppe

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1632, during the Eighty Years' War, a Dutch army led by Frederick Henry, Prince of Orange, successfully captures the city of Maastricht after a two-month siege, marking a significant victory for the Dutch forces.
events.name: Capture of Maastricht

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1632, the Battle of Castelnaudary occurs, where a rebellion against King Louis XIII of France is decisively crushed. The leader of the rebellion, Gaston, Duke of Orléans, surrenders, solidifying Louis XIII's control over France.
events.name: Battle of Castelnaudary

events.enhanced_description: On September 3, 1632, the last executions of Christians in Japan take place in Nagasaki, where four Spanish missionaries, including Augustinian friar Bartholomew Gutierrez, and two Japanese converts are burned alive. They are later beatified as martyrs.
events.name: Executions in Nagasaki

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1632, during the Thirty Years' War, the Battle of the Alte Veste takes place near Nuremberg. Swedish King Gustavus Adolphus attempts to break the siege laid by Wallenstein but is ultimately defeated, marking a setback for Swedish forces.

image.caption: Portrait of Albrecht von Wallenstein, reproduced from an old painting.
image.credit: Unidentified painter — photograph of old painting
image.date_qualification: The painting is dated circa 1700, after the 1632 battle; this is a portrait, not a contemporary event depiction.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of the Alte Veste

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1632, Yakutsk is founded by Pyotr Beketov as a fort and administrative center in Siberia. This establishment plays a crucial role in the Russian expansion into the Far East.
events.name: Yakutsk founded

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1632, the University of Tartu officially opens its doors, becoming a significant center of learning in the region. It plays an important role in the cultural and educational development of Estonia.
events.name: University of Tartu opens

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1632, Henri II de Montmorency is executed for his role in the rebellion against King Louis XIII of France. His execution serves as a warning to others who might oppose the king's authority.

image.caption: Design for Henri II de Montmorency’s funeral monument in Moulins, attributed to Michel Anguier.
image.credit: Michel Anguier (1612-86) — http://arts-graphiques.louvre.fr/fo/images-fo/d0014576-000.jpg
image.date_qualification: 17th century (the supplied image date is recorded as “17 th century date QS:P,+1650-00-00T00:00:00Z/7”); created after the 1632 execution.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Execution of Henri II de Montmorency

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1632, Wladyslaw IV Waza is elected king of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth following the death of Sigismund III Vasa. His reign is marked by efforts to strengthen the monarchy and the state.

image.caption: Portrait of Władysław Vasa as a boy, painted by Martin Kober.
image.credit: Martin Kober — Dorota Żołądź - Strzelczyk (2006). Dziecko w dawnej Polsce . Wydawnictwo Poznańskie. ISBN 83-71770-38-3
image.date_qualification: The portrait is dated 1596, not the 1632 election date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Wladyslaw IV Waza elected king

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1813, the Battle of Lützen took place, where Napoleon Bonaparte achieved a victory against a coalition of German forces. This battle was significant in the context of the Napoleonic Wars, demonstrating Napoleon's military prowess despite the growing opposition.
events.name: Battle of Lützen

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1632, a new Dutch settlement named Swanadael in New Netherland is wiped out by Indigenous peoples. This event highlights the ongoing conflicts between European settlers and Native Americans during the colonial period.
events.name: Swanadael settlement wiped out

events.enhanced_description: In a significant advancement for firefighting, fire engines were used for the first time in England to combat a fire at London Bridge. Despite their efforts, 43 houses were destroyed before the fire was brought under control.
events.name: Fire engines used in England

events.enhanced_description: In 1633, the Jewish community of Poznań was granted a significant privilege that allowed them to restrict Christian access to their quarter, reflecting the complex inter-religious dynamics of the time. This privilege was part of a broader trend of Jewish self-governance in various European cities during the early modern period.
events.name: The Jews of Poznań are granted the privilege of forbidding Christians to enter into their city quarter

events.enhanced_description: In 1633, Emperor Fasilides of Ethiopia expelled Jesuit missionaries from his realm, marking a significant moment in the history of Ethiopian Christianity and its relationship with European powers. This expulsion was part of Fasilides' efforts to reassert Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity against foreign influence.
events.name: Emperor of Ethiopia Fasilides expels Jesuit missionaries

events.enhanced_description: St Columb's Cathedral in Derry, completed in 1633, is notable for being the first post-Reformation Anglican cathedral built in the British Isles. Its construction marked a significant moment in the religious landscape of Ireland, symbolizing the Protestant Reformation's influence.
events.name: Completion of St Columb's Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: In 1633, Mission San Luis de Apalachee was established in what is now Tallahassee, Florida, by Spanish friars. This mission played a crucial role in the Spanish colonization efforts and the spread of Christianity among the indigenous Apalachee people.
events.name: Mission San Luis de Apalachee is built

events.enhanced_description: In 1633, English colonists settled in what would become Hingham, Massachusetts, contributing to the expansion of English settlements in New England. This settlement played a role in the early colonial history of the region.
events.name: English colonists settle Hingham, Massachusetts

events.enhanced_description: In 1633, the University of Cambridge established a professorship in Arabic studies, reflecting the growing interest in the Arabic language and Islamic culture during the early modern period. This initiative marked a significant step in the academic study of the Middle East in Europe.
events.name: Founding of a professorship in Arabic studies at the University of Cambridge

events.enhanced_description: In 1633, during the Trịnh–Nguyễn War, Trịnh Tráng launched an attack on Đàng Trong at the Nhật Lệ estuary, marking a significant clash in this civil war. This conflict was characterized by the struggle for power between the Trịnh and Nguyễn lords in Vietnam.
events.name: Trịnh–Nguyễn War: Attack on Đàng Trong

events.enhanced_description: Galileo Galilei, the renowned Italian astronomer, was summoned to Rome by Pope Urban VIII to answer charges of heresy. During his journey, he was quarantined for 22 days at Ponte a Centino due to a plague outbreak, delaying his arrival for the trial that would challenge his heliocentric views.
events.name: Galileo Galilei summoned to Rome

events.enhanced_description: The formal coronation of Władysław IV Vasa as King of Poland took place at Wawel Cathedral in Kraków. This event marked the official recognition of his kingship, following his election on November 8, 1632.
events.name: Coronation of Władysław IV Vasa

events.enhanced_description: The Duchy of Hesse-Cassel successfully captured the town of Dorsten from the Electorate of Cologne without facing any resistance. This event was part of the broader conflicts during the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Capture of Dorsten

events.enhanced_description: Galileo Galilei arrived in Rome to stand trial before the Inquisition, facing charges of heresy for his support of heliocentrism. This trial would have significant implications for the relationship between science and the Catholic Church.
events.name: Galileo Galilei arrives in Rome for trial

events.enhanced_description: Samuel de Champlain reclaimed his role as commander of New France, acting on behalf of Cardinal Richelieu. His leadership was crucial in the development and expansion of French interests in North America.
events.name: Samuel de Champlain reclaims command of New France

events.enhanced_description: Galileo Galilei was convicted of heresy by the Roman Catholic Church for advocating the heliocentric model of the solar system. This conviction marked a pivotal moment in the conflict between science and religious doctrine.
events.name: Galileo Galilei convicted of heresy

events.enhanced_description: Samuel de Champlain returned to Quebec after a four-year absence, taking on the role of Lieutenant General of the troops of New France. His return was significant for the French colonial efforts in North America.
events.name: Samuel de Champlain returns to Quebec

events.enhanced_description: Aurangzeb, the Crown Prince of the Mughal Empire, narrowly escaped death when an elephant stampede disrupted his encampment. He managed to defend himself with a lance, showcasing his bravery and quick thinking.
events.name: Aurangzeb escapes elephant stampede

events.enhanced_description: Charles I was crowned King of Scots at St Giles' Cathedral in Edinburgh, marking his first visit to Scotland since early childhood. Although he had been the Scottish monarch since 1625, this ceremony solidified his royal status.
events.name: Charles I crowned King of Scots

events.enhanced_description: Under pressure from the Roman Catholic Church, Galileo Galilei was forced to recant his heliocentric view of the solar system. Legend has it that after his recantation, he muttered 'Eppur si muove' ('And yet it moves').
events.name: Galileo Galilei recants heliocentric view

events.enhanced_description: The fleet of the Dutch East India Company, led by Hans Putmans, launched a surprise attack on the base of their ally Zheng Zhilong near Xiamen. This unexpected assault highlighted the complexities of alliances during the period.
events.name: Dutch East India Company attacks Zheng Zhilong's base

events.enhanced_description: During the Thirty Years' War, the Battle of Oldendorf saw Swedish forces defeat the Holy Roman Empire near Hessisch Oldendorf. This victory contributed to Sweden's growing influence in the conflict.
events.name: Battle of Oldendorf

events.enhanced_description: William Laud was appointed Archbishop of Canterbury, a position that would allow him to influence the Church of England significantly. His tenure was marked by efforts to enforce religious uniformity.
events.name: William Laud becomes Archbishop of Canterbury

events.enhanced_description: King Louis XIII of France entered Nancy, marking the occupation of the Duchy of Lorraine. This event was part of France's broader territorial ambitions during the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Louis XIII occupies Nancy

events.enhanced_description: A group from the Plymouth Colony established the first settlement in Windsor, Connecticut. This marked a significant step in the expansion of English colonial presence in New England.
events.name: First settlement in Connecticut

events.enhanced_description: During the Thirty Years' War, Spain successfully recaptured Rheinfelden from Swedish forces in a strategic siege. This event underscored the ongoing conflict between the two powers in the region.
events.name: Siege of Rheinfelden

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Liaoluo Bay, a large fleet of the Ming dynasty, commanded by Zheng Zhilong, defeated a Dutch East India Company fleet near the island of Quemoy. This battle highlighted the tensions between European powers and Asian empires.
events.name: Battle of Liaoluo Bay

events.enhanced_description: The Dutch expedition led by Jan Janszoon van Hoorn against Spanish pirates in Central America concluded successfully after six months. This mission underscored the ongoing conflicts between European colonial powers in the New World.
events.name: Dutch expedition against Spanish pirates

events.enhanced_description: Commissioned by Cecil Calvert, 2nd Baron Baltimore, the ships The Ark and Dove departed from Gravesend, England, to transport English colonists to the province of Maryland. This journey marked a significant moment in the establishment of English settlements in America.
events.name: The Ark and Dove depart for Maryland

events.enhanced_description: The Ark encountered a violent storm during its journey to America but managed to stay afloat. The ship's crew later discovered that the Dove had also survived the storms, and both vessels would arrive in Maryland on February 24, 1634.
events.name: The Ark survives storm on journey to America

events.enhanced_description: Francisco de Murga, the Governor of Cartagena, led a brutal crackdown on a revolt by escaped African slaves at the palenque of Limón. His actions resulted in the capture and execution of several rebels, reflecting the harsh realities of colonial rule.
events.name: Francisco de Murga crushes slave revolt

events.enhanced_description: In 1634, the Dutch captured the island of Curaçao, which became a significant point for trade and military strategy in the Caribbean. This event was part of the larger conflict between European powers vying for control over territories in the New World.
events.name: Capture of Curaçao by the Dutch

events.enhanced_description: In 1634, the English established a settlement at Cochin (modern-day Kochi) on the Malabar Coast of India, marking an important step in their colonial expansion in Asia. This settlement facilitated trade and interaction between England and the Indian subcontinent.
events.name: Establishment of English Settlement at Cochin

events.enhanced_description: In 1634, Emperor Fasilides of Ethiopia expelled Patriarch Afonso Mendes and several Jesuit missionaries, suspecting their involvement in the Portuguese assault on Mombasa. This event marked a significant shift in the relationship between Ethiopia and the Catholic Church.
events.name: Expulsion of Patriarch Afonso Mendes from Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: In 1634, Cardinal Richelieu formed the Académie Française, which would be formally established in 1635. This institution aimed to preserve and regulate the French language and literature, playing a crucial role in the cultural development of France.
events.name: Formation of the Académie Française

events.enhanced_description: The first performance of the Oberammergau Passion Play took place in 1634 in Oberammergau, Bavaria. This play, which depicts the Passion of Jesus Christ, has become a significant cultural and religious tradition in the region.
events.name: First Performance of the Oberammergau Passion Play

events.enhanced_description: In 1634, Moses Amyraut published his influential work, Traité de la predestination, which presented a unique perspective on predestination and free will within the context of Reformed theology. This publication contributed to ongoing theological debates in Europe.
events.name: Publication of Moses Amyraut's Traité de la predestination

events.enhanced_description: In 1634, the Paulaner Brewery was established in Munich by Minim friars, which would later become one of the most famous breweries in Germany. This brewery played a significant role in the development of the beer culture in Bavaria.
events.name: Establishment of the Paulaner Brewery

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1634, Albrecht von Wallenstein, the supreme commander of the Holy Roman Empire's army, demanded that his colonels sign a declaration of personal loyalty. This act was indicative of the tensions within the Imperial command during the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Albrecht von Wallenstein demands loyalty from his colonels

events.enhanced_description: On January 14, 1634, France's Compagnie normande secured a one-year monopoly on trade with the African kingdoms in Guinea. This monopoly was part of France's broader colonial ambitions in West Africa during the early 17th century.
events.name: Compagnie normande obtains trade monopoly

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1634, Charles IV, Duke of Lorraine, abdicated in favor of his brother Nicholas II, who would only hold the duchy for a brief period of 75 days. This political maneuvering reflects the instability of noble power in the region during this era.
events.name: Charles IV abdicates in favor of Nicholas II

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1634, Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand II signed a classified order dismissing Albrecht von Wallenstein, the supreme commander of the Imperial Army. This decision was pivotal in the context of the Thirty Years' War and reflected the growing tensions within the Imperial leadership.
events.name: Ferdinand II dismisses Albrecht von Wallenstein

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1634, the public announcement of Emperor Ferdinand II's dismissal of Albrecht von Wallenstein for high treason was made, along with an order for his capture. This event marked a significant turning point in the Thirty Years' War.
events.name: Wallenstein's dismissal made public

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1634, Albrecht von Wallenstein was assassinated by rebel Scots and Irish soldiers in Cheb. This assassination was a critical moment in the Thirty Years' War, significantly impacting the course of the conflict.
events.name: Assassination of Albrecht von Wallenstein

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1634, the Russians vacated their camp, effectively ending the Siege of Smolensk. This event marked a significant moment in the ongoing conflict between the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and Russia.
events.name: End of the Siege of Smolensk

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1634, Belgian scientist Jan Baptist van Helmont was interrogated by the Spanish Inquisition and placed under house arrest due to his controversial experiments in plant growth. This incident highlights the tension between scientific inquiry and religious authority during the period.
events.name: Jan Baptist van Helmont interrogated by the Spanish Inquisition

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1634, Leonard Calvert arrived in Maryland with Jesuit missionaries, establishing St. Mary's as the fourth permanent settlement in British North America. This settlement played a crucial role in the early development of the colony and the establishment of religious freedom.

locations.name: St. Mary's City, Maryland, United States

events.name: Leonard Calvert arrives in Maryland

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1634, Nicholas II, who had briefly ruled the Duchy of Lorraine, abdicated in favor of his brother Charles IV. This political shift underscores the instability and power struggles within the region's nobility.
events.name: Nicholas II abdicates in favor of Charles IV

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1634, the Battle of Amritsar commenced as Mughal Empire troops attempted to eliminate the Sikh leader Guru Hargobind. The Sikh defenders achieved a remarkable victory, marking a significant moment in the history of Sikh resistance against Mughal authority.
events.name: Battle of Amritsar begins

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1634, following the assassination of Albrecht von Wallenstein, Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand II took personal command of the Imperial Army. This decision was pivotal in the ongoing Thirty Years' War, as it marked a shift in leadership strategy.
events.name: Ferdinand II takes command of the Imperial Army

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1634, King Charles I of England and Scotland referred to the banner of the British Isles as the 'Union Flag' in a proclamation. This term would evolve into the description of the British flag as the 'Union Jack', symbolizing the political union of England and Scotland.

image.caption: Graphic depicting a proposed Union Jack design.
image.credit: RCraig09 — Own work
image.date_qualification: The image description identifies the proposal as circa 1604; the 2021-04-17 image date is not the depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Charles I refers to the Union Flag

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1634, the Treaty of Polyanovka was signed, concluding the Smolensk War between the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and the Tsardom of Russia. This treaty marked a significant shift in the balance of power in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Treaty of Polyanovka signed

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1634, the city of Trois-Rivières was founded in New France, in what is now Quebec, Canada. This settlement was one of the earliest in the region and played a crucial role in the French colonial efforts in North America.
events.name: Founding of Trois-Rivières

events.enhanced_description: In August 1634, Jean Nicolet became the first European to set foot in what is now Wisconsin, landing at Green Bay while searching for a water route to the Pacific. His journey marked an important moment in the exploration of North America.
events.name: Jean Nicolet reaches Wisconsin

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1634, Urbain Grandier was burned alive in Loudun, France, after being accused of wizardry. This event is emblematic of the witch hunts and religious fervor that characterized the period in Europe.
events.name: Urbain Grandier burned alive in Loudun

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Nördlingen, fought on September 6-7, 1634, marked a significant victory for the Imperial Army and Habsburg Spain against the Swedish forces and Protestant German troops during the Thirty Years' War. This battle not only shifted the balance of power in the conflict but also led to the withdrawal of Swedish forces from southern Germany.
events.name: The Battle of Nördlingen

events.enhanced_description: On September 12, 1634, a catastrophic explosion occurred at a gunpowder factory in Valletta, Malta, resulting in the deaths of 22 individuals and extensive damage to surrounding buildings. This incident highlighted the dangers associated with the storage and handling of gunpowder during the period.
events.name: Gunpowder Factory Explosion in Valletta

events.enhanced_description: The Burchardi flood, also known as the second Grote Mandrenke, struck the North Sea coast of Germany and Denmark on October 11, 1634, causing widespread devastation and resulting in the deaths of an estimated 8,000 to 12,000 people. This catastrophic event underscored the vulnerability of coastal communities to natural disasters.

image.caption: Retrospective map illustration titled “Strand before and Burchardi flood.”
image.credit: Joan Blaeu / After Danckwerth, Kaspar / After Johannes Mejer — This image has been extracted from another file
image.date_qualification: The image date is 1662, 28 years after the flood; do not present it as made during the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Burchardi Flood

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1634, the Irish House of Commons passed an Act for the Punishment of the Vice of Buggery, reflecting the legal and moral attitudes of the time towards homosexuality. This legislation was part of a broader trend in Europe during the early modern period to regulate sexual behavior through law.
events.name: Irish House of Commons Act for the Punishment of the Vice of Buggery

events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1634, Francesco Niccolini, an Italian diplomat, obtained an audience with Pope Urban VIII to advocate for the reconsideration of the Church's punishment of the astronomer Galileo Galilei. The Pope, while expressing esteem for Galileo, ultimately indicated that no changes would be made to the Church's stance.
events.name: Francesco Niccolini's Audience with Pope Urban VIII

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1634, Gregorio Panzani, an emissary of Pope Urban VIII, was welcomed in London by King Charles I, marking a significant diplomatic moment as it was the first time since England's break with the Roman Catholic Church that a monarch had received a representative from the Vatican.
events.name: Gregorio Panzani's Visit to England

events.enhanced_description: The Pearl Mosque, also known as the Moti Masjid, was commissioned by Shah Jahan and completed in 1635 within the Lahore Fort. This exquisite mosque is a prime example of Mughal architecture, showcasing intricate marble inlay work and a serene ambiance, reflecting the artistic achievements of the Mughal Empire.
events.name: Consecration of Shah Jahan's Pearl Mosque

events.enhanced_description: In 1635, Shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu issued the Sakoku Edict, which outlawed Christianity and enforced a policy of isolationism in Japan. This edict was a pivotal moment in Japanese history, leading to over two centuries of limited foreign contact and the suppression of Christianity.
events.name: Shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu issues the Sakoku Edict of 1635

events.enhanced_description: In 1635, France began the colonization of Guadeloupe and Martinique, establishing a foothold in the Caribbean. This marked the beginning of French colonial expansion in the region, which would have lasting impacts on the islands' demographics and culture.
events.name: Colonization of Guadeloupe and Martinique

events.enhanced_description: In 1635, France claimed the island of Dominica, furthering its colonial ambitions in the Caribbean. This claim would lead to conflicts with other colonial powers and shape the island's future.
events.name: Claiming of Dominica by France

events.enhanced_description: In 1635, the Ottomans were expelled from Yemen, marking a significant shift in control over the region. This expulsion was part of the broader conflicts involving the Ottoman Empire and local powers.
events.name: Expulsion of Ottomans from Yemen

events.enhanced_description: In 1635, the Sakoku Edict was enforced in Japan, instituting a policy of isolationism that prohibited Japanese citizens from traveling abroad and restricted foreign access to the country. This edict marked a significant turning point in Japan's foreign relations and cultural exchange.
events.name: Sakoku Edict of 1635

events.enhanced_description: In 1635, the Pearl Mosque, commissioned by Shah Jahan, was completed at Lahore Fort. This mosque is renowned for its exquisite architecture and reflects the grandeur of Mughal design during Shah Jahan's reign.
events.name: Completion of Shah Jahan's Pearl Mosque

events.enhanced_description: In 1635, Nagyszombat University, the predecessor of Budapest University, was established in what is now Trnava, Slovakia. This institution played a crucial role in the educational landscape of Hungary and Central Europe.
events.name: Establishment of Nagyszombat University

events.enhanced_description: In 1635, Willem and Joan Blaeu published the first edition of their Atlas Novus in Amsterdam. This work became a significant contribution to cartography and was widely recognized for its detailed maps and artistic quality.
events.name: Publication of Atlas Novus

events.enhanced_description: The Great Colonial Hurricane struck Narragansett Bay on August 25, 1635, causing significant destruction and resulting in the deaths of over 46 people. This hurricane is noted for its intensity, possibly reaching Category 3 status, and it impacted the early colonial settlements in New England.
events.name: The Great Colonial Hurricane

events.enhanced_description: On September 12, 1635, the Treaty of Sztumska Wieś was signed, marking a significant peace agreement between Sweden and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. This treaty concluded hostilities that had arisen during the Polish–Swedish War, establishing a temporary peace in the region.
events.name: The Treaty of Sztumska Wieś

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1635, Roger Williams, a religious dissident and advocate for the separation of church and state, was banished from the Massachusetts Bay Colony. His outspoken criticism of the colony's policies regarding religious punishment and land dealings with Native Americans led to his expulsion, ultimately resulting in the founding of Rhode Island.

image.caption: Roger Williams Landing Place monument in Slate Rock Park, Providence, Rhode Island.
image.credit: Kenneth C. Zirkel — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2022-01-11; this is a later site monument, not a depiction of the 1635 banishment.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Banished of Roger Williams

events.enhanced_description: Thomas Parr, who was claimed to have lived to the age of 152, was buried in Westminster Abbey on November 15, 1635. His extraordinary age and the circumstances of his life drew significant public interest, and his burial in such a prestigious location underscored his unique status.
events.name: Burial of Thomas Parr

events.enhanced_description: The Dutch pacification campaign against Taiwanese aborigines began on November 22, 1635, as part of the Dutch colonial efforts in Formosa. This campaign aimed to assert control over the island and subdue local resistance, marking a significant moment in the history of Dutch colonialism in Asia.
events.name: Dutch pacification campaign on Formosa

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1635, Shah Jahan, the Mughal Emperor, issued a decree against Portuguese Jesuits, ordering the demolition of the Agra Church and prohibiting their attempts to convert Hindus and Muslims. This decree reflected the tensions between the Mughal Empire and European colonial powers regarding religious influence.
events.name: Shah Jahan's decree against Portuguese Jesuits

events.enhanced_description: In 1636, Anthony van Diemen took office as Governor-General of the Dutch East Indies, a position he would hold until his death in 1645. His administration was marked by significant expansion of Dutch influence in the region.
events.name: Anthony van Diemen takes office

events.enhanced_description: The year 1636 marked the beginning of French intervention in the Thirty Years' War, as France sought to counter Habsburg power in Europe. This intervention would significantly alter the course of the conflict and the political landscape of the continent.
events.name: French intervention in the Thirty Years' War

events.enhanced_description: The Manchus occupied the Liaoning region in northern China and established Shenyang (then known as Mukden) as their capital, marking the proclamation of the Qing dynasty. This event was pivotal in the transition of power in China from the Ming to the Qing dynasty.
events.name: Manchus occupy Liaoning region

events.enhanced_description: The Kohra estate was founded by Babu Himmat Sah, contributing to the socio-political landscape of the region. This establishment reflects the patterns of land ownership and governance in early modern India.
events.name: Kohra estate founded

events.enhanced_description: The shōgun of Japan issued a decree forbidding Japanese citizens from traveling abroad and preventing those already abroad from returning home. This policy marked the beginning of Japan's isolationist period, which would last for over two centuries.
events.name: Shōgun forbids Japanese travel abroad

events.enhanced_description: Emperor Fasilides founded the city of Gondar, which would serve as the capital of Ethiopia for the next two centuries. This establishment marked a significant development in Ethiopian history, influencing its political and cultural landscape.
events.name: Emperor Fasilides founds Gondar

events.enhanced_description: Henry Adams, the first American ancestor of the future U.S. President John Adams, emigrated to Massachusetts, marking the beginning of the Adams family's significant role in American history. This migration reflects the broader patterns of settlement and family lineage in colonial America.
events.name: Henry Adams emigrates to Massachusetts

events.enhanced_description: The Kahal Zur Israel Synagogue was founded in Recife by the Dutch, becoming the first synagogue in the New World. This establishment played a crucial role in the history of Jewish communities in the Americas.
events.name: Kahal Zur Israel Synagogue founded

events.enhanced_description: On January 18, 1636, 'The Duke's Mistress,' the last play by James Shirley, was performed for the first time in London. This performance marked the culmination of Shirley's contributions to English drama during the early 17th century.
events.name: First performance of The Duke's Mistress

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1636, Al Walid ben Zidan, the Sultan of Morocco, was assassinated by French renegades. This event highlighted the political instability in Morocco and the influence of foreign powers in the region.
events.name: Assassination of Al Walid ben Zidan

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1636, Nimi a Lukeni a Nzenze a Ntumba was installed as King Alvaro VI of Kongo, ruling over a region that is now part of Angola. His reign would last until his death in 1641, during a period of significant change in Central Africa.
figures: Nimi a Lukeni a Nzenze a Ntumba
events.name: Installation of Nimi a Lukeni a Nzenze a Ntumba as King Alvaro VI of Kongo

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1636, King Christian IV of Denmark and Norway issued an order mandating that able-bodied beggars be sent to Brinholmen to work on shipbuilding or as galley rowers. This decree was part of his broader efforts to address social issues in his kingdom.
events.name: Order by King Christian IV regarding beggars

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1636, a 'great charter' was granted to the University of Oxford, establishing the Oxford University Press as the second privileged press in England. This marked a significant development in the publishing industry and academic dissemination of knowledge.
events.name: Establishment of Oxford University Press

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1636, Utrecht University was founded in the Dutch Republic, becoming one of the leading institutions of higher education in the Netherlands. Its establishment marked an important milestone in the development of academic scholarship in Europe.
events.name: Founding of Utrecht University

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1636, the nine-month Siege of Schenkenschans concluded when forces of the Dutch Republic successfully recaptured the strategically important fort from the Spanish during the Eighty Years' War. This victory was significant for the Dutch in their struggle for independence.
events.name: Siege of Schenkenschans

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1636, William Pynchon and his men established the settlement of Agawam Plantation, now known as Springfield, Massachusetts. This settlement was negotiated for purchase from the Agawam people, marking an important moment in colonial expansion in New England.
events.name: Establishment of Agawam Plantation

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1636, Roger Williams and other Puritan settlers founded the colony of Providence Plantations, which would later become part of Rhode Island. This colony was established on principles of religious freedom and separation of church and state.
events.name: Founding of Providence Plantations

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1636, the Battle of Tornavento was fought in north-west Italy during the Thirty Years' War, as French and Savoyard forces responded to an attack by Spain. Although the battle ended in a stalemate, it resulted in significant damage to the nearby city of Castano Primo.
events.name: Battle of Tornavento

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1636, the Senate of the Venetian Republic voted overwhelmingly in favor of renewing the charter for Jewish merchants to sell within the city, after a delay of nearly six months. This decision reflected the complex dynamics of commerce and religious tolerance in early modern Venice.
events.name: Renewal of charter for Jewish merchants in Venice

events.enhanced_description: The Pequot War commenced in New England following the killing of John Oldham and his crew during an attack on their ship by allies of the Narragansett Indians at Block Island. This event marked the beginning of a violent conflict between the Pequot tribe and English settlers, significantly impacting Native American populations in the region.

locations.name: Block Island, Rhode Island, United States

events.name: The Pequot War begins

events.enhanced_description: In France, Cardinal Richelieu successfully persuaded King Louis XIII to issue an ordonnance that allowed the French nobility to be excused from military service if they paid a tax. This tax was intended to fund the hiring of paid cavalry, reflecting the shifting dynamics of military obligations in early 17th-century France.
events.name: Cardinal Richelieu's ordonnance

events.enhanced_description: The Spanish forces laid siege to Corbie, a strategic town in northern France, during the Thirty Years' War. This siege was part of the broader conflict involving multiple European powers, highlighting the intense military struggles of the period.
events.name: The Spanish besiege Corbie

events.enhanced_description: The covenant of the Town of Dedham, Massachusetts Bay Colony, was first signed, establishing a framework for governance and community organization. This event is significant in the context of early colonial self-governance in New England.
events.name: Covenant of the Town of Dedham signed

events.enhanced_description: The Great and General Court of the Massachusetts Bay Colony voted to establish New College, which would later be known as Harvard University, marking the foundation of the first institution of higher education in the United States. This event laid the groundwork for the development of higher education in America.
events.name: Establishment of New College (Harvard University)

events.enhanced_description: During the Thirty Years' War, the Battle of Wittstock took place, where a Swedish-allied army achieved a decisive victory over a combined Imperial-Saxon force. This battle was significant in altering the balance of power in the ongoing conflict.
events.name: Battle of Wittstock

events.enhanced_description: On Guy Fawkes Day, English theologian Henry Burton delivered two sermons that were sharply critical of the Anglican bishops, leading to his summons before the Star Chamber. This event exemplified the tensions between religious authority and dissenting voices in early 17th-century England.
events.name: Henry Burton's sermons

events.enhanced_description: The Massachusetts Bay Colony organized three militia regiments to defend against the Pequot Indians, an action recognized as a foundational moment for the United States National Guard. This organization reflected the growing need for structured military defense in colonial America.

locations.name: Massachusetts Bay Colony, Massachusetts, United States

events.name: Massachusetts Bay Colony organizes militia

events.enhanced_description: In 1637, Pierre de Fermat famously made a notation in the margin of a document, claiming to have proof of what would later be known as Fermat's Last Theorem. This assertion would remain unproven for over 350 years, becoming one of the most famous problems in mathematics.
events.name: Fermat's Last Theorem notation

events.enhanced_description: In 1637, René Descartes published his influential work, Discourse on the Method, in Leiden. This text introduced the Cartesian coordinate system and emphasized the importance of rational thought and scientific inquiry, laying the groundwork for modern philosophy and mathematics.
events.name: René Descartes publishes Discourse on the Method

events.enhanced_description: In 1637, France began placing a few missionaries in the Ivory Coast, marking the start of a long-term religious and colonial presence in the region. This early missionary work would eventually lead to significant cultural and religious changes in the area over the following centuries.
events.name: French missionaries in Ivory Coast

events.enhanced_description: In 1637, Scottish army officer Robert Monro published Monro, His Expedition With the Worthy Scots Regiment Called Mac-Keys in London. This work is recognized as the first military history written in English, providing insights into military campaigns and the experiences of soldiers during the period.
events.name: Robert Monro publishes military history

events.enhanced_description: In 1637, Elizabeth Poole became the first female founder of a town in the Americas when she established Taunton, Massachusetts. Her pioneering role in colonial America highlights the contributions of women in early American history.
events.name: Elizabeth Poole founds Taunton

events.enhanced_description: In 1637, Richard Norwood published The Seaman's Practice, a significant work that contributed to the field of navigation and maritime practices. This publication was instrumental for sailors and navigators of the time, enhancing their understanding of sea travel.
events.name: Publication of The Seaman's Practice

events.enhanced_description: The tragicomedy 'Le Cid' by Pierre Corneille was first performed in Paris, marking a significant moment in French literature and theater. This play is often credited with influencing the development of French drama and the genre of tragicomedy.
events.name: Le Cid first performed

events.enhanced_description: The siege of Nagpur concluded with the surrender of Kok Shah, the King of Deogarh, to the Mughal Empire. This event marked a significant expansion of Mughal influence in the region and the consolidation of power in central India.
events.name: Siege of Nagpur ends

events.enhanced_description: John Maurice, Prince of Nassau-Siegen, arrived from the Netherlands to take on the role of Governor of Dutch Brazil, where he would extend the colony's range over the next six years. His governance is noted for its cultural and scientific advancements in the region.
events.name: John Maurice arrives in Dutch Brazil

events.enhanced_description: The Manchu armies completed their invasion of northern Korea, culminating in the surrender of King Injo of the Joseon Kingdom. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics in East Asia, leading to the eventual establishment of the Qing dynasty's influence over Korea.
events.name: Manchu invasion of northern Korea

events.enhanced_description: The phenomenon known as Tulip mania, characterized by the speculative trading of tulip bulbs in the Dutch Republic, collapsed, leading to significant economic repercussions. This event is often cited as one of the first recorded speculative bubbles in history.
events.name: Tulip mania collapses

events.enhanced_description: Ferdinand III ascended to the position of Holy Roman Emperor following the death of his father, Ferdinand II, although his formal coronation would occur later in the year. This transition marked a significant moment in the Habsburg dynasty's influence over European politics.

image.caption: Portrait of Ferdinand III, Holy Roman Emperor, by Frans Luycx.
image.credit: Frans Luycx — [1] .
image.date_qualification: Before 1668; this is a portrait, not a depiction of the 1637 accession event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ferdinand III becomes Holy Roman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: During the Eighty Years' War, the Battle off Lizard Point occurred off the coast of Cornwall, where a Spanish fleet intercepted an Anglo-Dutch merchant convoy, destroying or capturing a significant portion of it. This battle underscored the ongoing naval conflicts between Spain and the Dutch Republic.

locations.name: Lizard Point, Cornwall, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Battle off Lizard Point

events.enhanced_description: The world's first opera house, Teatro San Cassiano, opened in Venice, featuring the premiere of 'L'Andromeda' with music by Francesco Manelli. This event marked a significant development in the history of opera and theatrical performance.
events.name: Teatro San Cassiano opens

events.enhanced_description: The Blessed Virgin was proclaimed Queen of Genoa, reflecting the city's deep religious traditions and the significance of Marian devotion in the region. This proclamation was part of the broader context of Catholicism's influence in Italy during the 17th century.
events.name: The Blessed Virgin proclaimed Queen of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: Plymouth Colony granted the 'tenn menn of Saugust' a new settlement on Cape Cod, which would later be named Sandwich. This event illustrates the ongoing expansion and development of colonial settlements in New England.
events.name: Plymouth Colony grants new settlement

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1637, King Charles I of England issued a proclamation aimed at curbing the emigration of his subjects to the North American colonies. This move was part of his broader efforts to maintain control over the population and suppress dissent during a period of rising tensions between the monarchy and Parliament.
events.name: King Charles I of England issues a proclamation, attempting to stem emigration to the North American colonies

events.enhanced_description: In May 1637, Chinese encyclopedist Song Yingxing published his seminal work, Tiangong Kaiwu ("Exploitation of the Works of Nature"), which is regarded as one of the most valuable encyclopedias of classical China. This comprehensive text covers various aspects of agriculture, industry, and technology, reflecting the advanced knowledge of the time.
events.name: Song Yingxing publishes Tiangong Kaiwu

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1637, during the Pequot War, English settlers led by Captain John Mason, along with their Narragansett and Mohegan allies, attacked a fortified village of the Mashantucket Pequot Tribe near the Mystic River. The assault resulted in the deaths of between 400 and 700 Pequot, primarily women, children, and the elderly, marking a significant and brutal episode in the conflict.
events.name: Pequot War – Mystic massacre

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1637, Captain John Weddell led the first English venture to China, sailing into the ports of Macau and Guangzhou during the late Ming Dynasty. His expedition aimed at establishing trade relations, and he notably brought with him a large shipment of eyeglasses, marking a significant moment in European trade with China.
events.name: Captain John Weddell's venture to China

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1637, after a protracted court battle, King Charles I of England transferred the title of the North American colony of Massachusetts to Sir Ferdinando Gorges, a key figure in the early colonial administration and one of the founders of the Plymouth Council for New England. This decision reflected the ongoing complexities of colonial governance and land rights during this period.
events.name: King Charles I hands over title to Massachusetts

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1637, Adam Olearius, along with Philipp Crusius and Otto Bruggemann, was welcomed by Shah Safi in Isfahan, the capital of the Safavid Empire. Their mission, sent by the Duke of Holstein-Gottorp, aimed to establish a trade agreement, highlighting the growing interest in Persian trade during this era.
events.name: Adam Olearius welcomed by Shah Safi

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1637, during the Eighty Years' War, a Spanish force of 17,000 troops, commanded by Don Fernando de Austria, successfully recaptured the city of Venlo from the Dutch Republic after a five-day siege. This event underscored the ongoing military struggles in the region as both sides vied for control.
events.name: Eighty Years' War: Recapture of Venlo
