events.name: Founding of Sharon, Massachusetts

events.enhanced_description: Around 1650, Istanbul is estimated to have become the largest city in the world, surpassing Beijing. This transition marked a significant moment in urban history, reflecting the city's importance as a cultural and political center in the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Istanbul becomes the largest city in the world

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1650, Louis I, Prince of Anhalt-Köthen, passed away after a reign of over 63 years. His long rule significantly influenced the political landscape of the region, and his death marked a transition in leadership.
events.name: Louis I, Prince of Anhalt-Köthen dies

events.enhanced_description: On January 18, 1650, Cardinal Jules Mazarin, the Chief Minister of France, arrested several nobles, including the Prince de Condé, which incited a rebellion against the Crown. This event was a pivotal moment in the Fronde, a series of civil wars in France that challenged royal authority.
events.name: Mazarin arrests nobles, prompting rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On January 28, 1650, Sultan bin Saif of Oman successfully expelled the Portuguese colonial government from Muscat, ending 35 years of occupation. This event marked a significant turning point in Omani history, restoring local control and sovereignty.
events.name: Sultan bin Saif expels Portuguese from Muscat

events.enhanced_description: The French verse play 'Andromède', commissioned by Cardinal Mazarin and written by Pierre Corneille, premiered at the Théâtre Royal de Bourbon in Paris. The production featured elaborate sets designed by Giacomo Torelli, showcasing the artistic and cultural advancements of the time.
events.name: Premiere of Andromède

events.enhanced_description: On February 13, 1650, Oliver Cromwell's troops bombarded Kiltinan Castle in County Tipperary during their campaign in Ireland. This event marked a significant moment in the conflict between Cromwell's forces and Irish royalists.
events.name: Bombardment of Kiltinan Castle

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1650, Jacob van Kittensteyn succeeded Joan Maetsuycker as the Dutch Governor of Zeylan, now known as Sri Lanka. His governance was part of the Dutch colonial efforts in South Asia during the 17th century.
events.name: Jacob van Kittensteyn becomes Governor of Zeylan

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1650, João Rodrigues de Vasconcelos, the Portuguese Count of Castelo Melhor, was appointed as the new Governor of Brazil. His leadership came during a period of significant colonial expansion and conflict in the region.
events.name: João Rodrigues de Vasconcelos becomes Governor of Brazil

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Kilkenny concluded on March 28, 1650, when royalist Sir Walter Butler surrendered the city to Oliver Cromwell's forces after six days of intense conflict. This event was pivotal in the English Civil War's Irish campaign.
events.name: Siege of Kilkenny ends

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Carbisdale commenced on April 27, 1650, when a Royalist army invaded mainland Scotland from the Orkney Islands. The Royalists faced defeat at the hands of a Covenanter army, marking a significant moment in the Scottish Civil War.
events.name: Battle of Carbisdale begins

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1650, during the Siege of Clonmel, a quarter of the New Model Army was trapped and killed, highlighting the fierce resistance faced by Oliver Cromwell's forces in Ireland.
events.name: Siege of Clonmel

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1650, the Harvard Corporation was established as the more powerful of the two administrative boards of Harvard University, making it the first legal corporation in the Americas. This marked a significant development in the governance of higher education in the New World.
events.name: Establishment of the Harvard Corporation

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1650, Charles II arrived in Scotland at Garmouth, the only kingdom that had accepted him as ruler. This marked a significant moment in his efforts to reclaim the throne during the tumultuous period of the English Civil War.
events.name: Charles II arrives in Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1650, Italian priest and astronomer Gerolamo Sersale created an extremely detailed lunar map during a full moon in Naples. This map was later engraved and reproduced, contributing to the field of astronomy.
events.name: Gerolamo Sersale draws lunar map

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1650, after completing his invasion of Ireland, General Oliver Cromwell crossed from Northumberland at Berwick-upon-Tweed into Berwickshire, initiating military actions against the Kingdom of Scotland as he led his troops toward Edinburgh.
events.name: Cromwell begins war against Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On July 29, 1650, William II, Prince of Orange, attempted to conquer the rest of the Netherlands and staged a coup d'état against the Dutch Republic. This action reflected the ongoing power struggles within the region during the 17th century.
events.name: William II's coup attempt

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1650, Colonel George Monck formed Monck's Regiment of Foot, which would become the forerunner of the Coldstream Guards. This regiment played a crucial role in the military history of England.
events.name: Formation of Monck's Regiment of Foot

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1650, the Kolumbo volcano on Santorini experienced a massive eruption, classified as a Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) of 6. This eruption had significant geological and environmental impacts on the region.

image.caption: NOAA map of the Kolumbo submarine crater and nearby volcanic cones.
image.credit: NOAA graphics — https://oceanexplorer.noaa.gov/explorations/06blacksea/logs/summary_thera/summary_thera.html
image.date_qualification: A map of the Kolumbo volcanic area, not a depiction of the 1650 eruption. Image date: 2006-08-23.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Eruption of Kolumbo volcano

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1650, Henry Robinson opened his Office of Addresses and Encounters in Threadneedle Street, London. This establishment served as an early form of employment exchange, reflecting the evolving economic landscape of the time.
events.name: Opening of Office of Addresses and Encounters

events.enhanced_description: On October 17, 1650, members of the Parliament of Scotland signed the Western Remonstrance, condemning the recognition of Charles II as King of Scotland and pledging allegiance to Oliver Cromwell. This act was a significant political statement during the English Civil War.
events.name: Signing of the Western Remonstrance

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1650, Queen Christina of Sweden held an elaborate coronation ceremony at Jacobsdal Castle near Stockholm. This event marked a significant moment in her reign, which had been delayed due to the war with Denmark-Norway.
events.name: Coronation of Queen Christina of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1650, the Commonwealth of England passed a law prohibiting trade between English merchants and colonies that sided with Charles II over Oliver Cromwell. This law specifically targeted Virginia, the Somers Isles, Barbados, and Antigua, marking a significant economic measure during the civil unrest.
events.name: Trade prohibition law passed

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1650, William III of Orange was born, becoming Prince of the House of Orange at the moment of his birth. His birth marked a significant moment in Dutch history, as he would later play a crucial role in the political landscape of the Netherlands.
events.name: Birth of William III of Orange

events.enhanced_description: On December 14, 1650, Anne Greene was hanged at Oxford Castle for infanticide after concealing an illegitimate stillbirth. Remarkably, she revived the following day in the dissection room and was later pardoned, living until 1659.
events.name: Execution of Anne Greene

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1650, Thomas Cooper was hanged as a Royalist rebel in London. His execution underscored the tensions and divisions within England during the Civil War.
events.name: Execution of Thomas Cooper

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1651, Charles II was crowned King of Scots at Scone, marking his first crowning. This event was significant in the context of the English Civil War and the ongoing struggles for power in Britain.
events.name: Charles II crowned King of Scots

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Upton, fought in early 1651, saw Scottish forces under Major General Edward Massey defeated by the English Parliamentarians led by John Lambert. This defeat was pivotal, clearing the way for the Parliamentarian advance towards Worcester.
events.name: Battle of Upton

events.enhanced_description: In October 1651, an English diplomatic team led by Oliver St John traveled to The Hague to negotiate an alliance between the Commonwealth of England and the Dutch Republic. This diplomatic effort was crucial in shaping the political landscape of Europe during the period.
events.name: Diplomatic negotiations in The Hague

events.enhanced_description: The Keian Uprising, an insurrection against the Tokugawa shogunate, failed in 1651, reflecting the ongoing struggles for power in Japan during this period. The uprising's failure further solidified the shogunate's control over the country.
events.name: Keian Uprising fails

events.enhanced_description: In 1651, the first coffee house in England opened in Oxford, marking the beginning of a new social trend that would spread across Europe. This establishment became a hub for intellectual discussion and social interaction, reflecting the growing popularity of coffee in European culture.
events.name: First coffee house in England

events.enhanced_description: The Madanmohan-jiu Temple was constructed in 1651 in Samta, a village in the Howrah district of West Bengal, India. This temple is significant in the cultural and religious landscape of the region, reflecting the architectural styles and spiritual practices of the time.
events.name: Madanmohan-jiu Temple built

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1651, the Parliament of Boroa took place in Chile, where Spanish and Mapuche authorities convened to renew the fragile peace established in previous parliaments. This meeting was crucial in maintaining a tenuous balance between the two groups during a period of conflict.
events.name: Parliament of Boroa in Chile

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1651, St. Peter's Flood struck the North Sea, causing catastrophic flooding along the German coast and resulting in thousands of deaths. This natural disaster highlighted the vulnerability of coastal communities to storm surges.
events.name: St. Peter's Flood

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1651, another storm tide from St. Peter's Flood struck the Netherlands, leading to severe flooding in Amsterdam. The disaster underscored the ongoing challenges faced by the Dutch in managing their low-lying geography.
events.name: St. Peter's Flood in the Netherlands

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1651, Count Per Brahe the Younger founded the town of Kajaani in Finland. This establishment was part of broader efforts to develop the region and enhance its strategic importance within the Swedish Empire.
events.name: Founding of Kajaani

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1651, Prince Aisin Gioro Fulin became the Shunzhi Emperor of China at the age of 13, following a regency after his father's death. His ascension marked the beginning of a new era in the Qing dynasty, which would see significant changes in Chinese governance.
events.name: Shunzhi Emperor ascends the throne

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1651, the Spanish ship San José, laden with silver, wrecked on the southern coast of Chile due to strong winds. The surviving crew faced dire consequences as they were killed by indigenous Cuncos, illustrating the dangers of maritime trade and colonial encounters.
events.name: Wreck of the San José

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1651, Shunzhi, the Emperor of China, issued an edict promising to purge corruption from the government. This declaration was part of his efforts to consolidate power and restore integrity within the Qing administration.

image.caption: Portrait of the Shunzhi Emperor in court dress, a 17th-century painting.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — https://www.dpm.org.cn/court/lineage/226262.html
image.date_qualification: 17th century (image date metadata: 1650; the image is not dated to the 1651 edict).
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Shunzhi Emperor's edict against corruption

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1651, Thomas Hobbes published his influential political treatise, Leviathan, in England. This work laid the foundation for modern political philosophy, advocating for a strong central authority to avoid chaos and maintain social order.
events.name: Publication of Leviathan

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1651, General Marcin Kalinowski of Poland achieved victory at the Battle of Kopychyntsi against Zaporozhian Cossacks led by Asand Demka. This battle was part of the Khmelnytsky Uprising, a significant conflict in Eastern European history.
events.name: Battle of Kopychyntsi

events.enhanced_description: On May 21, 1651, the Sovereign Military Order of Malta purchased several Caribbean islands from France's Compagnie des Îles de l'Amérique. This acquisition was part of the Order's efforts to expand its influence and economic power in the New World.
events.name: Purchase of Caribbean islands by the Order of Malta

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1651, during the Franco-Spanish War, a squadron of Spanish galleys led by John of Austria the Younger captured the French galleon Lion Couronné off the coast of Formentera. This event underscored the naval conflicts between Spain and France during this period.
events.name: Capture of Lion Couronné

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1651, the Battle of Berestechko took place, one of the largest land battles of the 17th century, involving approximately 205,000 troops. The Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth Army achieved a decisive victory over the Zaporozhian Cossacks, significantly impacting the Khmelnytsky Uprising.
events.name: Battle of Berestechko

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1651, the Battle of Inverkeithing occurred, where the English Parliamentarian New Model Army, commanded by Major-General John Lambert, defeated a Scottish Covenanter army led by Sir John Brown of Fordell. This battle was a crucial moment in the English Civil War, solidifying Parliamentarian control.
events.name: Battle of Inverkeithing

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1651, the Battle of Warrington Bridge marked the last victory of Scotland over England, where the troops of King Charles II forced the retreat of English Commonwealth forces. This battle was significant in the context of the ongoing conflicts between the two nations.
events.name: Battle of Warrington Bridge

events.enhanced_description: The Onfall of Alyth occurred in early 1651 when members of Scotland's Committee of States were betrayed to English forces. Key Scottish leaders, including the Earls of Leven and Crawford, were captured, significantly weakening the Scottish resistance against the English Parliament.
events.name: Onfall of Alyth

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1651, the siege of Dundee concluded with the English Parliamentarian army, led by General Monck, decisively defeating the Covenanters. This battle marked the end of significant military engagements in the Wars of the Three Kingdoms in Scotland.

image.caption: A 1693 drawing of Dundee, Angus, Scotland, by John Slezer.
image.credit: John Slezer — This image is available from the National Library of Scotland From John Slezer's Theatrum Scotiae [1]
image.date_qualification: Depicts Dundee in 1693, 42 years after the siege concluded on 1 September 1651.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Siege of Dundee

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1651, Kösem Sultan was assassinated by her daughter-in-law, Turhan Sultan, in a power struggle within the Ottoman Empire. This event highlighted the intense political intrigue and rivalry within the imperial court during this period.
events.name: Assassination of Kösem Sultan

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Worcester, fought on September 3, 1651, marked the final confrontation of the English Civil War. Charles II, leading a largely Scottish army, faced defeat against the New Model Army commanded by Oliver Cromwell, leading to his subsequent flight and the consolidation of Parliamentarian control over England.
events.name: Battle of Worcester

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1651, laws were enacted in Massachusetts prohibiting the poor from adopting extravagant styles of dress. This legislation reflected the Puritanical values of the colony, aiming to maintain social order and discourage ostentation.
events.name: Laws forbidding excessive dress styles

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1651, Charles II of England fled to France after his defeat at the Battle of Worcester. This escape marked a significant moment in his life, leading to years of exile before his eventual restoration to the throne.
events.name: Charles II escapes to France

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1651, the Manx Rebellion concluded with the surrender of the Isle of Man to Oliver Cromwell's forces. The Countess of Derby negotiated terms for safe passage for herself and her family, marking a significant moment in the consolidation of Cromwell's power.
events.name: End of the Manx Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1651, Qing dynasty forces led by Shang Kexi captured Guangzhou from the Southern Ming, resulting in a massacre that claimed the lives of approximately 70,000 people over 11 days. This event underscored the brutal nature of the conflict during this period in Chinese history.
events.name: Capture of Guangzhou

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1651, Castle Cornet, the last royalist stronghold in the Third English Civil War, surrendered to Parliamentarian forces. This event marked the effective end of royalist resistance in the Channel Islands.
events.name: Surrender of Castle Cornet

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Plymouth was a naval engagement during the First Anglo-Dutch War, where a fleet from the Commonwealth of England attacked a Dutch convoy. The Dutch fleet, commanded by Vice-Commodore Michiel de Ruyter, managed to escape despite being outnumbered.
events.name: First Anglo-Dutch War: Battle of Plymouth

events.enhanced_description: The Guo Huaiyi Rebellion was a peasant uprising against Dutch colonial rule in Taiwan. The rebellion was suppressed within four days, highlighting the tensions between local populations and colonial authorities.
events.name: The Guo Huaiyi Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: The Great Fire of Oulu devastated the town, destroying nearly all bourgeois houses, provision warehouses, and the drawbridge of Oulu Castle. This catastrophic event marked a significant moment in the town's history, leading to reconstruction efforts.
events.name: The Great Fire of Oulu

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of the Kentish Knock was a naval engagement in the North Sea during the First Anglo-Dutch War. The battle resulted in a Dutch withdrawal, showcasing the ongoing naval rivalry between England and the Netherlands.
events.name: First Anglo-Dutch War: Battle of the Kentish Knock

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Dungeness was a significant naval battle during the First Anglo-Dutch War, resulting in a Dutch victory over the English Royal Navy. This victory allowed the Dutch to gain control over the English Channel.

image.caption: Retrospective portrait of English naval commander Robert Blake, painted by Henry Perronet Briggs.
image.credit: Henry Perronet Briggs — EXTRACTED FROM: en:File:Robert Blake, General at Sea, 1598-1657 RMG BHC2558.tiff ; original file at: http://collections.rmg.co.uk/collections/objects/14032
image.date_qualification: Painted and commissioned in 1829, approximately 177 years after the battle; it is a retrospective portrait, not a contemporary event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Dungeness

events.enhanced_description: The defeat at the Battle of Dungeness prompted the Commonwealth of England to undertake significant reforms of its navy. This event underscored the challenges faced by England in the ongoing conflict with the Dutch.
events.name: First Anglo-Dutch War: Defeat at the Battle of Dungeness

events.enhanced_description: The Swiss Peasant War began when magistrates in Lucerne refused to address grievances from financially distressed peasants. This conflict highlighted the socio-economic tensions in 17th-century Switzerland.

image.caption: Edict of the Bern city authorities devaluing the Batzen, a copper coin.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Immediate image source: Muster, E.: Texte und Bilder zum Grossen Schweizerischen Bauernkrieg von 1653 ("Texts and images on the great Swiss peasant war of 1653"). Secondary source: State archive of Berne.
image.date_qualification: Contemporary official document identified as the immediate cause of the Swiss peasant war; it is not a depiction of the revolt itself. Document date given as December 2, 1652 (Gregorian); November 22, 1652 (Julian).
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Swiss Peasant War

events.enhanced_description: The Morning Star Rebellion erupted in Närke, Sweden, as peasants revolted against Queen Christina's rule. The rebellion was brutally suppressed, leading to the execution of its leader, Olof Mårtensson.
events.name: Morning Star Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: In 1653, Marcello Malpighi, an Italian pioneer in the field of microscopical anatomy, received his medical degree. His groundbreaking work laid the foundation for modern histology and significantly advanced the understanding of human anatomy.
events.name: Marcello Malpighi Becomes Doctor of Medicine

events.enhanced_description: In 1653, Stephen Bachiler, a clergyman and early advocate for the separation of church and state, returned to England after spending over 20 years in the Massachusetts Bay Colony. His experiences abroad influenced his views on religious freedom.
events.name: Stephen Bachiler Returns to England

events.enhanced_description: In 1653, the gardens surrounding the Taj Mahal mausoleum were completed in Agra. These gardens are an integral part of the monument's design, symbolizing paradise on earth and enhancing the beauty of this iconic structure.
events.name: Completion of Taj Mahal Gardens

events.enhanced_description: The Coonan Cross Oath was a pivotal moment for the Eastern Church in India, as it marked their declaration of independence from Portuguese colonial influence. This event was significant in shaping the identity of the Indian Christian community.
events.name: Coonan Cross Oath

events.enhanced_description: New Amsterdam, now known as New York City, was granted municipal rights through a charter from Governor Peter Stuyvesant. This event marked an important step in the development of the city’s governance.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: New Amsterdam Receives Municipal Rights

events.enhanced_description: Cardinal Mazarin returned to Paris from exile, reestablishing his influence in French politics during a tumultuous period marked by the Fronde. His return signaled a shift in the power dynamics of the French court.
events.name: Cardinal Mazarin Returns to Paris

events.enhanced_description: Peasants from the Entlebuch valley gathered at Heiligkreuz to organize a tax strike against the authorities in Lucerne. This assembly was a key moment in the Swiss Peasant War, which saw increasing unrest among the rural population.
events.name: Swiss Peasant War of 1653

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Leghorn, a Dutch fleet achieved victory over the English in the Mediterranean. However, the Dutch commander Johan van Galen succumbed to his wounds shortly after the battle, marking a bittersweet victory.
events.name: Battle of Leghorn

events.enhanced_description: Oliver Cromwell expelled the Rump Parliament in a decisive move that reshaped the political landscape of England. This action was part of Cromwell's broader efforts to consolidate power during the Commonwealth.
events.name: Oliver Cromwell Expels the Rump Parliament

events.enhanced_description: The Great Fire of Marlborough devastated the town, destroying 224 houses and significant textile businesses. This disaster had a profound impact on the local economy and community.
events.name: The Great Fire of Marlborough

events.enhanced_description: Ferdinand IV was elected King of the Romans, positioning him to succeed his father as Holy Roman Emperor. Unfortunately, he would not live to fulfill this role, dying shortly thereafter.
events.name: Ferdinand IV Elected King of the Romans

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of the Gabbard was a significant naval engagement during the First Anglo-Dutch War, where the English navy defeated the Dutch fleet after a two-day battle. This victory was crucial for England's naval dominance.
events.name: Battle of the Gabbard

events.enhanced_description: The Swiss Peasant War concluded with the suppression of the last rebels in the Entlebuch Valley by Swiss Army troops under Sebastian Peregrin Zwyer. This marked the end of significant peasant unrest in Switzerland.
events.name: End of the Swiss Peasant War

events.enhanced_description: Barebone's Parliament, named after Puritan member Praise-God Barebone, convened in London with the aim of passing laws for the Commonwealth of England. This assembly represented a unique moment in the political landscape of the time.
events.name: Barebone's Parliament Opens

events.enhanced_description: John Thurloe was appointed as Oliver Cromwell's head of intelligence, playing a crucial role in the administration of the Commonwealth. His work in intelligence would have lasting impacts on the governance of England.
events.name: John Thurloe Becomes Cromwell's Head of Intelligence

events.enhanced_description: Frederick William, Elector of Brandenburg, reaffirmed the nobility's tax exemptions in exchange for a significant financial grant. This agreement solidified the power dynamics between the nobility and the elector.
events.name: Frederick William Reaffirms Nobility's Tax Exemptions

events.enhanced_description: The petite post, a revolutionary system of postage using prepaid labels and post boxes, was inaugurated in Paris by Jean-Jacques Renouard de Villayer. This innovation significantly improved mail delivery within the city.
events.name: Inauguration of the Petite Post

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Scheveningen marked the final naval confrontation of the First Anglo-Dutch War, where the English Navy achieved a tactical victory over the Dutch fleet after three days of intense fighting.
events.name: Battle of Scheveningen

events.enhanced_description: A violent storm off the west coast of Scotland resulted in the sinking of the English Navy warship Swan and several commandeered merchant ships. The disaster claimed the lives of 23 crew members from the ship Speedwell.
events.name: Storm Sinks English Navy Ships

events.enhanced_description: The Mughal Empire's third and final attempt to recapture Kandahar from the Safavid Empire ended in failure, despite the mobilization of 70,000 soldiers under Prince Dara Shukoh. This defeat marked a significant setback for the Mughal ambitions in the region.
events.name: Mughal Empire's Failed Attempt to Recapture Kandahar

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1653, the Zemsky Sobor, the national assembly of the Russian Empire, convened in Moscow to declare war against the Kingdom of Poland. This assembly marked a significant moment in Russian political history as it sought to unify the nation against external threats.
events.name: Zemsky Sobor Session Opening

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1653, the Battle of Bordeaux took place in the Gironde estuary, where Spanish warships, commanded by Álvaro de Bazán y Manrique de Lara, decisively defeated the French fleet led by César, Duke of Vendôme. This battle was a crucial engagement in the ongoing Franco-Spanish War.
figures: Álvaro de Bazán y Manrique de Lara
events.name: Battle of Bordeaux

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1653, Erdeni Bumba, the chief consort of the Shunzhi Emperor of China, was demoted from her position as empress to that of a concubine. This event reflected the complex dynamics of power and favor within the imperial court during the Qing dynasty.
events.name: Demotion of Erdeni Bumba

events.enhanced_description: On October 29, 1653, Pierre-Esprit Radisson, a French Canadian teenager, escaped captivity from a Mohawk raiding party in what is now New York. His experiences would later contribute to his significant role in the fur trade and exploration of North America.

locations.name: New York, New York, United States

events.name: Escape of Pierre-Esprit Radisson

events.enhanced_description: In November 1653, John Casor, an African servant, left Anthony Johnson's farm after claiming his indenture had expired. This led to a landmark court case that would establish a precedent for the status of African Americans in colonial Virginia.
events.name: John Casor's Landmark Case

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1653, the Battle of Arronches occurred near the town of Arronches, where the Portuguese Army successfully outflanked and defeated a larger Spanish force. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts during the Portuguese Restoration War.
events.name: Battle of Arronches

events.enhanced_description: On November 16, 1653, the Krishnanattam, a series of eight dance dramas depicting the life of the Hindu god Krishna, was completed by Mana Veda, the Zamorin of Calicut. This artistic achievement is significant in the cultural heritage of Kerala.
events.name: Completion of Krishnanattam

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1653, Jacques Dyel du Parquet completed his payments to become the exclusive owner of the Caribbean islands of Martinique, Grenada, Saint Lucia, and the Grenadines. This acquisition was pivotal in the French colonial expansion in the Caribbean.
events.name: Jacques Dyel du Parquet's Ownership of Caribbean Islands

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1653, the Moti Masjid, an exquisite mosque made entirely of white marble, was dedicated by Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan within the Agra Fort. This architectural marvel exemplifies the grandeur of Mughal architecture.
events.name: Dedication of Moti Masjid

events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1653, Barebone's Parliament, a unique assembly during the Commonwealth of England, voted to dissolve itself after passing several laws. This marked a significant moment in the turbulent political landscape of England during this period.
events.name: Dissolution of Barebone's Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1653, the Instrument of Government was adopted in England, establishing the first written constitution of Britain. This document marked the beginning of Oliver Cromwell's rule as Lord Protector, reshaping the governance of England, Scotland, and Ireland.
events.name: Instrument of Government

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1654, Jaswant Singh of Marwar was elevated to the title of Maharaja by Emperor Shah Jahan. This elevation reflected the political dynamics and alliances within the Mughal Empire during this period.
events.name: Elevation of Jaswant Singh

events.enhanced_description: On January 11, 1654, during the Arauco War, the Battle of Río Bueno took place in southern Chile, where Indigenous Huilliche warriors successfully routed Spanish troops from Fort Nacimiento. This battle highlighted the resistance of Indigenous peoples against colonial forces.

locations.name: Río Bueno, Los Ríos Region, Chile

events.name: Battle of Río Bueno

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1654, Portugal recaptured the city of Recife from the Netherlands after a prolonged siege during the Dutch-Portuguese War. This event marked the end of Dutch rule in Brazil, significantly altering the colonial landscape.
events.name: Recapture of Recife

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1654, Spanish troops led by Don Gabriel de Rojas y Figueroa captured Fort Rocher, a pirate-controlled base on the Caribbean island of Tortuga. This victory was part of Spain's efforts to regain control over Caribbean territories.
figures: Don Gabriel de Rojas y Figueroa
events.name: Capture of Fort Rocher

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1654, the Battle of Tullich occurred in Aberdeenshire, Scotland, during Glencairn's rising, a royalist revolt against the Commonwealth of England. The battle ended indecisively, reflecting the ongoing conflict between royalists and parliamentarians.
events.name: Battle of Tullich

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1654, the Treaty of Pereyaslav was concluded in the city of Pereyaslav, marking a significant agreement between the Cossacks of the Zaporozhian Host and Tsar Alexey I of Russia. This treaty solidified the alliance between the Cossacks and Russia following the Khmelnytsky Uprising.
events.name: Treaty of Pereyaslav

events.enhanced_description: On February 19, 1674, England and the Netherlands signed the Treaty of Westminster, effectively ending the Third Anglo-Dutch War. The treaty's provisions were implemented gradually, marking a significant diplomatic resolution between the two nations.
events.name: Treaty of Westminster

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1654, a commercial treaty between England and Sweden was signed, facilitating trade and economic relations between the two nations. This agreement was part of the broader context of European diplomacy during the mid-17th century.
events.name: Commercial Treaty between England and Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1654, Oliver Cromwell established a union between England and Scotland, which included Scottish representation in the Parliament of England. This union was a significant political development during the Commonwealth period.
events.name: Union between England and Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1654, Cromwell's Act of Grace was proclaimed at the Mercat Cross in Edinburgh, offering pardons to those who had opposed the Commonwealth. This act was part of Cromwell's efforts to stabilize his rule in Scotland.
events.name: Cromwell's Act of Grace

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1654, Otto von Guericke demonstrated the power of atmospheric pressure using his vacuum pump and the Magdeburg hemispheres before Ferdinand III, Holy Roman Emperor, in Regensburg. This demonstration was pivotal in advancing the understanding of physics and the nature of vacuums.

image.caption: Title page of Otto von Guericke’s *Experimenta Nova (ut vocantur) Magdeburgica de Vacuo Spatio*.
image.credit: Otto von Guericke — https://libserv.aip.org/ipac20/ipac.jsp?session=F663470U76581.251418&profile=rev-nbl&source=~!horizon&view=subscriptionsummary&uri=full=3100006~!44257~!5&ri=1&aspect=power&menu=search&ipp=20&spp=20&staffonly=&term=guericke&index=.GW&uindex=&aspect=power&menu=search&ri=1
image.date_qualification: The image description and image_date identify the copy as 1672, 18 years after the stated event date; it is not an event photograph or a contemporaneous depiction of the demonstration.

events.name: Otto von Guericke's Demonstration

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1654, Louis XIV was crowned King of France in a lavish ceremony at Reims Cathedral, symbolizing the divine right of kings and the centralization of royal power in France. This event marked the beginning of his long reign, which would significantly shape French history and culture.
events.name: Louis XIV of France is crowned at Reims

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1654, Charles X Gustav ascended to the Swedish throne following the abdication of his cousin Christina, who converted to Catholicism shortly thereafter. His reign would be marked by military conflicts and territorial expansion.
events.name: Charles X Gustav succeeds Christina on the Swedish throne

events.enhanced_description: The Thirteen Years' War began on July 5, 1654, as the Russian Army camped outside Smolensk, initiating a conflict with Poland over control of Ukraine. This war would significantly alter the balance of power in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Thirteen Years' War starts between Russia and Poland

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1654, Peter Vowell and John Gerard were executed in London for their involvement in a plot to assassinate Oliver Cromwell, the Lord Protector of England. Their execution underscored the tensions and political strife of the period.
events.name: Execution of Peter Vowell and John Gerard

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Shklow occurred on August 12, 1654, during a total solar eclipse, marking one of the first significant clashes of the Russo-Polish War. The Russian forces faced a retreat, highlighting the challenges they encountered in the conflict.
events.name: Battle of Shklow

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1654, Oliver Cromwell initiated the Western Design, appointing Admiral William Penn to lead an expedition against Spanish territories in the Caribbean. This marked the beginning of the Anglo-Spanish War, which would last until after the English Restoration.
events.name: Oliver Cromwell launches the Western Design

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1654, a group of 23 Sephardic Jews arrived in New Amsterdam as refugees from Brazil, establishing the foundation for what would become the second largest urban Jewish community in history, and leading to the formation of Congregation Shearith Israel, the first synagogue in North America.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Jewish arrival in New Amsterdam

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1654, Russian forces achieved a decisive victory against the Polish Army in the Battle of Shepeleviche, further asserting their dominance in the ongoing conflict of the Russo-Polish War.
events.name: Battle of Shepeleviche

events.enhanced_description: The First Protectorate Parliament convened on September 3, 1654, marking a significant moment in the governance of England under Oliver Cromwell's rule. This assembly aimed to establish a new political order following the English Civil War.
events.name: First Protectorate Parliament assembles

events.enhanced_description: On September 12, 1654, Oliver Cromwell ordered the exclusion of 120 members of Parliament who were deemed hostile to his rule. This action reflected the ongoing political tensions and Cromwell's efforts to consolidate power.
events.name: Cromwell orders exclusion of hostile members from Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1654, after a prolonged siege lasting nearly three months, Smolensk fell to the Russian Army. This victory was a pivotal moment in the Thirteen Years' War, significantly impacting the conflict's trajectory.
events.name: Smolensk falls to the Russian Army

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1654, the Delft Explosion devastated the city, resulting in over 100 fatalities, including the renowned painter Carel Fabritius. This tragic event highlighted the dangers of munitions storage and had a lasting impact on the city's history.
events.name: Delft Explosion

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1654, Ferdinand Maria was crowned Elector of Bavaria, establishing an absolutist style of leadership that would influence the governance of Germany for years to come. His reign was marked by efforts to strengthen the state's power and stability.
events.name: Ferdinand Maria crowned Elector of Bavaria

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1654, Blaise Pascal experienced a profound mystical vision that deeply influenced his philosophical and religious beliefs. This event marked a turning point in his life, leading him to focus on theology and the defense of Christianity.
events.name: Blaise Pascal experiences mystical vision

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1654, Sir William Petty was awarded the contract by the Commonwealth of England to conduct a comprehensive survey of Ireland. This survey would later become a foundational work in the field of statistics and land management.
events.name: William Petty wins contract for survey of Ireland

events.enhanced_description: On December 14, 1654, Jerónimo de Ataíde was appointed as the new Governor-General of Brazil, succeeding João Rodrigues de Vasconcelos e Sousa. His administration would face challenges in managing colonial affairs and relations with indigenous peoples.
events.name: Jerónimo de Ataíde becomes Governor-General of Brazil

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1654, an English Navy fleet, commanded by Admiral William Penn, set sail from Portsmouth to launch a surprise attack on Spanish colonies in the Caribbean. This operation was part of Oliver Cromwell's broader strategy to expand English influence overseas.
events.name: English Navy fleet departs for the Caribbean

events.enhanced_description: In 1655, Stephan Farffler, a paraplegic watchmaker from Nuremberg, innovatively designed the world's first self-propelling chair. This remarkable device utilized a three-wheel chassis and a system of cranks and cogwheels, resembling a hand bike more than a traditional wheelchair.
events.name: Stephan Farffler builds the world's first self-propelling chair

events.enhanced_description: The Bibliotheca Thysiana, constructed in 1655, stands as the only surviving 17th-century building in the Netherlands specifically designed as a library. This architectural gem reflects the cultural and intellectual aspirations of its time.
events.name: Erection of the Bibliotheca Thysiana

events.enhanced_description: In 1655, a plague outbreak resulted in the deaths of 20 individuals, highlighting the ongoing public health challenges of the period. The specific location and context of this outbreak remain undocumented.

locations.name: Unknown location, Unknown region, Unknown country

events.name: Plague outbreak

events.enhanced_description: In 1655, Frederick III of Denmark-Norway transferred control of the Faroe Islands to Christoffer Gabel and his son, establishing a governance that would last until 1709. This decision was part of broader administrative changes in the Danish realm.
events.name: Frederick III gives control of the Faroe Islands

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1655, English Admiral Robert Blake led his fleet to a decisive victory against the Barbary pirates at Porto Farina, near Tunis. This battle was part of the broader conflict between England and the Barbary States, showcasing Blake's naval prowess and the growing power of the English navy.
events.name: Battle of Porto Farina

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1655, Fabio Chigi was elected as Pope Alexander VII, succeeding Pope Innocent X. His papacy would be marked by efforts to strengthen the Catholic Church's influence and address various political and religious challenges of the time.
events.name: Pope Alexander VII succeeds Pope Innocent X

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1655, the Piedmontese Easter Massacre occurred when Charles Emmanuel II, Duke of Savoy, ordered the slaughter of approximately 1,500 Waldensians, including men, women, and children. This tragic event highlighted the religious persecution faced by the Waldensians and was later memorialized in John Milton's sonnet.
events.name: Piedmontese Easter Massacre of the Waldensians

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1655, the Dutch West India Company rejected Governor Peter Stuyvesant's request to exclude Jews from settling in New Amsterdam. This decision marked a significant moment in the history of religious tolerance in the early American colonies.
events.name: Dutch West India Company denies Peter Stuyvesant's request

events.enhanced_description: On April 28, 1655, Admiral Robert Blake's fleet inflicted significant damage on the arsenal of the Bey of Tunis. This action was part of Blake's campaign against the Barbary pirates, further asserting English naval power in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Admiral Blake damages the arsenal of the Bey of Tunis

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1655, during the Anglo-Spanish War, forces of the English Protectorate led by William Penn and Robert Venables successfully captured Jamaica from Spanish control. This invasion marked a significant expansion of English influence in the Caribbean.
events.name: Invasion of Jamaica

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1655, Adriana Nooseman-van de Bergh became the first actress to perform in a theater in Amsterdam, marking a significant milestone in the history of performing arts in the Netherlands. Her performance paved the way for the acceptance of women in theatrical roles.
events.name: First actress in Amsterdam theater

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1655, the Amsterdam Town Hall, now known as the Royal Palace, was inaugurated. This architectural masterpiece symbolized the wealth and power of Amsterdam during the Dutch Golden Age.
events.name: Inauguration of the Amsterdam Town Hall

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1655, the Jewish community in New Amsterdam petitioned for a separate cemetery, reflecting their growing presence and the need for designated burial grounds in the colony. This petition was a significant step towards religious and cultural recognition.
events.name: Jews in New Amsterdam petition for cemetery

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1655, Dutch troops captured Fort Assahudi on the island of Seram, part of the Maluku Islands in Indonesia. This event was part of the Dutch colonial expansion in the region, aiming to control the lucrative spice trade.
events.name: Dutch troops capture Fort Assahudi Seram

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1655, during the Russo-Polish War, the Russian army entered Vilnius, the capital of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and held it for six years. This occupation was a significant event in the conflict between Russia and Poland.
events.name: Russian army enters Vilnius

events.enhanced_description: In August 1655, Governor Peter Stuyvesant of New Netherland launched an attack against the New Sweden colony in Delaware. This military action was part of the larger conflict for control over North American territories between the Dutch and the Swedes.
events.name: Stuyvesant attacks New Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On August 9, 1655, Lord Protector Oliver Cromwell divided England into 11 districts, each governed by major-generals. This administrative change aimed to strengthen control over the country and enforce Puritan moral standards.
events.name: Cromwell divides England into districts

events.enhanced_description: On August 28, 1655, New Amsterdam's Governor Peter Stuyvesant barred colonial Jews from military service, reflecting the tensions and prejudices of the time. This decision was part of a broader pattern of discrimination against Jewish settlers in the colony.
events.name: New Amsterdam bars Jews from military service

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1655, Swedish King Karl X Gustav occupied Warsaw, Poland, during the Second Northern War. This occupation was a pivotal moment in the conflict, leading to significant territorial changes in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Karl X Gustav occupies Warsaw

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1655, Peter Stuyvesant successfully recaptured Fort Casimir from the Swedish forces, solidifying Dutch control over the region. This victory was part of the broader struggle between the Dutch and Swedish colonies in North America.
events.name: Stuyvesant recaptures Fort Casimir

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1655, a tragic massacre of Jews occurred in Lublin, Poland, during the chaos of the Second Northern War. This event underscored the vulnerability of Jewish communities in times of conflict and persecution.
events.name: Massacre of Jews in Lublin

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1655, Swedish King Karl X Gustav occupied Kraków during the Second Northern War. This occupation was part of Sweden's aggressive military campaign in Poland, significantly impacting the region's political landscape.
events.name: Karl X Gustav occupies Kraków

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1655, England and France signed military and economic treaties, strengthening their alliance during a time of European conflict. These agreements were crucial for both nations as they navigated the complexities of 17th-century geopolitics.
events.name: England and France sign treaties

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1655, Lord Protector Oliver Cromwell announced measures against the Laudian party, a faction within the Church of England. These measures were part of Cromwell's broader efforts to consolidate power and enforce Puritan reforms.
events.name: Cromwell announces measures against Laudian party

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1655, the city of Middelburg in the Netherlands forbade the construction of a synagogue, reflecting the religious tensions and restrictions faced by Jewish communities in the region during this period.
events.name: Middelburg forbids synagogue construction

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1655, the Whitehall Conference concluded with the determination that there was no legal barrier preventing Jews from re-entering England after the Edict of Expulsion in 1290. This decision marked a significant step towards the eventual readmission of Jews to England.
events.name: Whitehall Conference on Jewish re-entry

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1655, during the Second Northern War, monks at the Jasna Góra Monastery in Czestochowa successfully defended against a month-long siege. This event became a symbol of Polish resistance and faith during a tumultuous period in Polish history.
events.name: Siege of Jasna Góra Monastery

events.enhanced_description: In 1656, the Stockholm Banco was founded in Stockholm, Sweden, becoming the first bank to issue banknotes. This innovation marked a significant development in the history of banking and finance.
events.name: Founding of Stockholm Banco

events.enhanced_description: In 1656, the only English fifty shilling coin was minted, representing a unique moment in the history of English currency. This coin would become a collector's item due to its rarity.
events.name: Minting of fifty shilling coin

events.enhanced_description: In 1656, Konoike Zen'amon founded a baking and money-changing business in Osaka, Japan. This enterprise would grow to become a significant player in the financial and commercial landscape of the region.
events.name: Founding of Konoike Zen'amon's business

events.enhanced_description: In 1656, Adams' Grammar School was founded in Newport, Shropshire, England, by William Adams. This institution would play a crucial role in the education of young men in the region.
events.name: Founding of Adams' Grammar School

events.enhanced_description: In 1656, Samuel Stockhausen, a physician from the metal mining town of Goslar, published his groundbreaking work, 'Libellus de lithargyrii fumo noxio morbifico,' which examined the health impacts of toxic fumes from mining operations, particularly focusing on miners' asthma. This treatise is considered one of the earliest studies on occupational diseases, highlighting the dangers faced by workers in hazardous environments.
events.name: Publication of Libellus de lithargyrii fumo noxio morbifico

events.enhanced_description: The First War of Villmergen erupted on January 5, 1656, as a civil conflict between Protestant and Roman Catholic cantons in Switzerland. The war was characterized by battles involving major cities like Zurich and Bern against Catholic cantons.
events.name: The First War of Villmergen begins

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1656, the Treaty of Königsberg was signed, establishing a strategic alliance between Charles X Gustav of Sweden and Frederick William, Elector of Brandenburg. This alliance aimed to strengthen their positions during the ongoing conflicts in Northern Europe.
events.name: Treaty of Königsberg signed

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1656, Spanish Chilean troops, reinforced by soldiers from the Viceroyalty of Peru, achieved a significant victory against the indigenous Mapuche warriors at San Fabián de Conuco. This battle marked a turning point in the ongoing Mapuche uprising.

locations.name: San Fabián de Conuco, Ñuble, Chile

events.name: Battle at San Fabián de Conuco

events.enhanced_description: In 1656, Jacob Lumbrozo made history as the first Jewish doctor to arrive in the Thirteen Colonies, landing in Maryland. His arrival marked a significant moment in the cultural and medical landscape of early America.

locations.name: St. Mary's City, Maryland, United States

events.name: Jacob Lumbrozo arrives in Maryland

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1656, the Battle of Golab marked a significant engagement during the Swedish Deluge, where Swedish Empire troops led by King Carl X Gustav defeated the forces of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth commanded by General Stefan Czarniecki.
events.name: Battle of Golab

events.enhanced_description: On February 23, 1656, London's Lord Mayor Christopher Packe proposed to Oliver Cromwell that he should restore the monarchy with himself as King. Cromwell declined the offer, but it set the stage for future political developments in the Commonwealth.
events.name: Cromwell's Monarchy Proposal

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1656, the Çınar incident occurred when Turkish soldiers rebelled after being denied payment by a palace guard for Sultan Mehmet IV. The rebellion resulted in the execution of 30 officials identified by the rebels as responsible for the non-payment.
events.name: Çınar Incident

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1656, Fyodor Baykov, the first envoy from the Russian Empire, was admitted to the Forbidden City in Beijing. He was sent by Tsar Alexis to negotiate a trade agreement with Emperor Shunzi, marking a significant moment in Sino-Russian relations.
events.name: Russian envoy admitted to Forbidden City

events.enhanced_description: The First War of Villmergen concluded on March 7, 1656, with a peace agreement mediated by France and the Duchy of Savoy. This agreement ended the civil conflict between Protestant and Roman Catholic cantons in Switzerland.
events.name: End of the First War of Villmergen

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1656, the Battle of Jaroslaw saw Polish and Lithuanian troops, commanded by Stefan Czarniecki, defeat the Swedish Army led by King Karl X Gustav. This battle was a significant counter-offensive in the ongoing conflict known as the Swedish Deluge.
events.name: Battle of Jaroslaw

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1656, Pope Alexander VII issued a decree resolving the Chinese Rites controversy, allowing Jesuit missionaries to accept practices favorable to Chinese customs, including Confucianism and ancestor worship, as compatible with Catholic rites.
events.name: Pope Alexander VII's decree on Chinese Rites

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1656, King John II Casimir Vasa crowned the Black Madonna of Częstochowa as Queen and Protector of Poland in Lviv Cathedral. This event was a pivotal moment during the Second Northern War, symbolizing the nation's spiritual resilience.
events.name: Coronation of the Black Madonna

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1656, the Treaty of Brussels was signed, forging an alliance between Philip IV of Spain and the exiled Royalists of the British Isles, led by Charles II. This treaty was part of the broader political maneuvers during the English Civil War.
events.name: Treaty of Brussels signed

events.enhanced_description: On April 28, 1656, the Dutch East India Company ship Vergulde Draeck wrecked off Ledge Point, Western Australia, resulting in the loss of 118 crew members. The ship was en route from the Cape of Good Hope to Batavia, carrying valuable cargo.
events.name: Wreck of the Vergulde Draeck

events.enhanced_description: On May 7, 1656, nine days after the wreck of the Vergulde Draeck, a steersman and six crew members were dispatched to Batavia to seek help. The remaining survivors awaited rescue at Ledge Point but were never seen again.
events.name: Dispatch for help after the wreck of the Vergulde Draeck

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1656, the Dutch captured the city of Colombo, marking the beginning of their colonial rule over Dutch Ceylon. This event was significant in the context of European colonial expansion in Asia.
events.name: Dutch capture of Colombo

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1656, Francesco Cornaro was elected as the Leader of the Venetian Republic, defeating Bertuccio Valier. Cornaro's leadership was short-lived as he passed away less than three weeks later.
events.name: Election of Francesco Cornaro as Leader of Venice

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1656, Bertuccio Valier was elected as the new Doge of the Venetian Republic. His election came after a period of political instability and was part of the ongoing governance of Venice.
events.name: Bertuccio Valier elected as Doge of Venice

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1656, after a 41-day voyage, a seven-member team reached Batavia to inform Dutch East India Company officials about the wreck of the Vergulde Draeck. This led to the dispatch of rescue ships to assist the stranded crew in Western Australia.
events.name: Rescue mission after the wreck of the Vergulde Draeck

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1656, Warsaw was recaptured by King John II Casimir Vasa of Poland, nearly a year after it fell to Swedish forces. This event marked a significant turning point in the ongoing conflicts of the Second Northern War.
events.name: Recapture of Warsaw

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of the Dardanelles, fought from June 27-28, 1656, resulted in a significant defeat for the Ottoman Navy against the combined forces of Venice and Malta. The Ottomans lost 82 out of 98 ships, while Venice suffered minimal losses, marking a pivotal moment in naval warfare.
events.name: Battle of the Dardanelles

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1656, the Treaty of Marienburg was signed, establishing a military alliance between Sweden and Brandenburg-Prussia during the Second Northern War. This treaty was crucial in shaping the power dynamics in Northern Europe.
events.name: Treaty of Marienburg

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1656, a search party from the rescue ship Goede Hoop was sent ashore to find survivors of the shipwrecked Vergulde Draeck. Despite their efforts, no trace of the ship or its crew would be found for over three centuries.
events.name: Search for survivors of the Vergulde Draeck

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1656, a Writ of Excommunication was issued against the philosopher Baruch Spinoza by the Jewish community of Amsterdam. This act reflected the tensions between Spinoza's radical ideas and the traditional beliefs of his community.
events.name: Excommunication of Baruch Spinoza

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1656, Swedish and Brandenburger troops, led by King Charles X Gustav, defeated the forces of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth near Warsaw, recapturing the capital. This battle was a key moment in the Second Northern War.
events.name: Battle near Warsaw

events.enhanced_description: King Prasat Thong of the Ayutthaya Kingdom died on August 8, 1656, after a reign of over 25 years. His death led to a power struggle, as his eldest son was quickly crowned but faced threats from within the royal family.
events.name: Death of King Prasat Thong

events.enhanced_description: On August 9, 1656, Prince Si Suthammaracha staged a coup d'état, overthrowing his nephew King Sanpet VI of Ayutthaya. This power grab led to the execution of Sanpet and a brief reign for Suthammaracha.
events.name: Coup d'état in Ayutthaya

events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1656, Russian troops captured the Swedish-controlled city of Kokenhusen during the Russo-Swedish War. Tsar Alexis renamed the city Tsarevich-Dmitriev in memory of his deceased son, marking a significant territorial gain for Russia.
events.name: Capture of Kokenhusen

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1656, the Treaty of Butre was signed between the Dutch West India Company and the Ahanta Kingdom, establishing a protectorate over the Dutch Gold Coast, which is now part of modern Ghana.
events.name: Treaty of Butre

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1656, Köprülü Mehmed Pasha was appointed Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire, a position he would use to implement significant reforms and strengthen the empire's military and administrative structures.
events.name: Köprülü Mehmed Pasha becomes Grand Vizier

events.enhanced_description: On October 26, 1656, Prince Narai overthrew King Si Suthammaracha of Ayutthaya, just weeks after Suthammaracha had seized the throne. Narai's ascension marked a significant shift in the kingdom's leadership.
events.name: Coup d'état by Prince Narai

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1656, the Truce of Vilna was signed between Russia and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, establishing a temporary ceasefire and mutual defense against Swedish aggression.
events.name: Truce of Vilna

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1656, Ali Adil Shah II ascended to the throne as Sultan of Bijapur following the death of his father, Mohammed Adil Shah. His reign would be marked by challenges from rival powers in the Deccan.
events.name: Ali Adil Shah II becomes Sultan

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1656, at just 13 years old, Afonso VI became King of Portugal following the death of his father, King João IV. Due to his youth and mental disability, his mother, Queen Luisa, acted as regent during his early reign.

events.name: Afonso VI becomes King of Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On November 20, 1656, the Treaty of Labiau was signed between Charles X Gustav of Sweden and Frederick William, Elector of Brandenburg, solidifying their alliance during the Second Northern War.
events.name: Treaty of Labiau

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1656, a treaty of alliance was signed between the Holy Roman Empire and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, aimed at countering Swedish expansion during the Second Northern War.
events.name: Alliance between Holy Roman Empire and Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1656, the Treaty of Radnot was signed among Sweden, the Electorate of Brandenburg, Transylvania, and Polish rebel groups, outlining the division of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in the event of victory in the Second Northern War.
events.name: Treaty of Radnot

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1656, English Quaker James Nayler was convicted of blasphemy but spared the death penalty. This case highlighted the tensions between religious dissenters and the established authorities in England.
events.name: Conviction of James Nayler

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1656, King Frederick III of Denmark and Norway decreed that loan repayments would be made on two specific days, known as Fandens fødselsdag or 'Devil's Birthday'. This decree was part of his broader financial reforms.
events.name: Fandens fødselsdag decree

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1656, Christiaan Huygens invented the pendulum clock, achieving unprecedented accuracy by losing only 10 seconds per day. This invention revolutionized timekeeping and laid the groundwork for modern horology.
events.name: Invention of the pendulum clock

events.enhanced_description: In September 1657, Shah Jahan, the Mughal Emperor, fell ill, which allowed his son, Aurangzeb, to begin taking control of the Mughal Empire. This shift in power dynamics would lead to significant changes in the empire's governance and policies.
events.name: Shah Jahan's illness

events.enhanced_description: In 1657, the Accademia del Cimento was founded in Florence, Italy, as one of the first scientific societies in Europe. This institution played a crucial role in the advancement of experimental science and the promotion of empirical research during the Scientific Revolution.
events.name: Foundation of the Accademia del Cimento

events.enhanced_description: In 1657, England's first chocolate house opened in London, marking a significant cultural shift as chocolate became a fashionable drink among the elite. This year also saw the introduction of tea in England and coffee in France, reflecting the growing influence of global trade on European lifestyles.
events.name: England's first chocolate house is opened in London and introduction of tea in England while coffee is introduced to France

events.enhanced_description: In 1657, Dutch mathematician Christiaan Huygens published 'De ratiociniis in ludo aleae', the first book on probability theory, laying the groundwork for modern probability and statistics. This work emerged during a period of significant mathematical advancement in Europe.

image.caption: A pendulum clock designed by Christiaan Huygens and his treatise *Horologium Oscillatorium* on display at Museum Boerhaave in Leiden.

events.name: Christiaan Huygens writes the first book to be published on probability theory, De ratiociniis in ludo aleae

events.enhanced_description: In 1657, the German playwright Andreas Gryphius published his drama 'Katharina von Georgien' in Breslau, which showcased the Baroque style and reflected the tumultuous historical context of the Thirty Years' War. Gryphius is considered one of the most important figures in German literature.
events.name: Andreas Gryphius' drama Katharina von Georgien is published in Breslau

events.enhanced_description: In 1657, 'Women Beware Women', a tragedy by Thomas Middleton, was published posthumously in London. The play explores themes of gender, power, and morality, and is considered a significant work in the canon of English drama.
events.name: Thomas Middleton's tragedy Women Beware Women is published posthumously in London

events.enhanced_description: On January 8, 1657, Miles Sindercombe and a group of disaffected Levellers were arrested after their plot to assassinate Oliver Cromwell by blowing up Whitehall Palace was foiled. This event underscored the political tensions in England during the Interregnum, as various factions vied for power and influence.
events.name: Assassination attempt on Oliver Cromwell

events.enhanced_description: On January 29, 1657, the Rule of the Major-Generals, a military government established by Oliver Cromwell to maintain order, was abolished. This marked a significant shift in governance as Cromwell sought to restore a more traditional form of rule amidst growing discontent with military oversight.
events.name: Abolition of the Rule of the Major-Generals

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1657, Oliver Cromwell assured Antonio Fernandez Carvajal and the Jewish community of their right to remain in England, marking a pivotal moment in the resettlement of Jews in the country after centuries of expulsion. This event signified a shift towards religious tolerance during Cromwell's rule.
events.name: Resettlement of the Jews in England

events.enhanced_description: On February 23, 1657, the Humble Petition and Advice was presented to Oliver Cromwell, offering him the crown of England. This proposal reflected the ongoing debate about the future of governance in England following the Civil War and Cromwell's role as Lord Protector.
events.name: Humble Petition and Advice offered to Cromwell

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1657, the Great Fire of Meireki devastated Edo (modern-day Tokyo), destroying a significant portion of the city and damaging Edo Castle. The fire resulted in the tragic loss of an estimated 100,000 lives, highlighting the vulnerabilities of urban centers in the 17th century.
events.name: Great Fire of Meireki

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1657, during the Anglo-Spanish War, English Admiral Robert Blake led an attempt to seize a Spanish treasure fleet at the Battle of Santa Cruz de Tenerife. This naval engagement was part of England's broader strategy to disrupt Spanish maritime trade.

locations.name: Santa Cruz de Tenerife, Canary Islands, Spain

events.name: Battle of Santa Cruz de Tenerife

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1657, Oliver Cromwell confirmed his refusal of the English crown, opting instead to retain the title of 'Lord Protector.' This decision reflected his desire to maintain a republican form of government while navigating the complexities of power in post-Civil War England.
events.name: Cromwell refuses the crown

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1657, King Frederick III of Denmark signed a manifesto effectively declaring war on Sweden. This act initiated a conflict that would become part of the larger Northern Wars, significantly impacting the balance of power in Scandinavia.
events.name: Denmark declares war on Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1657, the ship Les Armes d'Amsterdam arrived at Quebec, New France, carrying Michel Mathieu Brunet dit Lestang, a notable colonist and explorer. His journey contributed to the exploration and settlement of North America, particularly in the Great Lakes region.
events.name: Arrival of Les Armes d'Amsterdam at Quebec

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1657, Brandenburg and Poland signed the Treaty of Wehlau, which marked a significant diplomatic agreement between the two powers. This treaty was part of the broader context of territorial disputes and alliances in Eastern Europe during the 17th century.
events.name: Treaty of Wehlau

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1657, the first autopsy and coroner's jury verdict in the Colony of Maryland were recorded, marking a significant development in the understanding of forensic science and legal procedures in the early American colonies.
events.name: First autopsy in Maryland

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1657, the Treaty of Raalte was signed, resulting in William III, Prince of Orange, losing his position as stadtholder of Overijssel. This treaty was part of the broader political maneuvers in the Dutch Republic during a time of internal conflict and power struggles.
events.name: Treaty of Raalte

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1657, French troops occupied Mardyck, a strategic location during the conflicts of the time. This occupation was part of France's military campaigns during the ongoing wars in Europe, particularly against Spain.
events.name: French occupation of Mardyck

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1657, the Treaty of Bromberg was signed between Brandenburg and Poland, concluding a series of conflicts and territorial disputes. This treaty was significant in shaping the political landscape of Eastern Europe during the 17th century.
events.name: Treaty of Bromberg

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1657, Christina, the former Queen regnant of Sweden, had Gian Rinaldo Monaldeschi killed in her presence at the Palace of Fontainebleau. This shocking act was rooted in personal betrayal and political intrigue, reflecting the tumultuous nature of Christina's reign.
events.name: Monaldeschi's execution

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1657, the Flushing Remonstrance was signed in New Amsterdam, advocating for religious freedom and tolerance. This document is considered a precursor to the principles of religious liberty in America, highlighting the diverse beliefs present in the early colonial period.

locations.name: Flushing, New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Signing of the Flushing Remonstrance

events.enhanced_description: In July 1658, the Manchu fleet led by Šarhūda decisively defeated Onufriy Stepanov's Russian flotilla on the Amur River. This battle underscored the growing tensions and conflicts in the region as both powers sought to expand their influence.
events.name: Manchu fleet annihilates Russian flotilla on the Amur River

events.enhanced_description: In early 1658, Dutch forces expelled Portuguese traders from Ceylon, marking a significant shift in control over trade routes in the region. This event was part of the larger conflict between European colonial powers in Asia.
events.name: Expulsion of Portuguese traders from Ceylon

events.enhanced_description: In 1658, the Dutch in the Cape Colony began importing slaves from India and Southeast Asia, marking the start of a grim chapter in South African history. This practice would later expand to include slaves from Madagascar and other regions.
events.name: Importation of slaves to the Cape Colony

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1658, Edward Sexby, a former soldier and conspirator against Oliver Cromwell, died in the Tower of London. His death marked the end of a controversial figure who had played a significant role in the political upheavals of the English Civil War.
events.name: Edward Sexby dies in the Tower of London

events.enhanced_description: On January 30, 1658, the 'March Across the Belts' commenced, where Swedish King Karl X Gustav led his troops across the frozen waters of the Danish straits. This strategic maneuver allowed Sweden to capture several Danish islands, significantly altering the balance of power in the region.
events.name: The March Across the Belts begins

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1658, Prince Muhi al-Din Muhammad, one of the sons of Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan, declared himself Emperor after his father named his older brother, Dara Shikoh, as regent. This proclamation initiated a power struggle within the Mughal Empire.

image.caption: Bhavanidas’s painting depicts Emperor Aurangzeb being carried in a palanquin.
image.credit: Bhavanidas — https://www.metmuseum.org/Collections/search-the-collections/140012467?rpp=20&pg=1&ft=bhavanidas&pos=4
image.date_qualification: Retrospective painting of Aurangzeb, not a depiction of his 1658 proclamation; the image is dated circa before 1720.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Prince Muhi al-Din Muhammad proclaims himself Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1658, Swedish troops under King Charles X Gustav successfully crossed The Great Belt, utilizing the frozen sea to advance into Danish territory. This maneuver was pivotal in Sweden's military campaigns during the Second Northern War.
events.name: Swedish troops cross The Great Belt

events.enhanced_description: On March 8, 1658, the Treaty of Roskilde was signed, concluding peace between Sweden and Denmark-Norway. Under the treaty, Denmark ceded significant territories to Sweden, marking a high point in Swedish territorial expansion during the period.
events.name: Treaty of Roskilde is concluded

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1658, the Battle of Dharmat occurred in modern-day Madhya Pradesh, India, where Prince Muhi al-Din Muhammad led 30,000 troops to victory against 22,000 forces led by Jaswant Singh and Ratan Singh Rathore. This battle was crucial in the power struggle for the Mughal throne.
events.name: Battle of Dharmat is fought

events.enhanced_description: On April 16, 1658, representatives of the nobility from the provinces of Blekinge, Halland, and Scania gathered in Malmö to swear allegiance to King Charles X Gustav of Sweden. This event symbolized the consolidation of Swedish power in the recently acquired territories.
events.name: Nobility of Skåneland swear allegiance to King Charles X Gustav

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1658, Thomas Browne published 'Hydriotaphia, Urn Burial' and 'The Garden of Cyrus' in England. These works reflect Browne's interests in archaeology, philosophy, and the natural world, contributing significantly to English literature and thought.
events.name: Thomas Browne publishes works in England

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1658, Aurangzeb emerged victorious in the Battle of Samugarh against his brother Dara Shikoh, who was defending the Mughal capital of Agra. This decisive battle paved the way for Aurangzeb to ultimately seize the Mughal throne.
events.name: Aurangzeb wins the Battle of Samugarh

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1658, Pope Alexander VII appointed François de Laval as vicar apostolic of New France, marking a significant step in the Catholic Church's efforts to establish a strong presence in North America. Laval would go on to become the first bishop of Quebec.
events.name: Pope Alexander VII appoints François de Laval

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1658, during the Anglo-Spanish War and Franco-Spanish War, the Battle of the Dunes took place near Dunkirk. A combined French and English force defeated the Spanish, leading to England's acquisition of Dunkirk as a strategic port.
events.name: Battle of the Dunes

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1658, the Battle of Rio Nuevo occurred, where a Spanish invasion force attempted to recapture Jamaica from English control but was ultimately unsuccessful. This battle was part of the larger Anglo-Spanish War.
events.name: Battle of Rio Nuevo

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1658, the Siege of Toruń commenced as troops from the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth and Austria sought to reclaim the city from Swedish control. The siege would last several months, culminating in the surrender of the Swedish garrison.
events.name: Siege of Toruń begins

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1658, Prince Leopold of the House of Habsburg was elected as the new Holy Roman Emperor. His election marked a significant moment in the Habsburg dynasty's influence over European politics during the 17th century.
events.name: Prince Leopold elected as Holy Roman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1658, after the completion of the Taj Mahal, Aurangzeb deposed his father, Shah Jahan, as ruler of the Mughal Empire. This act marked a significant shift in power and initiated a new era in Mughal history.
events.name: Aurangzeb deposes Shah Jahan
