events.name: During war between the Russian Empire and the Ottoman Empire, Russian troops arrive at Chigirin

events.enhanced_description: Henry Purcell, a prominent English composer, was appointed as a musician to the court of Charles II, marking a significant moment in the history of English music. His work during this period would later influence the development of English opera and choral music.
events.name: Henry Purcell is appointed a musician to the court of Charles II of England

events.enhanced_description: In a military campaign, Danish troops invaded the Swedish island of Rügen, driving out the local population. This event was part of the larger conflict known as the Scanian War, which saw multiple shifts in territorial control in Northern Europe.
events.name: Troops from Denmark invade and capture the Swedish island of Rügen

events.enhanced_description: The Kangxi Emperor of China formally granted titles and ranks to all of his wives, elevating Empress Xiaozhaoren to the status of consort. This act was significant in the context of Qing dynasty court politics and the status of women in imperial China.
events.name: Kangxi Emperor grants titles and ranks to his wives

events.enhanced_description: Michel le Tellier was appointed Chancellor of France, a position that placed him at the center of French political power during the reign of Louis XIV. His tenure was marked by significant administrative reforms and the strengthening of royal authority.
events.name: Michel le Tellier becomes Chancellor of France

events.enhanced_description: The marriage of Mary II of England to William of Orange was a politically significant union that would later lead to the Glorious Revolution. This event solidified William's claim to the English throne and marked a pivotal moment in the history of the British monarchy.
events.name: Mary II of England marries William of Orange

events.enhanced_description: French troops occupied Freiburg during the ongoing conflicts in Europe, asserting French dominance in the region. This occupation was part of the larger context of the Franco-Dutch War and the struggle for territorial control in the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: French troops occupy Freiburg

events.enhanced_description: Belgian missionary Louis Hennepin became the first known European to discover Niagara Falls, documenting his observations in his book. His accounts brought significant attention to the natural wonder, influencing future exploration and tourism.

image.caption: Portrait of Louis Hennepin.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — http://millcitytimes.com/news/father-louis-hennepin-man-myth-legend.html http://static1.1.sqspcdn.com/static/f/436570/28178760/1566831406360/Louis+Hennepin+Portrait+-+1694.jpg?token=66qmcTNv37z7gDqzu38MhYNivVQ%3D
image.date_qualification: The portrait is dated 1694, after the event date stated in the record (1677-12-07); it is not a contemporary event photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: Niagara Falls, New York, United States

events.name: Louis Hennepin discovers Niagara Falls

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Stettin concluded after nearly five months with the surrender of the Swedish garrison to Frederick William, Elector of Brandenburg. This event marked a significant territorial gain for Prussia during the Scanian War.

image.caption: Anonymous period plate depicting the Siege of Stettin during the Scanian War.
image.credit: Anonymous plate — https://www.europeana.eu/portal/record/92034/D31C1B6E8FB481F9CE38258E4F3E0C101EFFACFB.html?query=stettin+1675&start=1&startPage=1&view=table&pageId=brd
image.date_qualification: The supplied image date is a broad 17th-century date, not a date for the depicted surrender; the article states the siege ran until 26 December 1677.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Siege of Stettin ends with Sweden's surrender

events.enhanced_description: In 1678, approximately 1,200 Irish families migrated from Barbados to Virginia and the Carolinas. This movement was part of the broader patterns of migration during this period, contributing to the demographic changes in the American colonies.
events.name: Irish families migrate from Barbados

events.enhanced_description: In 1678, the vacant Bishopric of Leighlin was given to the Bishop of Kildare in commendam. This appointment was significant as it later contributed to the formation of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Kildare and Leighlin.
events.name: Bishopric of Leighlin appointed

events.enhanced_description: In a strategic move against France, England and the Dutch Republic signed a mutual defense treaty, solidifying their alliance during a period of heightened tensions in Europe. This agreement was crucial for the balance of power in the region.
events.name: England and the Dutch Republic sign a mutual defense treaty

events.enhanced_description: The establishment of the first fire engine company in North America in Boston marked a significant advancement in public safety and urban management. This development laid the groundwork for modern firefighting practices in the United States.
events.name: The first fire engine company in North America goes into service

events.enhanced_description: The first part of John Bunyan's Christian allegory, 'The Pilgrim's Progress', was published in London in 1678. This seminal work has since become one of the most significant works of English literature, illustrating the spiritual journey of a character named Christian as he seeks salvation.
events.name: The Pilgrim's Progress published

events.enhanced_description: Thomas Shadwell's comedy 'A True Widow' premiered at The Duke's Theatre in London on March 21, 1678. This performance marked a significant moment in Restoration theatre, showcasing Shadwell's comedic style and contributing to the vibrant cultural scene of the time.

locations.name: The Duke's Theatre, London, Greater London, England

events.name: A True Widow first performance

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1678, Wu Sangui, a rebel general in southern China, declared himself the monarch of 'The Great Zhou' during the Revolt of the Three Feudatories. His reign was short-lived, as he succumbed to dysentery later that year, marking a significant moment in the struggle against the Qing dynasty.
events.name: Wu Sangui declares himself monarch

events.enhanced_description: The city of Ypres fell to the French Army on March 25, 1678, after a seven-day siege during the Franco-Dutch War. This event highlighted the ongoing conflict in the Spanish Netherlands, which would later see Ypres returned to Dutch control and eventually become part of modern Belgium.
events.name: Siege of Ypres

events.enhanced_description: Polish astronomer Johannes Hevelius discovered nova V529 Orionis on March 28, 1678. This discovery contributed to the field of astronomy and showcased Hevelius's significant role in the scientific community of the 17th century.
events.name: Discovery of nova V529 Orionis

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1678, Ignatius Gregory Peter VI Shahbaddin was enthroned as the Patriarch of the Syriac Catholic Church in Aleppo, receiving recognition from both Ottoman Sultan Mehmed IV and Pope Innocent XI. This event marked a significant moment in the history of the Syriac Catholic Church.
events.name: Enthronement of Ignatius Gregory Peter VI

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Casco Bay was signed on April 12, 1678, between officials of the Province of New York and the Penobscot tribe, along with the Wabanaki Confederacy. This treaty aimed to end hostilities following King Philip's War and established terms for land rights and rent payments.
events.name: Treaty of Casco Bay signed

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1678, French admiral Jean d'Estrees ran his fleet aground in the Las Aves Archipelago while attempting to reach Curaçao. This incident underscored the challenges faced by naval forces during the conflicts of the era.
events.name: French fleet runs aground

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1678, French buccaneer Michel de Grammont launched a daring raid on Spanish-held Venezuela, arriving with a formidable fleet. He captured Maracaibo on June 14, marking a significant moment in the history of piracy in the Caribbean.
events.name: Michel de Grammont's raid on Venezuela

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1678, Elena Lucrezia Cornaro Piscopia became the first woman to be awarded a university degree, receiving a doctorate in philosophy from the University of Padua. This groundbreaking achievement paved the way for future generations of women in academia.
events.name: Elena Lucrezia Cornaro Piscopia awarded doctorate

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Ortenbach, fought on July 23, 1678, near Offenburg, was one of the last major engagements of the Franco-Dutch War. French forces under François de Créquy decisively defeated a larger contingent of Holy Roman Empire troops led by Duke Karl V Leopold.
events.name: Battle of Ortenbach

events.enhanced_description: On July 29, 1678, Muhammad Azam Shah was appointed as the Mughal Governor of Bengal by his father, Emperor Aurangzeb. His tenure was brief, lasting just over a year before he was recalled, reflecting the turbulent political landscape of the Mughal Empire.
events.name: Muhammad Azam Shah appointed Governor of Bengal

events.enhanced_description: The Treaties of Nijmegen, signed on August 10, 1678, marked the end of the Franco-Dutch War. The agreements resulted in territorial changes, including the cession of the County of Burgundy to France, reshaping the political landscape of Europe.
events.name: Treaties of Nijmegen signed

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Saint-Denis occurred on November 10, 1567, where Anne de Montmorency led 16,000 Royalists against the 3,500 Huguenots commanded by Louis, Prince of Condé. Despite being outnumbered, the Huguenots put up a fierce resistance before being ultimately defeated, and Montmorency was mortally wounded.
events.name: Battle of Saint-Denis

events.enhanced_description: The Kediri campaign commenced on August 21, 1678, as forces from the Mataram Sultanate and the Dutch East India Company, led by VOC Captain François Tack, marched from Jepara toward Kediri to suppress the Trunajaya rebellion. This campaign was crucial in restoring Mataram authority in the region.
events.name: Kediri campaign begins

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1678, Sultan Amangkurat II of Mataram set off from Jepara with a significant force to lead the Kediri campaign against the Trunajaya rebellion. He was accompanied by VOC forces under Anthonio Hurdt, marking a collaborative effort to restore order in the region.
events.name: Sultan Amangkurat II leads Kediri campaign

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1678, Titus Oates began presenting allegations of the 'Popish Plot', claiming a Roman Catholic conspiracy to assassinate King Charles II of England. This sensational claim fueled anti-Catholic sentiment and led to widespread panic and persecution.
events.name: Titus Oates presents Popish Plot allegations

events.enhanced_description: The Franco-Dutch War officially ended on September 17, 1678, with the signing of the Treaties of Nijmegen. This conclusion brought a ceasefire after more than six years of conflict, significantly altering the balance of power in Europe.
events.name: Franco-Dutch War ends

events.enhanced_description: On October 17, 1678, Sir Edmund Berry Godfrey, an English magistrate, was found murdered in Primrose Hill, London. His death was perceived as evidence of the 'Popish Plot', intensifying the already heightened tensions between Catholics and Protestants in England.
events.name: Sir Edmund Berry Godfrey found murdered

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1678, England's House of Commons voted to initiate impeachment proceedings against five Roman Catholic members of the House of Lords, accused of involvement in the 'Popish Plot'. This marked a significant escalation in the political and religious tensions of the time.
events.name: House of Commons votes for impeachment

events.enhanced_description: The Kediri campaign successfully concluded on November 25, 1678, with Anthonio Hurdt and Sultan Amangkurat II capturing Kediri and forcing the rebel Prince Trunajaya to flee. This victory restored Mataram's control over the region and marked a significant achievement for the Dutch East India Company.
events.name: Kediri campaign concludes

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1678, William Staley, an English banker and Roman Catholic, became the first person executed in connection with the 'Popish Plot' arrests. His execution highlighted the severe consequences of the anti-Catholic hysteria gripping England at the time.
events.name: William Staley executed

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1678, the Test Act was enacted, requiring members of both the House of Lords and House of Commons in England to swear an anti-Catholic oath before taking office. This legislation further entrenched the anti-Catholic sentiment in English politics.
events.name: Test Act enacted

events.enhanced_description: In 1679, a peace treaty was signed in Tunis between Ali Bey al-Muradi, who had overthrown his brother Muhammad Bey al-Muradi, and their uncle Muhammad al-Hafsi al-Muradi, the Pasha of Tunis. This agreement was facilitated by the Dey of Algiers, reflecting the complex political dynamics of North Africa at the time.
events.name: Peace Treaty in Tunis

events.enhanced_description: The Tibet–Ladakh–Mughal War commenced in 1679 with the Tibetan invasion of Ladakh, marking a significant conflict involving regional powers. This war would have lasting implications for the political landscape of the region.
events.name: Beginning of the Tibet–Ladakh–Mughal War

events.enhanced_description: In 1679, French explorer Daniel Greysolon, Sieur du Lhut, explored the Saint Louis River, which would later lend its name to the city of Duluth, Minnesota. His expeditions were crucial in establishing French presence and influence in the region.
events.name: Exploration of the Saint Louis River

events.enhanced_description: In 1679, the Malpas Tunnel on the Canal du Midi in Hérault, France, was excavated by Pierre-Paul Riquet, marking the construction of Europe's first navigable canal tunnel. This engineering feat was pivotal in enhancing trade and transportation in the region.
events.name: Excavation of Malpas Tunnel

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1679, King Charles II of England dissolved the Cavalier Parliament, which had been in session for nearly 18 years. This dissolution was part of the ongoing political struggles of the time, particularly concerning the Exclusion Crisis and the king's desire to maintain control over Parliament.
events.name: Dissolution of the Cavalier Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1679, Moroccan troops from Fez, led by Commander Moussa ben Ahmed ben Youssef, were engaged in a battle against rebels in the Jbel Saghro mountain range. Despite suffering losses, Sultan Ismail Ibn Sharif successfully negotiated a ceasefire, allowing the remaining troops to return home safely.
events.name: Battle in Jbel Saghro

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Celle was signed on February 5, 1679, between France and Sweden on one side and the Holy Roman Empire on the other. This treaty confirmed Sweden's sovereignty over Bremen-Verden while ceding Thedinghausen and Dörverden to the Germans, marking a significant shift in territorial control in Northern Europe.
events.name: Treaty of Celle

events.enhanced_description: On February 19, 1679, Ajit Singh Rathore ascended to the throne as the new Maharaja of Jodhpur State, a prominent principality in India known as Marwar. His reign would contribute to the rich history and culture of the region.
events.name: Ajit Singh Rathore becomes Maharaja

events.enhanced_description: The Habeas Corpus Parliament, also known as the First Exclusion Parliament, was opened on March 6, 1679, in England. This parliament was significant in the context of the Exclusion Crisis, which sought to prevent the Catholic Duke of York from ascending to the throne.
events.name: Opening of the Habeas Corpus Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1679, Catherine Deshayes Monvoisin, known as La Voisin, was arrested outside the Church of Notre-Dame-de-Bonne-Nouvelle in Paris. Accused of being a notorious poisoner responsible for the deaths of over 1,000 people, she was imprisoned for 11 months before being executed.
events.name: Arrest of La Voisin

events.enhanced_description: On April 3, 1679, Aurangzeb, the Mughal Emperor, decreed the re-imposition of the jizya tax on non-Muslims, primarily targeting Hindus. This decision marked a significant shift in policy, reversing the earlier abolition of the tax by his great-grandfather, Akbar.
events.name: Imposition of the Jizya Tax

events.enhanced_description: On April 8, 1679, a devastating landslide in the Italian region of Piedmont caused the village of Bosia to sink and become buried, resulting in the deaths of approximately 200 inhabitants. The village was later rebuilt at a different location.
events.name: Landslide in Bosia

events.enhanced_description: On March 30, 1680, a total eclipse of the Sun occurred, with totality visible over the Opala Territory in the modern-day Democratic Republic of the Congo. This astronomical event would have been significant for both scientific observation and cultural interpretation.

locations.name: Opala Territory, Democratic Republic of the Congo

events.name: Total Eclipse of the Sun

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1679, James Sharp, the Archbishop of St Andrews and a prominent figure in the Church of Scotland, was assassinated at Magus Muir by a group of Scottish Covenanters. This event was part of the larger conflict between the Covenanters and the royal government.
events.name: Assassination of James Sharp

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1679, the Parliament of England passed the Habeas Corpus Act, aimed at securing the liberty of individuals against unlawful detention. This act was a significant development in the evolution of legal rights in England.
events.name: Passage of the Habeas Corpus Act

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1679, the Battle of Drumclog took place, where a group of 200 Scottish Covenanters, led by William Cleland, overwhelmed a small unit of the Scottish Army pursuing them for the murder of Archbishop Sharp. The Covenanters achieved a notable victory, killing 36 soldiers.
events.name: Battle of Drumclog

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1679, a 6.4 magnitude earthquake struck near Yerevan, which was then part of the Persian Empire. This natural disaster would have had significant impacts on the local population and infrastructure.
events.name: Earthquake in Armenia

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1679, the Battle of Bothwell Bridge occurred, where royal forces led by James Scott, 1st Duke of Monmouth, and John Graham of Claverhouse confronted the Scottish Covenanters. This battle was a decisive moment in the conflict between the Covenanters and the crown.
events.name: Battle of Bothwell Bridge

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1679, King Charles II dissolved the Habeas Corpus Parliament while it was in recess. This action was taken to prevent the passage of a bill that would exclude non-Anglicans from the succession to the throne, particularly targeting his Catholic brother, James, Duke of York.
events.name: Dissolution of the Habeas Corpus Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1679, the brigantine Le Griffon was towed to the southern end of the Niagara River, marking it as the first ship to sail the upper Great Lakes of North America. This expedition was led by French explorer René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle.
figures: René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle

locations.name: Niagara River, New York, United States

events.name: Launch of Le Griffon

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1679, a devastating 8.0 Mw magnitude earthquake struck Beijing and the surrounding Hebei region in China. This earthquake caused significant destruction and loss of life in the area.
events.name: Sanhe-Pinggu Earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1679, the Province of New Hampshire was officially separated from the Massachusetts Bay Colony. This separation marked a significant administrative change in colonial governance in New England.
events.name: Separation of New Hampshire

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1679, Bil'arab bin Sultan ascended to the position of Imam of Oman following the death of his father, Sultan bin Saif. His leadership would play a crucial role in the political landscape of Oman.
events.name: Bil'arab bin Sultan becomes Imam of Oman

events.enhanced_description: On October 6, 1679, Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb returned control of Bengal to the local Nawab of Murshidabad after removing his son, Prince Qutb-ud-Din Muhammad Azam, from the governorship of Dhaka. This decision reflected the complexities of Mughal administration in the region.
events.name: Return of Bengal to Nawab of Murshidabad

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1679, representatives of the Dutch Republic and the Kingdom of Sweden signed the last of the nine Treaties of Nijmegen, effectively ending the conflicts that had begun during the Franco-Dutch War. This marked a significant moment in European diplomatic history.
events.name: Signing of the Treaties of Nijmegen

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1679, a naval battle occurred between England's Royal Navy and the Maratha Empire's navy, commanded by Mai Nayak Bhandari. The English bombardment successfully drove the Marathas from the island fortress at Khanderi, marking a significant military engagement in the region.
events.name: Sea Battle at Khanderi

events.enhanced_description: On November 27, 1679, a catastrophic fire in Boston, Massachusetts, destroyed all warehouses, 80 houses, and all ships in the dockyards. This disaster had a profound impact on the local economy and infrastructure.
events.name: Boston Fire

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1679, French explorers René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, and Henri de Tonti embarked on the first European expedition to explore the upper Mississippi River. This journey would pave the way for future exploration and settlement in the region.
figures: René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle
events.name: Exploration of the Upper Mississippi River

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1679, Oliver Plunkett, the Roman Catholic Primate of All Ireland and Archbishop of Armagh, was arrested on false charges related to the so-called 'Popish Plot', which alleged a conspiracy to aid a French invasion of the British Isles. His subsequent execution in 1681 and canonization in 1975 highlight the enduring significance of his legacy in Irish Catholic history.
events.name: Arrest of Oliver Plunkett

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1679, more than 200 captives aboard the ship The Crown of London, all Scottish Covenanters arrested after the Battle of Bothwell Bridge, were killed when the ship wrecked on the Orkney Islands while transporting them to exile in North America. This tragic event highlighted the brutal consequences of the political turmoil in Scotland.
events.name: Shipwreck of The Crown of London

events.enhanced_description: The Trunajaya rebellion in Java concluded on December 26, 1679, when Prince Panembahan Maduretno surrendered to Sultan Amangkurat II of Mataram. Although initially treated with respect, Maduretno was killed shortly after by the Sultan, marking a significant moment in the power struggles of the region.
events.name: End of the Trunajaya Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: In May 1680, the volcano Krakatoa erupted, likely on a small scale. This event was one of the early signs of the volcanic activity that would later lead to the catastrophic eruption in 1883.
events.name: Eruption of Krakatoa

events.enhanced_description: On January 2, 1680, King Amangkurat II of Mataram invited Trunajaya, the leader of a failed rebellion, for a ceremonial visit to the royal palace. This visit ended tragically when Amangkurat stabbed Trunajaya, reflecting the brutal nature of political power struggles in the region.
events.name: Ceremonial Visit of Trunajaya

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1680, William Harris, an English Puritan and co-founder of the Providence Plantations, was captured by Algerian pirates while returning to England. He was sold into slavery until a ransom was paid, highlighting the dangers faced by seafarers of the time.
events.name: Capture of William Harris

events.enhanced_description: On February 12, 1680, Charles Colbert, Marquis de Croissy, was appointed as France's Minister of Foreign Affairs, a position he held for 16 years until his death. His tenure was marked by significant diplomatic engagements that shaped France's foreign policy.
events.name: Charles Colbert becomes Minister of Foreign Affairs

events.enhanced_description: On February 16, 1680, Rev. Ralph Davenant's will provided for the establishment of the Davenant Foundation School for poor boys in Whitechapel, London. This initiative reflected the growing concern for education and social welfare in 17th-century England.
events.name: Foundation of the Davenant Foundation School

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1680, Catherine Deshayes Monvoisin, a fortune teller implicated in the 'Affair of the Poisons', was burned at the stake after being convicted of witchcraft. Her trial and execution were part of a larger witch hunt that resulted in the deaths of many others.
events.name: Execution of Catherine Deshayes Monvoisin

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1680, the Duchy of Saxe-Coburg was divided among the sons of the late Ernest I, Duke of Saxe-Gotha. This division reflected the fragmentation of territories in the Holy Roman Empire during this period.
events.name: Division of the Duchy of Saxe-Coburg

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1680, the Earl of Shaftesbury informed the Privy Council of England about a supposed rebellion by Roman Catholics in Ireland, allegedly backed by France. This led to the arrest and eventual execution of Archbishop Oliver Plunkett, highlighting the tensions of the period.
events.name: Earl of Shaftesbury's Warning

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1680, troops sent by Sultan Ismail Ibn Sharif of Morocco began a blockade of the port of Tangier, which was occupied by the English. Palmes Fairborne was dispatched to defend the port, illustrating the ongoing conflicts in North Africa.
events.name: Blockade of Tangier

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1680, the London Penny Post delivery service commenced operations, created by Robert Murray and William Dockwra. This innovative service allowed letters to be delivered anywhere in London for just one penny, revolutionizing communication in the city.
events.name: Establishment of the London Penny Post

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1680, Prince Rajaram Bhosle, the 10-year-old son of Shivaji, was installed as the new Emperor of the Maratha Empire in Raigad, Maharashtra, shortly after his father's death. This event marked a significant transition in leadership amidst ongoing power struggles.
events.name: Installation of Rajaram Bhosle

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1680, Prince Sambhaji Bhosle and fellow prisoners executed the commander of the Panhala prison and seized control of the fort. This act was part of Sambhaji's plans to reclaim power in the Maratha Empire following his brother's ascension to the throne.
events.name: Sambhaji's Escape from Panhala

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1680, the first group of French Huguenots arrived in Charleston, South Carolina, aboard the ship Richmond. This migration was part of a larger movement of religious exiles seeking refuge from persecution in Europe.
events.name: Arrival of French Huguenots in Charleston

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1680, King Charles XI of Sweden married Princess Elonora, the daughter of the late King Frederick III of Denmark-Norway. This marriage was significant for strengthening ties between the two kingdoms.
events.name: Marriage of Charles XI of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1680, Tokugawa Tsunayoshi ascended to the position of Shōgun of Japan following the death of his older brother, Tokugawa Ietsuna. His rule would be marked by significant cultural developments and strict policies.
events.name: Tokugawa Tsunayoshi becomes Shōgun

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1680, England and Spain signed a mutual defense treaty, reflecting the shifting alliances and geopolitical strategies of European powers during this period.
events.name: Mutual Defense Treaty between England and Spain

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1680, Elizabeth Cellier, an English Catholic midwife, was tried and acquitted of treason for her pamphleting against the government. Her trial highlighted the tensions between Catholics and the state during this period.
events.name: Trial of Elizabeth Cellier

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1680, Sambhaji Bhosle captured Raigad, the capital of the Maratha Empire, and declared himself Chhatrapati, effectively deposing his younger brother Rajaram I. This event marked a significant shift in power within the Maratha leadership during a tumultuous period of resistance against Mughal rule.
events.name: Sambhaji Bhosle captures Raigad

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1680, the Sanquhar Declaration was publicly read by Michael Cameron in Sanquhar, Scotland, asserting the Covenanters' opposition to the religious control imposed by King Charles II. This declaration was a pivotal moment in the Scottish Covenanter movement, emphasizing their commitment to religious freedom.
events.name: Sanquhar Declaration

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1680, an auto-da-fé, a public ceremony of the Spanish Inquisition, took place in the Plaza Mayor of Madrid. These events were notorious for their role in the persecution of heretics and were emblematic of the religious intolerance of the period.
events.name: Auto-da-fé in Madrid

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1680, the first documented tornado in America struck Cambridge, Massachusetts, resulting in the death of a servant. This event marked a significant moment in meteorological history as it was one of the earliest recorded instances of tornado activity in the New World.
events.name: First documented tornado in America

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1680, Popé, a Pueblo medicine man, initiated a coordinated attack against Spanish outposts in what is now New Mexico. This marked the beginning of the Pueblo Revolt, a significant uprising against Spanish colonial rule that aimed to restore indigenous autonomy.
events.name: Pueblo Revolt begins

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1680, the settlement of Karlskrona was founded in Sweden as the Royal Swedish Navy relocated there. This establishment was crucial for the naval power of Sweden and played a significant role in the country's maritime history.
events.name: Foundation of Karlskrona

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1680, during the Pueblo Revolt, the native Pueblo people successfully captured Santa Fe from Spanish colonists. This event was a critical turning point in the revolt, showcasing the Pueblo's resistance against colonial oppression.
events.name: Capture of Santa Fe

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1680, Comédie-Française was founded by decree of King Louis XIV as La maison de Molière in Paris. This establishment became a cornerstone of French theatrical culture and remains one of the oldest active theaters in the world.
events.name: Foundation of Comédie-Française

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1680, following the expiration of a four-month truce, Alcaid Omar, the Viceroy of Morocco, initiated a bombardment of the English fort at Tangier. This event marked a significant escalation in hostilities between England and Morocco during this period.
events.name: Bombardment of Tangier

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1680, Spanish troops launched a counterattack on Santa Fe, allowing the remaining Spanish forces in the besieged city to escape to El Paso, Texas. This event highlighted the ongoing conflict during the Pueblo Revolt and the struggle for control in the region.
events.name: Spanish counterattack on Santa Fe

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1680, Robert Boyle deposited his findings on the manufacturing of phosphorus from bone ash with The Royal Society of London for Improving Natural Knowledge. This discovery contributed significantly to the field of chemistry and the understanding of chemical processes.
events.name: Robert Boyle's phosphorus discovery

events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1680, the Great Comet of 1680 was first sighted by Gottfried Kirch, marking it as the first comet discovered by telescope. This event was significant in the field of astronomy and expanded the understanding of celestial phenomena.
events.name: Great Comet of 1680 sighted

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1680, the Green Ribbon Club, a precursor to the British Whigs, organized a procession in London to burn an effigy of the Pope for the second consecutive year. This event reflected the political and religious tensions of the time, particularly anti-Catholic sentiments.
events.name: Green Ribbon Club procession

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1680, the trial for treason of William Howard, 1st Viscount Stafford, concluded in the House of Lords after seven days. The Lords voted to convict him, leading to his execution on December 29, marking a significant moment in the political landscape of England.
events.name: Trial of William Howard

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1681, Prince Muhammad Akbar, son of Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb, initiated a civil war in India, declaring himself the new Mughal Emperor with the support of Rajput troops. This conflict highlighted the internal strife within the Mughal Empire during a period of significant political upheaval.
events.name: Civil War initiated by Muhammad Akbar

events.enhanced_description: In 1681, collections were made in England to support needy French refugees fleeing persecution. This act of charity reflected the social and political climate of the time, as well as the growing humanitarian efforts in England.
events.name: Collections for French Refugees

events.enhanced_description: In 1681, Welsh Quakers founded the communities of Havertown and Bryn Mawr in Pennsylvania. These settlements became important centers for Quaker culture and influence in the region.
events.name: Founding of Havertown and Bryn Mawr

events.enhanced_description: In 1681, the bell Emmanuel in Notre-Dame de Paris was recast, an important event for the iconic cathedral. This bell has since become a symbol of the church and its historical significance.
events.name: Recasting of the Bell Emmanuel

events.enhanced_description: In 1681, the Port of Honfleur in France was remodeled by the naval officer Abraham Duquesne. This project aimed to enhance the port's capacity and strategic importance.
events.name: Remodeling of the Port of Honfleur

events.enhanced_description: In 1681, the basilica of Santa Maria della Salute in Venice, designed by Baldassare Longhena, was dedicated. This baroque church remains a significant architectural landmark in the city.

image.caption: Santa Maria della Salute basilica in Venice.

events.name: Dedication of Santa Maria della Salute

events.enhanced_description: In 1681, the dodo, a flightless bird native to Mauritius, became extinct due to overhunting and habitat destruction. This event serves as a poignant reminder of the impact of human activity on biodiversity.
events.name: Extinction of the Dodo

events.enhanced_description: On January 3, 1681, the Treaty of Bakhchisarai was signed between the Ottoman vassal Crimean Khanate and the Russian Empire. This treaty was significant in shaping the geopolitical landscape of Eastern Europe and the Black Sea region.
events.name: Treaty of Bakhchisarai signed

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1681, King Charles II of England granted a land charter to William Penn to settle a debt of £16,000. This charter established the territory that would become Pennsylvania, a significant colony known for its religious tolerance and democratic principles.
events.name: Land Charter Granted to William Penn

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, 1681, King Charles II summoned the 'Oxford Parliament' to convene in Oxford instead of Westminster. However, this parliament was short-lived, being dissolved just seven days later, marking a significant moment in the political turmoil of the time.
events.name: Oxford Parliament Summoned

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1681, following the death of its last count, the territory of Palatinate-Landsberg passed into the possession of King Charles XI of Sweden. This transfer was part of the broader political landscape of Europe during the late 17th century.
events.name: Palatinate-Landsberg Succession

events.enhanced_description: The Canal du Midi, originally known as the Canal Royal de Languedoc, was officially opened on May 15, 1681. This engineering marvel connected the Mediterranean Sea to the Atlantic Ocean, facilitating trade and transportation in France.
events.name: Opening of the Canal du Midi

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1681, the Church of the East experienced a significant split when Pope Innocent XI proclaimed Mar Yousip as Joseph I, creating the 'Josephite line' of the Chaldean Catholic Church. This division added to the complexities of Christian leadership in the region.
events.name: Split of the Church of the East

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1681, Oliver Plunkett, the Roman Catholic Archbishop of Armagh, was executed at Tyburn after being falsely convicted of treason. His martyrdom marked a significant moment in the history of Catholicism in England, and he was canonized in 1975.
events.name: Execution of Oliver Plunkett

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1681, the Bombardment of Chios occurred during the French-Tripolitania War, part of France's broader campaign against the Barbary Pirates. This military action highlighted the ongoing conflicts in the Mediterranean region during the late 17th century.
events.name: Bombardment of Chios

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1681, English sea captain Robert Knox published his book 'An Historical Relation of the Island Ceylon,' detailing his 20-year imprisonment and escape from Ceylon. This work provided valuable insights into the island's culture and society during that period.
events.name: Publication of Robert Knox's Book

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1681, Gadadhar Singha ascended the throne as the Ahom King, taking the Tai name Supaatphaa. His reign marked a significant period in the history of the Ahom Kingdom in Assam, India.
events.name: Ascension of Gadadhar Singha

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1681, Titus Oates, known for his perjured testimony during the Popish Plot, was ordered to leave his state apartments in Whitehall. His declining fame led to his arrest and imprisonment for sedition, marking the end of his influence.
events.name: Titus Oates Arrested

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1681, France officially annexed the city of Strasbourg, which had previously been a free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire. This event was part of Louis XIV's expansionist policies in Europe.
events.name: Annexation of Strasbourg

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1681, Sir John Child was appointed as the new Governor of Bombay province, effectively becoming the Governor-General of all East India Company settlements in India. His tenure was marked by territorial expansion and conflict with the Mughal Empire.
events.name: John Child Becomes Governor of Bombay

events.enhanced_description: On November 20, 1681, Don Melchor de Navarra, Duke of Palata, arrived in Lima after a nearly 10-month voyage from Spain to assume the role of Viceroy of Peru. He succeeded Archbishop Melchor Liñán y Cisneros, who had governed since 1678.
events.name: Arrival of Don Melchor de Navarra in Lima

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1681, Cornelis Speelman was appointed as the new Governor-General of the Dutch East Indies. He formed an alliance with Sultan Amangkurat II and led military actions to suppress a rebellion, solidifying Dutch control in the region.
events.name: Cornelis Speelman Becomes Governor-General of Dutch East Indies

events.enhanced_description: On November 29, 1681, a storm struck the Isthmus of Panama, sinking the Spanish Navy's ship Nuestra Señora de Encarnación in the Chagres River. The wreckage was discovered in 2011, nearly 340 years later, largely intact with its cargo.
events.name: Storm Sinks Spanish Navy Ship

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1681, another ship from the Spanish Navy's Flota de Tierra Firma, Nuestra Señora de la Soledad, sank in the Chagres River, resulting in the loss of its 280 crew members. This disaster highlighted the perils faced by maritime expeditions during this period.
events.name: Nuestra Señora de la Soledad Sinks

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1681, Wu Shifan, the grandson of the Chinese general Wu Sangui, committed suicide in Kunming, effectively ending the eight-year Revolt of the Three Feudatories against the Kangxi Emperor and the Qing dynasty. This event marked a significant consolidation of Qing power in China.

image.caption: Map of the Revolt of the Three Feudatories in the Qing dynasty.
image.credit: SY — Own work
image.date_qualification: Created 2017-07-15; this is not the depicted event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: End of the Revolt of the Three Feudatories

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1681, King Charles II signed a warrant for the construction of the Royal Hospital Chelsea in London, intended to care for wounded and retired soldiers. This institution became a significant symbol of the British commitment to its veterans.
events.name: Royal Hospital Chelsea Warrant Signed

events.enhanced_description: In 1682, Celia Fiennes, a noblewoman and traveler, embarked on her extensive journeys across Britain, aiming to document the towns, cities, and great houses of the country. Her travels would continue until at least 1712, significantly contributing to the understanding of English geography and society during that period.
events.name: Celia Fiennes begins her journeys across Britain

events.enhanced_description: In 1682, the Richard Wall House was constructed in Pennsylvania, which is believed to be the longest continuously inhabited residence in the United States. This historic structure reflects the early colonial architecture and lifestyle of the time.
events.name: The Richard Wall House is built

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1682, the Republic of Genoa imposed a ban on unauthorized printing of newspapers and handwritten newssheets. This ban was lifted after three months, reflecting the tensions between censorship and the press during this period.
events.name: Genoa's Printing Ban

events.enhanced_description: James Renwick, a Scottish minister and prominent Covenanter, published the Declaration of Lanark as a statement of resistance against the oppressive policies of the Scottish government towards dissenting religious views. This declaration called for the preservation of the Presbyterian faith and highlighted the injustices faced by the Covenanters.
events.name: Declaration of Lanark

events.enhanced_description: In preparation for a conflict with the Holy Roman Empire, the Ottoman Empire mobilized its army, marking the beginning of military actions that would culminate in the significant Battle of Vienna in 1683. This mobilization was part of the broader tensions between the Ottoman Empire and European powers during this period.
events.name: Mobilization of the Ottoman Army

events.enhanced_description: The Opéra du Quai au Foin opened its doors in Brussels, becoming the first public theater in the city. This establishment marked a significant development in the cultural landscape of Brussels, providing a venue for theatrical performances and contributing to the flourishing arts scene of the time.
events.name: Opening of the Opéra du Quai au Foin

events.enhanced_description: A major fire swept through Edo (modern-day Tokyo) on the 28th day of the 12th month in the year Tenna 1, causing widespread destruction. This event highlighted the vulnerability of urban centers to fire disasters during this period in Japan.
events.name: Great Fire of Edo

events.enhanced_description: Thomas Otway's classic play 'Venice Preserv'd or A Plot Discover'd' premiered at the Duke's Theatre in London. This play is notable for its exploration of themes such as love, betrayal, and political intrigue, and it remains a significant work in the canon of English drama.
events.name: First Performance of Venice Preserv'd

events.enhanced_description: Construction began on the Royal Hospital Chelsea, a facility designed to care for elderly soldiers in London. This institution was part of a broader movement to provide support and care for veterans, reflecting the changing attitudes towards military service and welfare.
events.name: Construction of the Royal Hospital Chelsea

events.enhanced_description: René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, successfully navigated the waterways of North America and reached the mouth of the Mississippi River. This exploration was crucial in establishing French claims to the territory and expanding European knowledge of the region.
figures: René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle

image.caption: Portrait of René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, by Charles André Waltner.
image.credit: Charles André Waltner (1846-1925) — Sulte - Histoires des Canadiens-français, 1608-1880, tome II, 1882 (page 3)
image.date_qualification: 1882; portrait postdates the 1682 event by two centuries.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: René-Robert Cavelier reaches the Mississippi River

events.enhanced_description: At the mouth of the Mississippi River, near modern Venice, Louisiana, Robert de La Salle buried an engraved plate and a cross, claiming the territory for France as La Louisiane. This act symbolized France's territorial ambitions in North America and laid the groundwork for future colonization.
events.name: Claiming La Louisiane

events.enhanced_description: Louis XIV of France officially moved his court to the Palace of Versailles, a decision that would have profound implications for French politics and culture. This relocation symbolized the consolidation of royal power and the establishment of Versailles as the center of political life in France.
events.name: Louis XIV moves court to Versailles

events.enhanced_description: Upon the death of Tsar Feodor III of Russia, his younger brother Ivan was passed over in favor of their half-brother Peter, who was only 10 years old. This decision set the stage for a power struggle that would shape the future of the Russian monarchy.
events.name: Death of Tsar Feodor III and succession

events.enhanced_description: The Moscow Uprising of 1682 erupted when a mob, enraged by the rejection of Prince Ivan and rumors of his death, stormed the Kremlin. This violent revolt resulted in the lynching of boyars and military leaders, ultimately leading to the co-rule of Ivan V and Peter I as a compromise between their respective factions.
events.name: Moscow Uprising of 1682

events.enhanced_description: The English trading freighter Johanna was wrecked off the coast of South Africa, marking a significant loss for Britain's East India Company. This incident highlighted the dangers faced by maritime traders during this era and the challenges of navigating treacherous waters.
events.name: Wreck of the Johanna

events.enhanced_description: The city of Bandar Lampung was founded on the island of Sumatra, Indonesia. This establishment marked an important development in the region's urbanization and trade, contributing to the historical and cultural landscape of Sumatra.
events.name: Foundation of Bandar Lampung

events.enhanced_description: Ivan V and Peter I were crowned as joint Tsars of Russia at the Cathedral of the Dormition in Moscow. Their coronation was a result of the political compromise following the Moscow Uprising, with their older sister Sophia exercising actual power for the next seven years.
events.name: Coronation of Ivan V and Peter I

events.enhanced_description: Iyasus succeeded his father, Yohannes I, as Emperor of Ethiopia. His ascension marked a continuation of the Solomonic dynasty and was significant for the political and religious landscape of Ethiopia during this period.
events.name: Ascension of Emperor Iyasus

events.enhanced_description: The Ottoman Empire declared war on the Holy Roman Empire, initiating plans to attack Vienna. This declaration was part of the larger conflict that would lead to the pivotal Battle of Vienna in 1683, significantly impacting the balance of power in Europe.
events.name: Ottoman Declaration of War

events.enhanced_description: Mount Vesuvius began a period of volcanic activity that lasted for ten days, a reminder of the volcano's potential for catastrophic eruptions. This activity was closely monitored due to the historical significance of Vesuvius in the region.
events.name: Volcanic Activity of Vesuvius

events.enhanced_description: Comet Halley was observed from various locations on Earth after reaching a visible magnitude of 2. Notable astronomers such as Arthur Storer in Maryland and Johannes Hevelius in Danzig documented its appearance, contributing to the understanding of comets and their periodic nature.

image.caption: Babylonian tablet recording Halley’s Comet.
image.credit: The original uploader was Linguica at English Wikipedia . — Transferred from en.wikipedia to Commons by Calliopejen1 using CommonsHelper .
image.date_qualification: The image description identifies the tablet as recording an appearance in 164 BC, not the 1682 observation. Original image date is an upload date, not a depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Observation of Comet Halley

events.enhanced_description: Following the Bideford witch trial, three women were hanged in Exeter, marking one of the last known executions for witchcraft in England. This event reflects the intense social and legal pressures surrounding witchcraft accusations during this period.
events.name: Bideford Witch Trial Executions

events.enhanced_description: Bishop Gore School was founded in Swansea, Wales, contributing to the educational landscape of the region. This establishment reflects the growing emphasis on education during the period.
events.name: Foundation of Bishop Gore School

events.enhanced_description: Trinh Can ascended as the new ruler of Tonkin, located in northern Vietnam, following the death of his father, Trinh Tac. His reign initiated a series of reforms aimed at consolidating power and improving governance in the region.
events.name: Trinh Can becomes ruler of Tonkin

events.enhanced_description: Sultan Mehmed IV departed from Istanbul for Adrianople, marking a significant movement of the Ottoman leadership during a time of military preparations against the Holy Roman Empire. This journey was part of the broader strategic maneuvers leading up to the Battle of Vienna.
events.name: Departure of Sultan Mehmed IV

events.enhanced_description: Kara Mustafa, the Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire, departed with the Ottoman army to Adrianople, preparing for the impending conflict with the Holy Roman Empire. His leadership would play a crucial role in the events leading to the Battle of Vienna.
events.name: Departure of Kara Mustafa

events.enhanced_description: William Penn founded the city of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, as a place of religious freedom and tolerance. This city would later become a significant cultural and political center in the United States.
events.name: Founding of Philadelphia

events.enhanced_description: A devastating fire destroyed nearly 1,000 houses in Wapping, London, highlighting the ongoing risks of urban fires in densely populated areas. This event underscored the need for improved fire safety measures in the city.
events.name: Great Fire of Wapping

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1682, William Penn met with Charles Calvert, 3rd Baron Baltimore, to discuss the boundary between the colonies of Pennsylvania and Maryland. This meeting was crucial as it established the 40-degree north latitude line, which would limit Pennsylvania's access to the sea, prompting Penn to propose the purchase of some Maryland territory.
events.name: William Penn meets with Charles Calvert, 3rd Baron Baltimore

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1682, colonists from the German electorate of Brandenburg arrived at Akwidaa on the Brandenburger Gold Coast, present-day Ghana. They began constructing a fort at what is now known as Princes Town just five days later, marking a significant moment in the colonial expansion of Brandenburg.
events.name: Colonists from Brandenburg arrive at Akwidaa

events.enhanced_description: In 1683, Pedro II ascended to the throne of Portugal after serving as regent since 1668 for his older brother Afonso VI. His reign marked a significant period in Portuguese history, characterized by efforts to stabilize the kingdom and navigate the complexities of European politics.
events.name: Pedro II becomes King of Portugal

events.enhanced_description: In December 1683, the River Thames froze solid, allowing for a Frost Fair to be held on its surface. This event was part of a series of harsh winters in England and became a unique cultural phenomenon, showcasing the resilience and creativity of Londoners.

image.caption: Photograph of a Southwark memorial engraving about the River Thames frost fairs.
image.credit: Photograph by Mike Peel ( www.mikepeel.net ). Engraving by Richard Kindersley. — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photograph dated 2009-09-12; the image shows a later memorial engraving, not an event scene.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Frost Fair on the Thames

events.enhanced_description: In 1683, George Ducas, the Ottoman-installed Prince of Moldavia, was arrested by Polish authorities while returning to Bucharest after the defeat at the Battle of Vienna. His arrest marked a significant shift in power dynamics in the region following the battle.

image.caption: A seal of George Duca on a charter bearing the coats of arms of Moldavia and Wallachia.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — https://armyinform.com.ua/2022/02/19/george-duka-gospodar-moldovy-i-ukrayiny/
image.date_qualification: The seal is documented on a charter dated 1 June 1680, before the reported 1683 arrest; this is not a depiction of the arrest.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: George Ducas arrested

events.enhanced_description: By 1683, wild boars were hunted to extinction in Britain, marking a significant loss in biodiversity. This event reflects the broader trends of wildlife management and hunting practices in early modern England.
events.name: Extinction of wild boars in Britain

events.enhanced_description: On January 5, 1683, the Brandenburger-African Company signed a treaty with representatives of the Ahanta tribe to establish the fort and settlement of Groß Friedrichsburg in present-day Ghana. This fort was named in honor of Frederick William, Elector of Brandenburg, marking a significant moment in the colonial history of the region.
events.name: Treaty signed for the establishment of Groß Friedrichsburg

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1683, the tragic opera Phaëton, composed by Jean-Baptiste Lully with a libretto by Philippe Quinault, premiered at the Palace of Versailles. This opera is notable for its elaborate staging and music, reflecting the grandeur of the French Baroque period.
events.name: Premiere of the opera Phaëton

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1683, Gove's Rebellion erupted in the Province of New Hampshire as a revolt against the Royal Governor, Edward Cranfield. The rebellion was led by Edward Gove, who, along with most participants, was arrested and later convicted of treason, although he was pardoned three years later.
events.name: Gove's Rebellion breaks out

events.enhanced_description: On February 7, 1683, the opera Giustino, composed by Giovanni Legrenzi, premiered in Venice. This opera, which tells the story of the Byzantine Emperor Justin, showcases the rich musical traditions of the time and reflects the cultural vibrancy of Venice.
events.name: Premiere of the opera Giustino

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1683, Ageng Tirtayasa, the Sultan of Banten, was captured by soldiers hired by the Dutch East India Company. This event marked a significant moment in the struggle between local rulers and colonial powers in Indonesia.
events.name: Capture of Ageng Tirtayasa

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1683, a battle took place at Kalyan, near Bombay, between the Maratha Empire and the Mughal Empire. Maratha General Hambirrao Mohite achieved a decisive victory over the local Mughal official, Ranamast Khan, showcasing the growing power of the Maratha forces.
events.name: Battle at Kalyan

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1683, a great fire broke out in Newmarket, Suffolk, consuming half the houses in the town and forcing King Charles II, who was in residence, to flee. This event highlighted the vulnerabilities of urban centers in the 17th century.
events.name: Great fire in Newmarket

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1683, authorized representatives of King John III Sobieski of Poland and Emperor Leopold I of the Holy Roman Empire signed a military alliance treaty in Warsaw. This alliance would play a crucial role in the defense against the Ottoman Empire's advances into Europe.
events.name: Military alliance treaty signed

events.enhanced_description: On April 10, 1683, Charles V, Duke of Lorraine, was appointed commander of the Imperial Army of the Holy Roman Empire. His leadership would be pivotal in the military campaigns against the Ottoman forces during the Great Turkish War.
events.name: Charles V appointed commander of the Imperial Army

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1683, Sultan Mehmed IV of the Ottoman Empire entered Belgrade, a strategic city in the ongoing conflict with the Habsburg Monarchy. This event marked a significant moment in the Ottoman campaign in Central Europe.
events.name: Sultan Mehmed IV enters Belgrade

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1683, the Ashmolean Museum opened in Oxford, England, becoming the world's first university museum. It was established to house the collections of Elias Ashmole and has since played a significant role in the study of art and archaeology.
events.name: The Ashmolean Museum opens

events.enhanced_description: On June 12, 1683, the Rye House Plot to assassinate King Charles II of England was discovered. This conspiracy highlighted the political tensions of the time and led to significant repercussions for those involved.
events.name: Rye House Plot discovered

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1683, Admiral Shi Lang of the Qing dynasty led a fleet of 300 ships with 20,000 troops from Tongshan, Fujian, towards the Kingdom of Tungning in modern-day Taiwan. This military expedition aimed to quell the kingdom and assert Qing control over the region.
events.name: Admiral Shi Lang sails towards Tungning

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1683, a massive Ottoman force of 173,000 troops arrived at Vienna, initiating a siege that would become one of the pivotal moments in the struggle between the Ottoman Empire and the Habsburg Monarchy. The siege would ultimately lead to a significant turning point in European history.
events.name: Ottoman siege of Vienna begins

events.enhanced_description: On July 16, 1683, the Battle of Penghu took place, where Qing Chinese admiral Shi Lang decisively defeated the naval forces of Zheng Keshuang. This victory was instrumental in the Qing dynasty's efforts to consolidate control over Taiwan and its surrounding islands.
events.name: Battle of Penghu

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1683, Lord Russell was executed for his involvement in the Rye House Plot against King Charles II. The execution was carried out by the notorious royal executioner Jack Ketch, who infamously prolonged Russell's suffering during the beheading.
events.name: Execution of Lord Russell

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1683, Turhan, the Valide Sultan of the Ottoman Empire and mother of Sultan Mehmed IV, died at the age of 56. Her death marked the end of the Sultanate of Women, a period characterized by the significant influence of women in the Ottoman court.
events.name: Death of Turhan, Valide Sultan

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1683, Francesco Maria Imperiale Lercari was appointed as the new Doge of the Republic of Genoa. His leadership would influence the political landscape of Genoa during a time of significant change in the Mediterranean region.

image.caption: Claude-Guy Hallé’s painting of Doge Francesco Maria Imperiale Lercari making reparations to Louis XIV.
image.credit: Claude-Guy Hallé — w:de:Bild:Versailles1685.jpg . Voir aussi les Collections du château de Versailles .
image.date_qualification: Painted in 1715, depicting an event dated 15 May 1685; not contemporary with Lercari becoming Doge in 1683.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Francesco Maria Imperiale Lercari becomes Doge

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1683, Bahadur, the son of Emperor Aurangzeb of the Mughal Empire, was dispatched along with other nobles to invade Konkan, a region under the control of the Maratha Empire. This military action was part of the ongoing conflict between the Mughals and the Marathas.
events.name: Bahadur dispatched for invasion of Konkan

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1683, Thomas Dongan, the Earl of Limerick, was appointed as the new British Colonial Governor of the Province of New York. He implemented major reforms aimed at restoring public order and rescuing the province from financial instability.

locations.name: New York, New York, United States

events.name: Thomas Dongan takes office as Governor of New York

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1683, Qing Chinese admiral Shi Lang received the formal surrender of Zheng Keshuang, marking the collapse of the Kingdom of Tungning. This event led to the incorporation of Tungning into the Qing Empire, significantly altering the political landscape of Taiwan.
events.name: Zheng Keshuang surrenders to Shi Lang

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Vienna, fought on September 12, 1683, marked a decisive victory for the Holy League against the Ottoman Empire. The arrival of a coalition force led by Polish King Jan III Sobieski broke the siege of Vienna, halting the Ottoman advance into Central Europe and turning the tide in the struggle between the two powers.
events.name: Battle of Vienna

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1683, Shi Lang, a Chinese admiral, reached Taiwan and established control over the area, specifically modern-day Kaohsiung. This event marked a significant step in the Qing dynasty's efforts to assert dominance over Taiwan and integrate it into the Chinese empire.
events.name: Shi Lang occupies Taiwan

events.enhanced_description: Germantown, a neighborhood in Philadelphia, was founded on October 6, 1683, as the first permanent German settlement in North America. This settlement played a crucial role in the development of German-American culture and heritage in the United States.
events.name: Founding of Germantown

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1683, Louis XIV of France entered into a morganatic marriage with Madame de Maintenon in a secret ceremony following the death of his queen consort, Maria Theresa of Spain. This union reflected the complexities of royal marriages and the personal life of one of France's most famous monarchs.
events.name: Louis XIV's morganatic marriage

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1683, the English crown colony of the Province of New York was subdivided into 12 counties, including Albany, Dutchess, and Kings. This reorganization was part of the colonial administration's efforts to manage the growing population and land claims in the region.
events.name: Subdivision of Province of New York

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1683, Algernon Sidney, a prominent opponent of King Charles II of England, was executed after being found guilty of treason. His death marked a significant moment in the political landscape of England, reflecting the tensions between monarchy and republicanism.
events.name: Execution of Algernon Sidney

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1683, Kara Mustafa Pasha, the Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire, was executed on the orders of Sultan Mehmed IV after being blamed for the Ottoman defeat at the Battle of Vienna. His execution in Belgrade symbolized the internal strife within the Ottoman leadership following military failures.
events.name: Execution of Kara Mustafa Pasha

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1683, Richard Keigwin led a rebellion against the East India Company in Bombay, successfully ousting Governor Sir John Child. This revolt highlighted the tensions between colonial authorities and local leaders in India during the period of British expansion.
events.name: Richard Keigwin's rebellion

events.enhanced_description: In January 1684, a significant conversation took place in London among Edmond Halley, Christopher Wren, and Robert Hooke, where Hooke claimed to have derived the inverse-square law and other laws of planetary motion. This discussion highlighted the collaborative nature of scientific discovery during the period.
events.name: Conversation of Halley, Wren, and Hooke

events.enhanced_description: The Temnongata, the earliest form of what would later become the University of Tokyo, was established in 1684. This institution laid the groundwork for modern higher education in Japan, evolving significantly over the centuries.
events.name: Establishment of Temnongata, precursor to the University of Tokyo

events.enhanced_description: In 1684, Japanese poet Ihara Saikaku composed an astounding 23,500 verses in just 24 hours at the Sumiyoshi-taisha shrine in Osaka. This remarkable feat showcased his extraordinary talent and the cultural richness of the Edo period.
events.name: Ihara Saikaku's Verse Composition

events.enhanced_description: In 1684, the British East India Company received permission from Chinese authorities to establish a trading station in Canton. This marked a significant step in the expansion of British trade interests in China, particularly in tea.
events.name: British East India Company in Canton

events.enhanced_description: In 1684, John Bunyan published the second part of his influential work, The Pilgrim's Progress. This allegorical tale has had a lasting impact on Christian literature and continues to be widely read today.
events.name: Publication of The Pilgrim's Progress

events.enhanced_description: On January 5, 1684, King Charles II of England granted the title Duke of St Albans to his illegitimate son, Charles Beauclerk. This act reflected the complexities of royal lineage and the social dynamics of the English court.
events.name: Duke of St Albans title granted

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1684, a coach and six horses drove over the frozen River Thames, demonstrating its solidity during the Great Frost. This event led to the establishment of a Frost Fair, where streets of booths were set up, attracting thousands of visitors.
events.name: Thames Frost Fair

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1684, Marcantonio Giustinian was elected as the Doge of Venice. His election came during a time of political complexity for the Venetian Republic, as it navigated its position among European powers.
events.name: Election of Marcantonio Giustinian

events.enhanced_description: On February 7, 1684, Morocco regained control of Tangier from England, which had held the port since 1661. The English evacuation involved the destruction of fortifications built during their occupation, marking a significant shift in colonial power dynamics in North Africa.
events.name: Morocco retakes Tangier

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1684, Dumitrașcu Cantacuzino returned to the throne of Moldavia for a third time. His reign was short-lived, as he was overthrown just 14 months later, reflecting the turbulent political landscape of the region.
events.name: Dumitrașcu Cantacuzino returns to Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1684, the Great Frost that had frozen the River Thames and much of Britain came to an end. This event not only affected the environment but also had social implications, as the Frost Fair held during the freeze became a notable cultural event.
events.name: End of the Great Frost

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1684, a treaty was signed between German colonists from Brandenburg-Prussia and African chiefs in what is now Ghana, allowing the construction of a second fort on the Brandenburger Gold Coast. This event marked the expansion of European colonial interests in West Africa.
events.name: Treaty with African chiefs

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1538, the Holy League was formed, an alliance of Christian nations including the Papal States, the Republic of Venice, and Spain, directed by Pope Paul III and Venetian Senator Alvise Badoer. This coalition aimed to counter the Ottoman threat in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Formation of the Holy League

events.enhanced_description: On March 19, 1684, the Tenna era ended in Japan, marking the beginning of the Jōkyō era as royal astronomer Shibukawa Shunkai instituted a new calendar system. This change reflected Japan's efforts to modernize and align its timekeeping with scientific observations.
events.name: End of the Tenna era in Japan

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1684, the Republic of Venice declared war on the Ottoman Empire, marking the start of the Morean War. The conflict was primarily fought over control of the Peloponnese, a region of strategic importance in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Beginning of the Morean War

events.enhanced_description: Beginning on May 18, 1684, the French Navy, under the command of Abraham Duquesne, initiated a 10-day bombardment of Genoa during the War of the Reunions. The assault resulted in significant destruction, with two-thirds of the city damaged or destroyed.
events.name: Bombardment of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1684, after a six-week siege, Luxembourg City fell to the French Army, marking a significant territorial gain for France from Spain. This event was part of the larger conflict involving the Spanish Netherlands.
events.name: Siege of Luxembourg City

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1684, Francisco de Távora, the Viceroy of Portuguese India, issued an order prohibiting the use of the Konkani language among indigenous residents, mandating the adoption of Portuguese instead. This policy aimed to enforce cultural assimilation in the colony.
events.name: Prohibition of Konkani in Goa

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1684, René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, embarked on an expedition from France to establish a French colony at the mouth of the Mississippi River. He landed at Matagorda Bay, Texas, believing he was near the Mississippi, and established Fort St. Louis.
figures: René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle
events.name: René-Robert Cavelier's Expedition

events.enhanced_description: In August 1684, Edmond Halley visited Cambridge to engage in discussions with Isaac Newton regarding planetary motion. This meeting was pivotal in the development of Newton's theories that would later revolutionize the understanding of gravity.
events.name: Discussion on Planetary Motion

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1684, during the Morean War, the Republic of Venice successfully captured the Ottoman fortress of Santa Maura. This victory was part of Venice's broader campaign to reclaim territories in the Peloponnese.
events.name: Siege of Santa Maura

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1684, France under Louis XIV signed the Truce of Ratisbon with both the Holy Roman Empire and Spain, effectively ending hostilities in the War of the Reunions. This truce marked a significant diplomatic achievement for France.
events.name: Truce of Ratisbon

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1684, during the Morean War, the Republic of Venice captured the fortress town of Preveza from the Ottoman Empire. This strategic victory further solidified Venetian control over parts of Greece.
events.name: Capture of Preveza

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1684, Hotta Masatoshi, the Chief Minister of Japan, was assassinated. His death left Shōgun Tokugawa Tsunayoshi without adequate advisors, leading to a series of impractical edicts that caused hardships for the Japanese populace.
events.name: Assassination of Hotta Masatoshi

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1684, James Renwick, a Scottish minister and Covenanter, posted his 'Apologetical Declaration' on church doors and market crosses in Cambusnethan. This act was a significant protest against the attempts by the monarchy to control the church in Scotland.
events.name: James Renwick's Apologetical Declaration

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1684, Richard Keigwin, who had previously taken control of Bombay, returned authority to the East India Company and its envoy, Sir Thomas Grantham. This transfer marked a significant moment in the governance of Bombay.
events.name: Return of Control of Bombay

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1684, Isaac Newton's derivation of Kepler's laws from his theory of gravity was presented to the Royal Society by Edmond Halley. This work was foundational in the development of classical mechanics.
events.name: Newton's Laws of Planetary Motion

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1684, the Tibet–Ladakh–Mughal War concluded with the signing of a treaty at Tingmosgang between the 5th Dalai Lama and King Delek Namgyal of Ladakh. The agreement established respect for Ladakh's sovereignty in exchange for non-invitation of foreign armies.
events.name: End of the Tibet–Ladakh–Mughal War

events.enhanced_description: In 1685, the Qing dynasty's army attacked the Russian post at Albazin, during the reigns of the Kangxi Emperor and dual Russian rulers Ivan V and Peter I, leading to escalating tensions that would culminate in the Treaty of Nerchinsk in 1689.
events.name: Qing Dynasty Attack on Albazin

events.enhanced_description: In 1685, Adam Baldridge established a pirate base at Île Sainte-Marie, Madagascar, which became a notorious haven for pirates in the Indian Ocean, contributing to the region's maritime history.
events.name: Founding of Pirate Base at Île Sainte-Marie

events.enhanced_description: In 1685, Alice Molland was sentenced to death for witchcraft in Exeter, marking her as the last known person in England to face such a sentence, reflecting the waning but still present fears of witchcraft during this period.
events.name: Last Witchcraft Sentence in England

events.enhanced_description: In 1685, the Old Dutch Church was constructed in Sleepy Hollow, New York, later becoming famous as the setting for Washington Irving's tale of the Headless Horseman, intertwining local history with American folklore.

image.caption: Postcard depicting the Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow in Sleepy Hollow, New York.
image.credit: scanned by Dave Parker, cropped by Before My Ken — scnnned postcard, dated 1907
image.date_qualification: Image is dated 1907; it is not evidence of the church’s construction date.
image.image_date: original from 1907; scanned 10 June, 2007, cropped 6 February 2008
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Construction of the Old Dutch Church of Sleepy Hollow

events.enhanced_description: In February and March 1685, during the Morean War, the Ottoman serasker Halil Pasha led an invasion of the Mani Peninsula in Greece, compelling local leaders to surrender hostages as a demonstration of Ottoman authority in the region.
events.name: Morean War: Ottoman Invasion of Mani Peninsula

events.enhanced_description: In March 1685, Louis XIV of France enacted the Code Noir, a decree that regulated the treatment of enslaved people in French colonies, legitimizing the use of slavery and establishing harsh penalties for those who disobeyed its provisions.
events.name: Code Noir

events.enhanced_description: On March 28, 1685, an attack on Mughal envoy Khwajah Abdur Rahim outside Bijapur Fort led to a prolonged siege by forces under Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb, lasting 15 months before the city ultimately surrendered.
events.name: Siege of Bijapur

events.enhanced_description: On April 16, 1685, Wara Dhammaraza ascended to the throne as the new King of Arakan, following the death of his brother, Thiri Thuriya, marking a significant transition in the region's leadership.
events.name: Wara Dhammaraza Becomes King of Arakan

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1685, King James II of England was crowned at Westminster Abbey, alongside his Queen Consort, Mary of Modena, in a ceremony that underscored the political and religious tensions of the time.
events.name: Coronation of King James II

events.enhanced_description: On May 7, 1685, during the Morean War, Ottoman forces engaged and defeated Venetian irregulars in the Battle on Vrtijeljka, showcasing the ongoing conflict between the two powers in the region.
events.name: Battle on Vrtijeljka

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1685, during the period known as The Killing Time, five Covenanters, including Margaret Wilson, were executed in Wigtown, Scotland, for their refusal to acknowledge King James II as the head of the Church, becoming martyrs for their faith.
events.name: The Killing Time: Execution of Covenanters
