events.name: HMS Coronation and HMS Harwich are lost in a storm

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1691, during the War of the Grand Alliance, English and Dutch forces faced defeat against the French in the Battle of Leuze. This battle was part of the larger conflict involving multiple European powers.
events.name: War of the Grand Alliance: Battle of Leuze

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1691, the Treaty of Limerick was signed, effectively ending the Williamite War in Ireland and guaranteeing civil rights to Roman Catholics. This treaty was significant in the context of Irish history and the ongoing struggles for religious rights.
events.name: The Treaty of Limerick is signed

events.enhanced_description: On October 17, 1691, the Massachusetts Bay Colony and Plymouth Colony were united into a single entity by an act of the King and Queen of England. This unification was a significant step in the consolidation of colonial governance in New England.
events.name: Massachusetts Bay Colony and Plymouth Colony are united

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1691, a Form of Prayer and Thanksgiving was celebrated in all Anglican churches in Britain and Ireland by order of Archbishop Tillotson. This event reflected the religious sentiments of the time following the Williamite War.
events.name: A Form of Prayer and Thanksgiving is celebrated

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1691, during the Morean War, Captain Luca Dalla Rocca of Naples betrayed Venice by surrendering the fortress of Gramvousa to the Ottoman Turks in exchange for money and sanctuary. This act had significant implications for Venetian control in the region.

image.caption: Photograph of the Venetian fort on Gramvousa, with the sea.
image.credit: Levenius — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2007-08-16; depicts the site long after the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Captain Luca Dalla Rocca surrenders the fortress of Gramvousa

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1691, Patrick Sarsfield and 19,000 troops of the Irish Army, who had supported the Jacobite Rebellion, left Ireland to relocate to France. This exodus marked a significant moment in the aftermath of the Williamite War.
events.name: Patrick Sarsfield and troops relocate to France

events.enhanced_description: The Candlemas Massacre occurred on January 24, 1692, when French soldiers, led by missionary Louis-Pierre Thury, along with Abenaki and Penobscot warriors under Chief Madockawando, attacked the English settlement in York, Maine. This brutal assault resulted in the deaths of at least 75 residents, highlighting the violent conflicts during King William's War.
events.name: Candlemas Massacre

events.enhanced_description: On January 30, 1692, John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough, was dismissed from all his positions by the Earl of Nottingham on the orders of Queen Mary II. This event marked a significant political shift as Churchill was a key military leader and advisor to the crown during a tumultuous period in English history.
events.name: John Churchill is fired from his positions

events.enhanced_description: The Massacre of Glencoe took place on February 13, 1692, when forces loyal to Robert Campbell killed approximately 40 members of the Clan MacDonald of Glencoe. This brutal act was a result of political tensions and the delayed signing of an oath of allegiance to King William III, leading to one of Scotland's most infamous betrayals.

image.caption: Watercolour and bodycolour painting of Glencoe, Argyllshire, by Horatio McCulloch.
image.credit: The original uploader was Cactus.man at English Wikipedia . — Transferred from en.wikipedia to Commons by Off2riorob using CommonsHelper .
image.date_qualification: The image description gives “1864” for the depicted work; “21 January 2006” is identified as the original upload date, not the image date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Massacre of Glencoe

events.enhanced_description: The Salem witch trials commenced on March 1, 1692, in Salem Village, Massachusetts Bay Colony, when three women, including Tituba, were charged with witchcraft. This event marked the beginning of a series of trials that would lead to widespread hysteria and the execution of many accused individuals.

locations.name: Salem Village, Massachusetts Bay Colony, United States

events.name: Salem witch trials begin

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1692, the Kangxi Emperor of the Qing dynasty issued the Edict of Toleration, which recognized all members of the Roman Catholic Church and legalized their missionary activities in China. This edict marked a significant moment in the relationship between the Chinese state and foreign religions.
events.name: Kangxi Emperor issues Edict of Toleration

events.enhanced_description: On April 18, 1692, several residents of Salem, Massachusetts, including Giles Corey and Bridget Bishop, were arrested and charged with witchcraft. This event was part of the larger Salem witch trials, which led to a climate of fear and suspicion in the community.
events.name: Arrests during Salem witch trials

events.enhanced_description: The semi-opera The Fairy-Queen, composed by Henry Purcell and based on Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, premiered on May 2, 1692, at the Queen's Theatre in London. This performance is notable for its blend of music and drama, showcasing Purcell's significant contribution to English opera.
events.name: First performance of The Fairy-Queen

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1692, during the Nine Years' War, the Anglo-Dutch fleet achieved a significant victory at the Battle of Barfleur, breaking the French naval line and thwarting their plans to invade England. This battle was pivotal in maintaining naval supremacy in the region.
events.name: Battle of Barfleur

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1692, a devastating earthquake struck Port Royal, Jamaica, causing widespread destruction and a tsunami that submerged much of the city. The disaster resulted in an estimated 2,000 immediate deaths and led to further casualties from disease in the following months.

image.caption: Map showing shoreline changes caused by the 1692 Port Royal earthquake.
image.credit: I184.147.120.196 — Own work , based on information from the The College of Wooster
image.date_qualification: The map is dated 2011-10-10, not 1692.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Jamaica earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1692, during a famine in Mexico City, an angry mob set fire to the Viceroy's palace, igniting the archives within. Royal geographer Carlos de Sigüenza y Góngora played a crucial role in saving many important documents and artworks from destruction.
events.name: Mob torches Viceroy's palace in Mexico City

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1692, Bridget Bishop became the first victim of the Salem witch trials to be executed by hanging. Her trial and execution marked a turning point in the witch hunt hysteria that gripped the Massachusetts Bay Colony.
events.name: Bridget Bishop is hanged

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of La Hogue, which began on June 3, 1692, was a decisive naval engagement during the Nine Years' War, resulting in the further destruction of the French fleet. This battle solidified the Anglo-Dutch naval dominance in the conflict.
events.name: Battle of La Hogue

events.enhanced_description: The siege of Namur concluded on July 1, 1692, when Dutch General Menno van Coehoorn surrendered to King Louis XIV of France after five weeks of intense conflict. This event was part of the larger Nine Years' War, significantly impacting the balance of power in Europe.
events.name: Siege of Namur ends

events.enhanced_description: On July 5, 1692, wine shop owner Antoine Savetier and his wife were murdered in Lyon, leading to a notable investigation by peasant detective Jacques Aymar-Vernay. Aymar's efforts resulted in the capture of one perpetrator, showcasing early forms of detective work in criminal investigations.
events.name: Murder of Antoine Savetier and investigation

events.enhanced_description: The city of Ponce was founded on August 12, 1692, in Puerto Rico, becoming one of the island's most important urban centers. Its establishment marked a significant development in the Spanish colonization of the Caribbean.
events.name: Founding of Ponce

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1692, an earthquake measuring 5.8 on the Richter scale was felt across Brabant and parts of the Low Countries, Germany, and England. This seismic event caused significant alarm and damage in the affected regions.
events.name: Earthquake in Brabant

events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1692, Diego de Vargas led Spanish colonists in retaking Santa Fe, New Mexico, after a 12-year exile following the Pueblo Revolt of 1680. This event marked a significant moment in the Spanish reconsolidation of power in the region.

image.caption: Signature of Diego de Vargas Zapata Luján Ponce de León.
image.credit: Diego de Vargas Zapata Luján Ponce de León — National Park Service ( http://www.nps.gov/parkhistory/online_books/kcc/chap6e.htm )
image.date_qualification: A signature associated with Diego de Vargas, not a depiction of the 1692 retaking of Santa Fe. The saved image date is broad and does not support a display date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: Santa Fe, New Mexico, United States

events.name: Diego de Vargas retakes Santa Fe

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1692, Giles Corey was pressed to death in Salem, Massachusetts, as authorities attempted to coerce a confession of witchcraft from him during the infamous witch trials. His death became a symbol of the tragic consequences of the hysteria that gripped the community.
events.name: Giles Corey pressed to death

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1692, the last of those convicted of witchcraft during the Salem witch trials were hanged. By the end of the trials, a total of 14 women and 5 men had been executed, marking a dark chapter in colonial American history.
events.name: Last hangings of the Salem witch trials

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1692, the trial for sorcery of Anne Palles began in Denmark, where she confessed to giving her body and soul to Satan. The court found her guilty, and she was sentenced to death, reflecting the widespread fear of witchcraft in Europe during this period.
events.name: Trial of Anne Palles

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1692, a slave revolt in Barbados was violently suppressed by colonial authorities, highlighting the tensions and brutal realities of slavery in the Caribbean. This event marked a significant moment in the history of resistance against colonial oppression in the region.
events.name: Barbados Slave Revolt

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1692, the King of Spain officially donated lands that would become the municipalities of San Francisco and Mapulaca in Honduras. This act was part of the broader Spanish colonial efforts to establish and expand settlements in Central America.
events.name: Donation of Lands in Honduras

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1692, Mohamed bin Hajj Ali Thukkala ascended to the throne as Sultan Muhammad Ali IV of the Maldives. His reign marked a significant period in the history of the Maldives, characterized by political changes and interactions with colonial powers.
events.name: Sultan Muhammad Ali IV of the Maldives

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1692, William Mountfort's play 'Henry The Second, King Of England; With The Death Of Rosamond' premiered at the Drury Lane Theatre in London. This performance contributed to the rich tapestry of English theatre during the late 17th century.
events.name: First Performance of Henry The Second

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1692, John Goldsborough arrived in Madras as the new administrator of the British East India Company. His administration played a crucial role in the expansion of British influence in India during the late 17th century.
events.name: John Goldsborough in Madras

events.enhanced_description: On December 14, 1692, Maratha General Santaji Ghorpade achieved a significant victory against Mughal General Alimardan Khan, capturing him and bringing him back to fort Jinjee. This battle exemplified the ongoing conflict between the Maratha Empire and the Mughal Empire.
events.name: Battle of Jinjee

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1692, Nahum Tate was appointed as the new Poet Laureate of the United Kingdom, a position he held for 22 years. His tenure marked a significant period in English literature, contributing to the cultural landscape of the time.
events.name: Nahum Tate as Poet Laureate

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1692, the French ship Soleil Royal, a formidable three-decker warship armed with 104 guns, was launched at Brest Dockyard. This ship became a symbol of French naval power during the late 17th century.
events.name: Launch of Soleil Royal

events.enhanced_description: In a significant shift in trade policy, China centralized all foreign trade in Canton, restricting European ships from landing elsewhere. This decision had profound implications for international trade dynamics and colonial relations.
events.name: Concentration of foreign trade in Canton

events.enhanced_description: A significant religious schism occurred among Swiss and Alsatian Anabaptists, led by Jakob Ammann, resulting in the formation of the Mennonite Amish sect. This division reflected broader tensions within the Anabaptist movement regarding practices and beliefs.
events.name: Religious schism among Anabaptists

events.enhanced_description: The Knights of the Apocalypse were formed in Italy, reflecting the era's fascination with chivalric orders and religious themes. This organization contributed to the cultural landscape of the time.
events.name: Formation of the Knights of the Apocalypse

events.enhanced_description: The Academia Operosorum Labacensium was established in Ljubljana, Slovenia, contributing to the intellectual and cultural development of the region during the late 17th century.
events.name: Establishment of Academia Operosorum Labacensium

events.enhanced_description: Financier Richard Hoare relocated Hoare's Bank from Cheapside to Fleet Street in London, marking a significant development in the history of banking in England. This move reflected the growing importance of financial institutions in urban centers.

image.caption: The Golden Bottle sign at C. Hoare & Co., 37 Fleet Street, London.
image.credit: The wub — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2022-09-10; it does not depict the 1693 relocation.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Relocation of Hoare's Bank

events.enhanced_description: Italian barber Giovanni Paolo Feminis created Aqua Admirabilis, the earliest known form of eau de Cologne, which would later influence the fragrance industry significantly. This innovation marked a notable development in personal grooming and luxury goods.
events.name: Creation of Aqua Admirabilis

events.enhanced_description: John Locke published 'Some Thoughts Concerning Education,' a foundational text in educational philosophy that emphasized the importance of experience and environment in learning. This work influenced educational practices and theories for generations.
events.name: Publication of Some Thoughts Concerning Education

events.enhanced_description: William Penn published his proposal for a European federation in 'Essay on the Present and Future Peace of Europe,' advocating for peace and cooperation among nations. This work reflected his vision for a more harmonious international community.
events.name: William Penn's proposal for European federation

events.enhanced_description: Edmond Halley conducted a study of birth and death records in Breslau, producing a life table that consolidated data on mortality and longevity. This pioneering work laid the groundwork for modern actuarial science and demographic studies.
events.name: Edmond Halley's life table study

events.enhanced_description: Dimitrie Cantemir presented his work 'Kitâbu 'İlmi'l-Müsiki alâ Vechi'l-Hurûfât' to Sultan Ahmed II, which explored the melodic and rhythmic structures of Ottoman music. This comprehensive study included scores for around 350 works, showcasing Cantemir's contributions to musicology.
events.name: Presentation of Kitâbu 'İlmi'l-Müsiki alâ Vechi'l-Hurûfât

events.enhanced_description: On January 11, 1693, Mount Etna erupted, causing a devastating earthquake that resulted in the deaths of approximately 60,000 people in Sicily and Malta. This catastrophic event had profound effects on the local population and landscape.
events.name: Mount Etna Eruption

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1693, the College of William & Mary in Williamsburg, Virginia, was granted a Royal charter. This institution became one of the oldest colleges in the United States, playing a significant role in American education.
events.name: Royal Charter for College of William & Mary

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1693, the first women's magazine, titled 'The Ladies' Mercury,' was published in London by the Athenian Society. This publication marked a significant milestone in women's literature and media.
events.name: First Women's Magazine

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1693, Bozoklu Mustafa Pasha was appointed as the new Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire, succeeding Çalık Ali Pasha. His leadership was pivotal during a time of political and military challenges for the empire.
events.name: Bozoklu Mustafa Pasha as Grand Vizier

events.enhanced_description: In April 1693, Tituba, a slave convicted during the Salem witch trials, was released from jail in Boston after 13 months when an unknown purchaser paid her jail fees. Her case remains a significant part of American history regarding witchcraft and racial injustice.
events.name: Release of Tituba

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1693, Anne Palles became the last accused witch to be executed for witchcraft in Denmark. Convicted of sorcery, she was beheaded, marking the end of an era of witch trials in the country.
events.name: Execution of Anne Palles

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1693, King Louis XIV of France established the Order of Saint Louis, the first medal awarded to military personnel who were not members of the nobility. This order represented a significant shift in military honors and recognition.
events.name: Creation of the Order of Saint Louis

events.enhanced_description: On April 28, 1693, the 90-gun English Royal Navy warship HMS Windsor Castle was wrecked beyond repair on the Goodwin Sands. This incident underscored the dangers faced by naval vessels in treacherous waters.
events.name: Wreck of HMS Windsor Castle

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1693, forces of Louis XIV of France launched an attack on Heidelberg, the capital of the Electorate of the Palatinate. This military action was part of the broader conflicts of the Nine Years' War.
events.name: Louis XIV Attacks Heidelberg

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1693, Heidelberg was taken by invading French forces, leading to the surrender of Heidelberg Castle. The French subsequently destroyed parts of the castle using explosives, marking a significant event in the Nine Years' War.
events.name: Fall of Heidelberg Castle

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1693, the opera 'Didon' by French composer Henri Desmarets premiered at the Théâtre du Palais-Royal in Paris. This performance contributed to the rich cultural landscape of French opera during the Baroque period.
events.name: First Performance of Didon

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1759, the British fleet under Edward Boscawen defeated a French force commanded by Commodore Jean-François de La Clue-Sabran off the coast of Portugal in the Battle of Lagos. This engagement further weakened French naval capabilities during the Seven Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Lagos

events.enhanced_description: On July 17, 1693, a total lunar eclipse was visible in New Zealand and across the Pacific Ocean. This astronomical event was observed by many and contributed to the understanding of celestial phenomena.
events.name: Total Lunar Eclipse in New Zealand

events.enhanced_description: On July 29, 1693, during the Nine Years' War, William III of England faced defeat against French forces at the Battle of Landen, which included Irish Jacobite mercenaries. This battle was a critical moment in the ongoing conflict between England and France.
events.name: Battle of Landen

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1693, the Indian Ocean port of Pondicherry, the capital of French India, was captured by a 17-ship fleet from the Netherlands under the command of Laurens Pit the Younger. This event marked a significant shift in control over colonial territories in India.
events.name: Capture of Pondicherry

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1693, Francesco Invrea, King of Corsica, began a two-year term as the Doge of the Republic of Genoa. His leadership was significant in navigating the political landscape of the time.
events.name: Francesco Invrea as Doge of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: The siege of Charleroi marked a significant military engagement during the Nine Years' War, where French forces aimed to capture the strategically important fort from the Spanish. This event was part of a broader conflict involving multiple European powers vying for territorial control.
events.name: Siege of Charleroi

events.enhanced_description: King Louis XIV's letter to Pope Innocent XII signified a pivotal moment in the relationship between the French monarchy and the Catholic Church, as it marked the annulment of a previous declaration that had asserted the independence of the French clergy from papal authority.
events.name: Rescission of the Declaration of the Clergy of France

events.enhanced_description: King Manuel I of the Kingdom of Kongo was executed on the orders of his successor, Álvaro X, marking a violent transition of power within the kingdom. This event underscored the political instability and internal conflicts that plagued the Kongo during this period.

locations.name: Kingdom of Kongo, Zaire, Democratic Republic of the Congo

events.name: Execution of King Manuel I of Kongo

events.enhanced_description: William Congreve's comedy 'The Double-Dealer' premiered in London, showcasing the wit and social commentary characteristic of Restoration comedy. The play contributed to Congreve's reputation as a leading playwright of his time.

image.caption: Frontispiece illustration associated with William Congreve’s comedy The Double-Dealer.
image.credit: William Congreve — From frontispiece of comedy by Congreve dating back more than 200 years.
image.date_qualification: The image is a frontispiece associated with the play, not a depiction of its 1693 first performance; its depicted date is given as 1735–1740.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: First performance of The Double-Dealer

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Marsaglia, French forces under General Nicolas Catinat achieved a decisive victory over the Savoyard army, resulting in significant casualties for the latter. This battle was a critical moment in the ongoing conflicts of the Nine Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Marsaglia

events.enhanced_description: The fall of Charleroi to French forces marked a significant victory in the Nine Years' War, consolidating French control over the region and demonstrating the effectiveness of Louis XIV's military strategies.
events.name: Fall of Charleroi

events.enhanced_description: The Great Storm of 1693 caused extensive damage along the eastern coast of North America, altering river courses and reshaping coastlines from Virginia to Long Island. This natural disaster had lasting impacts on the geography and settlement patterns in the region.

locations.name: Virginia to Long Island, United States

events.name: The Great Storm

events.enhanced_description: King Charles II of Spain issued a royal edict that provided sanctuary in Spanish Florida for escaped slaves from the English colony of South Carolina, reflecting the complex social dynamics and colonial policies of the time.
events.name: Royal edict for escaped slaves

events.enhanced_description: General Santaji Ghorpade of the Maratha Empire faced defeat against General Himmat Khan of the Mughal Empire near Vikramhalli. This battle was part of the ongoing conflict between the Marathas and Mughals, showcasing the shifting power dynamics in India.
events.name: Defeat of General Santaji Ghorpade

events.enhanced_description: The Royal Navy frigate HMS Mordaunt, a 46-gun ship, tragically foundered off the coast of Cuba, highlighting the dangers faced by naval vessels during this period.

locations.name: Off the coast of Cuba, Cuba

events.name: Foundering of HMS Mordaunt

events.enhanced_description: A fleet of 30 English and Dutch ships successfully captured the French port of Saint-Malo, marking a significant naval victory during the Nine Years' War and demonstrating the effectiveness of allied maritime strategies.
events.name: Capture of Saint-Malo

events.enhanced_description: Diego de Vargas, the Spanish colonial governor, returned to Santa Fe and attempted to reassert control over the Pueblo people, leading to a siege that resulted in the surrender of the Pueblo defenders and the execution of rebels. This event highlighted the tensions between colonial authorities and indigenous populations.

locations.name: Santa Fe, New Mexico, United States

events.name: Siege of Santa Fe de Nuevo México

events.enhanced_description: The HMS Sussex, an 80-gun English Navy warship, embarked on its maiden voyage from Portsmouth, leading a fleet to the Mediterranean Sea. This voyage was significant for the Royal Navy's operational capabilities during the late 17th century.
events.name: Maiden voyage of HMS Sussex

events.enhanced_description: In 1694, the Lao empire of Lan Xang unofficially came to an end, marking a significant shift in the political landscape of Southeast Asia. This transition led to the fragmentation of the region into smaller principalities.
events.name: The Lao empire of Lan Xang unofficially ends

events.enhanced_description: In 1694, the infamous voyage of the English slave ship Hannibal concluded, resulting in the death of nearly half of the 692 enslaved individuals aboard. This event highlights the brutal realities of the Atlantic slave trade.
events.name: The notorious voyage of the English slave ship Hannibal ends

events.enhanced_description: In 1694, Rascians established a settlement on the banks of the Danube River, which would later develop into the city of Novi Sad. This settlement played a crucial role in the cultural and economic development of the region.
events.name: Rascians establish the settlement which will become Novi Sad

events.enhanced_description: In 1694, the Parker Tavern was constructed in Reading, Massachusetts, serving as a significant social and community hub in the early colonial period. The tavern became a gathering place for locals and travelers alike.

image.caption: Photograph of Parker Tavern, a historic house museum in Reading, Massachusetts.
image.credit: Swampyank at English Wikipedia — Own work
image.date_qualification: A 2008 photograph of the tavern, not a contemporary image of its construction in 1694.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Parker Tavern is built in Reading, Massachusetts

events.enhanced_description: On January 11, 1694, the Kiev Academy, which would later evolve into the National University of Ukraine, received official recognition from Tsar Ivan V of Russia. This marked a significant development in the educational landscape of Ukraine, establishing a foundation for higher education in the region.
events.name: Kiev Academy Recognition

events.enhanced_description: Francesco Morosini, the Doge of Venice, died after a tumultuous rule marked by military campaigns against the Ottoman Empire. His death marked the end of an era for Venice, which faced increasing challenges in maintaining its power and influence.
events.name: Death of Francesco Morosini

events.enhanced_description: Sir James Montgomery, arrested for conspiracy to restore King James to the throne, managed to escape custody and fled to France. This event underscored the political tensions and conflicts in Scotland during the late 17th century.
events.name: Escape of Sir James Montgomery

events.enhanced_description: On January 28, 1694, Alessandro Scarlatti's opera 'Pirro e Demetrio' premiered at the Teatro San Bartolomeo in Naples. This opera would later be adapted in London in 1708, becoming a significant work in the 18th-century operatic repertoire.
events.name: First Performance of Pirro e Demetrio

events.enhanced_description: On January 29, 1694, French missionary Jean-Baptiste Labat arrived in Martinique, marking his entry into the New World. His work in the Caribbean would significantly influence the spread of Catholicism and the cultural landscape of the region.
events.name: Jean-Baptiste Labat Arrives in the New World

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1694, the ship Ridderschap van Holland was lost at sea after departing from the Cape of Good Hope with a crew of 300, bound for Batavia (modern Jakarta, Indonesia). The ship never reached its destination and was never seen again, marking a tragic loss in maritime history.
events.name: Loss of the Ridderschap van Holland

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1694, the Quilombo dos Palmares, a settlement of escaped African slaves, was destroyed by bandeirantes led by Domingos Jorge Velho. The attack led to the flight of Zumbi, the last king of Palmares, who was later captured and executed, marking a significant event in the history of resistance against slavery in Brazil.
events.name: Destruction of Quilombo dos Palmares

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1694, Silvestro Valier was elected as the new Doge of Venice, succeeding the late Francesco Morosini. His election came during a period of political and economic challenges for the Venetian Republic.
events.name: Election of Silvestro Valier as Doge of Venice

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1694, the HMS Sussex treasure fleet, consisting of thirteen ships, was wrecked in the Mediterranean Sea off Gibraltar, resulting in the loss of approximately 1,200 lives. This disaster highlighted the perils of maritime trade during this period.
events.name: Wreck of the HMS Sussex Treasure Fleet

events.enhanced_description: On March 8, 1694, Peter II of Portugal established the Casa da Moeda do Brasil, a mint in Brazil that would play a crucial role in the colonial economy by producing currency for the region.
events.name: Formation of the Casa da Moeda do Brasil

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1694, Sheikh Yusuf, exiled from the Dutch East Indies, arrived at the Dutch Cape Colony aboard the ship De Voetboog. His arrival marked the introduction of Islam to South Africa, as he settled with his family and began to influence the local culture.
events.name: Sheikh Yusuf Arrives at the Dutch Cape Colony

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1694, the English Navy's 40-gun warship HMS Ruby captured the French privateer Entreprenant in battle. This event underscored the ongoing naval conflicts between England and France during this period.
events.name: Capture of the French Privateer Entreprenant

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1694, the French ship Diligente, commanded by René Duguay-Trouin, engaged in a battle against six Royal Navy ships led by David Mitchell. The encounter resulted in heavy losses for the Diligente's crew, and Duguay-Trouin was captured.

image.caption: Portrait of René Duguay-Trouin by Antoine Graincourt.
image.credit: Antoine Graincourt — Palace of Versailles
image.date_qualification: An 18th-century portrait of the battle commander, not a depiction of the 1694 naval engagement. The original image date is recorded as “18 th century date QS:P,+1750-00-00T00:00:00Z/7”; supported_display_date is null.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle involving the French ship Diligente

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1694, Frederick Augustus of Wettin ascended to the position of Elector of Saxony following the death of his brother, John George IV. His reign would later lead to his recognition as Augustus the Strong and his eventual kingship in Poland.
events.name: Frederick Augustus Becomes Elector of Saxony

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1694, the Battle of Torroella took place between the French and Spanish armies, each comprising around 24,000 troops. The French took advantage of fog to secure a victory, inflicting 3,000 casualties on the Spanish forces.
events.name: Battle of Torroella

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1694, the Tunisian-Algerian War commenced as Algerian troops crossed into Tunisia. This conflict marked a significant escalation in regional tensions and territorial disputes in North Africa.
events.name: Tunisian-Algerian War Begins

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1694, the Battle of Texel was fought near the Dutch island of Texel, where French Navy commander Jean Bart engaged a larger Dutch force. The battle resulted in the death of Dutch commander Hidde Sjoerds de Vries after being captured.
events.name: Battle of Texel

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1694, the Bank of England was founded through a Royal charter by the Whig-dominated Parliament, following a proposal by Scottish merchant William Paterson. This establishment marked the beginning of modern banking and government debt in England.
events.name: Foundation of the Bank of England

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1694, Sultan Husayn of the Safavid dynasty was crowned Shah of Persia in Isfahan, shortly after the death of his father, Suleiman I. His reign would be marked by internal strife and external pressures on the Safavid state.
events.name: Coronation of Sultan Husayn of Persia

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1694, the Dictionnaire de l'Académie française, the first official dictionary of the French language, was presented to King Louis XIV by Jacques de Tourreil and members of the Académie française. This work laid the groundwork for the standardization of the French language.
events.name: Presentation of the Dictionnaire de l'Académie française

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1694, the Great Fire of Warwick broke out, devastating half the town. The disaster prompted significant fundraising efforts for relief, including a notable contribution from Queen Anne.
events.name: Great Fire of Warwick

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1694, the Irpinia–Basilicata earthquake struck the Kingdom of Naples, causing widespread destruction and resulting in over 6,000 deaths. This earthquake was one of the deadliest natural disasters in the region's history.
events.name: Irpinia–Basilicata Earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1694, a hurricane struck Carlisle Bay in Barbados, sinking 27 British ships and resulting in approximately 3,000 casualties. This disaster highlighted the vulnerability of maritime activities in the Caribbean.
events.name: Hurricane Hits Carlisle Bay

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1694, a major windstorm began in the Scottish Highlands, spreading the Culbin Sands over a large area of farmland and burying the now-abandoned village of Culbin. This event had lasting effects on the local geography and agriculture.
events.name: Culbin Sands Windstorm

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1694, British/American colonial forces led by Sir William Phips attempted to seize Quebec from the French but ultimately failed. This event underscored the ongoing conflicts between British and French colonial powers in North America.
events.name: Failed Siege of Quebec

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1694, Queen Mary II of England established the Royal Hospital for Seamen at Greenwich, aimed at providing care for sick and injured sailors. This institution became a significant part of maritime healthcare in England.
events.name: Queen Mary II of England founds the Royal Hospital for Seamen at Greenwich

events.enhanced_description: On November 12, 1694, the Army of Algeria successfully captured Tunis after a three-month siege, marking the end of the Tunisian–Algerian War. The Bey of Tunis, Mohamed Bey El Mouradi, fled south, while Prince Muhammad ben Cheker was appointed as the new Dey.
events.name: The Army of Algeria captures Tunis

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1694, the Parliament of England enacted the Triennial Act, mandating that general elections be held every three years. This legislation aimed to ensure more regular accountability of the government to the electorate.
events.name: The Parliament of England passes the Triennial Act

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1694, Thomas Tenison was appointed as the Archbishop of Canterbury, a significant position in the Church of England. His tenure was marked by efforts to promote religious tolerance and reform within the church.
events.name: Thomas Tenison is appointed Archbishop of Canterbury

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1694, a total solar eclipse was visible across South America, captivating observers and contributing to the scientific understanding of celestial events. Such eclipses have historically been significant for both scientific inquiry and cultural interpretations.
events.name: A total solar eclipse is visible across South America

events.enhanced_description: The Great Famine of 1695–1697 severely impacted Scandinavia, leading to widespread food shortages and suffering. This famine was a significant event in the region's history, affecting population dynamics and social structures.
events.name: Great Famine of 1695–1697 in Scandinavia

events.enhanced_description: The Great Famine of Estonia (1695–1697) was part of a broader crisis affecting the region, leading to significant hardship and loss of life. This famine highlighted the vulnerabilities of agricultural societies in the face of climatic and economic challenges.
events.name: Great Famine of Estonia (1695–1697)

events.enhanced_description: On December 28, 1694 (O.S.), Queen Mary II of England passed away at the age of 32, marking the end of the last joint monarchy with her husband, King William III. Her death had significant implications for the English throne and the future of the monarchy.
events.name: The death of Queen Mary II of England

events.enhanced_description: On January 4, 1695 (O.S.), the Royal Navy warship HMS Nonsuch was captured near the Isles of Scilly by the French privateer Le Francois. The ship was subsequently sold to the French Navy and renamed Le Sans Pareil.
events.name: The capture of HMS Nonsuch by French privateer Le Francois

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1695, a devastating fire destroyed Milan's Court Theater, a significant cultural venue of the time. The loss of this theater impacted the artistic community and the cultural landscape of Milan.
events.name: Milan's Court Theater is destroyed in a fire

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1695, a flotilla of six Royal Navy warships, commanded by Commodore James Killegrew aboard HMS Plymouth, captured two French warships, Content and Trident, after the French mistakenly attacked them, believing they were merchant vessels.
events.name: The capture of two French warships by the Royal Navy

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1695, Mustafa II ascended to the throne as Sultan of the Ottoman Empire, succeeding his uncle Ahmed II. His reign would be marked by military conflicts and attempts at reform within the empire.
events.name: Mustafa II succeeds Ahmed II as Sultan of the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1695, the funeral of Queen Mary II took place in London, featuring music composed by Henry Purcell specifically for the occasion. This event marked a significant moment in the history of the English monarchy.
events.name: The funeral of Queen Mary II of England

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1695, John Trevor, the Speaker of the English House of Commons, was expelled after being found guilty of accepting a bribe of 1,000 pounds sterling from the City of London Corporation. This event underscored the issues of corruption within the political system.
events.name: John Trevor expelled from the House of Commons

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1695, during the War of the Grand Alliance, a significant battle occurred at Sant Esteve d'en Bas, where almost all 1,300 French troops under Brigadier General Urbain Le Clerc de Juigné were killed or captured by a smaller Spanish force led by Ramon de Sala i Saçala.
figures: Brigadier General Urbain Le Clerc de Juigné
events.name: Battle of Sant Esteve d'en Bas

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1695, Paul Foley was elected as the new Speaker of the House of Commons following the expulsion of John Trevor. His election marked a shift in leadership during a tumultuous period in English politics.
events.name: Paul Foley elected as new Speaker of the House

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1695, John Hungerford was expelled from the English House of Commons after being found guilty of accepting a bribe to promote the pending Orphans Bill. This incident highlighted ongoing concerns regarding corruption in the legislature.
events.name: John Hungerford expelled from the House of Commons

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1695, the House of Commons of England decided not to renew the Licensing Order of 1643, which lifted censorship and led to a significant increase in the number of printing houses. This decision fostered a more open society and a flourishing of print culture.
events.name: The House of Commons decides not to renew the Licensing Order of 1643

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1695, Sürmeli Ali Pasha was dismissed from his position as Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire following a disagreement with the new Sultan, Mustafa II. His dismissal marked a significant shift in the empire's leadership dynamics.
events.name: Sürmeli Ali Pasha is fired as Grand Vizier

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1695, during the Russo-Turkish War, Russia initiated the Azov campaigns against the Ottoman Empire, dispatching 31,000 troops to the fortress at Azov on the Don River. This marked a significant military engagement in the ongoing conflict.
events.name: Russia begins the Azov campaigns against the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1695, a devastating 7.8 magnitude earthquake struck Linfen in Shanxi Province, Qing Dynasty, resulting in the deaths of over 50,000 people. This disaster had a profound impact on the local population and infrastructure.
events.name: Linfen earthquake in Shanxi Province

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1695, an annular eclipse of the sun was visible across South America, drawing attention from astronomers and the general public alike. Such celestial events often inspired both scientific inquiry and cultural interpretations.
events.name: An annular eclipse of the sun is visible across South America

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1695, the Commission of Enquiry into the Massacre of Glencoe reported to the Parliament of England, attributing blame to Sir John Dalrymple and asserting that soldiers should refuse unlawful commands. This report had lasting implications for Scottish-English relations.
events.name: The Commission of Enquiry into the Massacre of Glencoe reports

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Namur commenced on July 12, 1695, during the Nine Years' War, as French forces attempted to capture the city from the Grand Alliance. The siege lasted for two months and was marked by intense fighting and significant casualties on both sides.
events.name: The Siege of Namur begins

events.enhanced_description: On July 15, 1695, the Russian Army began a siege of the Ottoman fortress at Azaq, aiming to secure a foothold on the Black Sea. The siege ultimately proved unsuccessful and was abandoned by October 2, 1695.
events.name: The siege of the Ottoman fortress at Azaq begins

events.enhanced_description: The Bank of Scotland was established on July 17, 1695, in Edinburgh, becoming one of the first banks in the world to issue banknotes. It played a crucial role in the development of the Scottish economy and banking system.

image.caption: Bank of Scotland building on Bank Street, Edinburgh.
image.credit: Reading Tom from Reading, UK — IMG_4133
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2014-05-26; this is a later site photograph, not a depiction of the bank’s 1695 founding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Bank of Scotland is founded

events.enhanced_description: Construction of the Wren Building at the College of William & Mary began on August 8, 1695. Designed in the style of Sir Christopher Wren, it is one of the oldest college buildings in the United States and remains a symbol of the institution.
events.name: The Wren Building is started

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1695, a naval skirmish occurred in the Strait of Dover between English and Swedish ships. This conflict was part of the broader tensions in Europe during the Nine Years' War.
events.name: Naval skirmish between English and Swedish ships

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1695, during the Nine Years' War, French troops bombarded Brussels as part of their military campaign against the Grand Alliance. The bombardment caused significant destruction and civilian casualties.
events.name: Brussels is bombarded by French troops

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1695, following a two-month siege, France surrendered the city of Namur to the forces of the Grand Alliance, led by King William III of England. This marked a significant victory for the Grand Alliance in the Nine Years' War.
events.name: France surrenders Namur

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1695, English pirate Henry Every captured the Grand Mughal ship Ganj-i-Sawai, marking one of the most profitable pirate raids in history. The raid prompted a furious response from Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb, who threatened to end all English trading in India.
events.name: Henry Every's raid on the Ganj-i-Sawai

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1695, the Royal Navy ship HMS Winchester foundered in the Florida Keys, resulting in the deaths of all but eight of its 305 crew members. The ship had been ravaged by yellow fever prior to the disaster.
events.name: HMS Winchester disaster

events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1695, King William III of England dissolved Parliament following a scandal involving former Speaker John Trevor and other Tory MPs. This act was part of the ongoing political turmoil in England during the late 17th century.
events.name: King William III dissolves Parliament

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1695, the 48-gun English Navy ship HMS Berkeley Castle was captured by the French Navy. This incident was part of the ongoing naval conflicts during the Nine Years' War.
events.name: HMS Berkeley Castle captured

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1695, King William III opened a new Parliament consisting of 513 members of the House of Commons. This Parliament was notable for its composition, with a majority of Whigs.
events.name: New Parliament opened by King William III

events.enhanced_description: On December 31, 1695, a window tax was imposed in England, leading some homeowners to brick up their windows to avoid the tax. This measure was part of the government's efforts to increase revenue.
events.name: Window tax imposed in England

events.enhanced_description: Colley Cibber's play 'Love's Last Shift' premiered in London, marking a significant moment in English theatrical history. The play contributed to the development of the comedy genre in the Restoration period.
events.name: First Performance of Love's Last Shift

events.enhanced_description: In a naval engagement known as the Battle of Dogger Bank, seven French ships attacked a convoy of Dutch merchant vessels, illustrating the ongoing maritime conflicts during the Nine Years' War.

locations.name: North Sea, near Dogger Bank, England

events.name: Battle of Dogger Bank

events.enhanced_description: The Great Famine of 1695–1697 devastated populations across Finland, Estonia, and Scotland, leading to significant loss of life and social upheaval. This period of famine highlighted the vulnerabilities of agrarian societies to climatic and economic pressures.
events.name: The Great Famine of 1695–1697

events.enhanced_description: Polish was established as an official language of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, replacing Ruthenian. This change reflected the cultural and political shifts within the region during the late 17th century.
events.name: Polish Language Official in Lithuania

events.enhanced_description: Abington, Pennsylvania, was settled, contributing to the expansion of colonial America. This settlement was part of the broader movement of European settlers into the New World during the late 17th century.
events.name: Settlement of Abington, Pennsylvania

events.enhanced_description: William Penn proposed an elaborate plan for intercolonial cooperation, focusing on trade, defense, and criminal matters. This initiative aimed to strengthen ties among the colonies and enhance their collective security.
events.name: William Penn's Plan for Intercolonial Cooperation

events.enhanced_description: Edward Lloyd likely began the publication of Lloyd's News, a precursor to Lloyd's List, in London. This publication played a significant role in maritime news and insurance, reflecting the growing importance of commerce and trade.
events.name: Publication of Lloyd's News

events.enhanced_description: The Window Tax was introduced in England and Wales, marking a significant shift in taxation policy that would remain in effect until 1851. This tax was based on the number of windows in a property, reflecting the economic challenges of the time.
events.name: Introduction of Window Tax

events.enhanced_description: William Whiston published 'A New Theory of the Earth', which received acclaim from intellectuals of the time. This work contributed to the scientific discourse on geology and the earth's formation.
events.name: Publication of A New Theory of the Earth

events.enhanced_description: The Bank of Scotland became the first bank in Europe to successfully issue paper currency, revolutionizing banking and commerce. This innovation laid the groundwork for modern financial systems.
events.name: Bank of Scotland Issues Paper Currency

events.enhanced_description: The HMS Royal Sovereign, originally launched as HMS Sovereign of the Seas in 1638, caught fire and was destroyed at Chatham after 57 years of service. This event marked the end of an era for one of the most famous ships of the Royal Navy.
events.name: HMS Royal Sovereign Catches Fire

events.enhanced_description: In response to new funeral reforms, undertakers in Amsterdam revolted against the changes imposed by the city authorities. This revolt highlighted the tensions between traditional practices and emerging regulations in urban Dutch society.
events.name: Undertakers Revolt in Amsterdam

events.enhanced_description: On January 29 (Old Style), Peter the Great became the sole Tsar of Russia following the death of his half-brother Ivan V. This transition marked a pivotal moment in Russian history as Peter embarked on extensive reforms to modernize the country.
events.name: Peter the Great Becomes Sole Tsar of Russia

events.enhanced_description: A plot to assassinate King William III of England was thwarted when he altered his usual route after a warning from his guard, William Bentinck. This incident underscored the ongoing political tensions and threats to William's reign.
events.name: Assassination Plot Against King William III Foiled

events.enhanced_description: A royal proclamation was issued to arrest Jacobite conspirators involved in a plot against King William III. Key figures such as Robert Charnock and John Fenwick were implicated, leading to their eventual execution.
events.name: Royal Proclamation to Arrest Jacobite Conspirators

events.enhanced_description: King William III of England departed from the Netherlands, marking a significant moment in his dual role as monarch of England and stadtholder of the Dutch Republic. His leadership was pivotal during this period of political complexity.
events.name: King William III Departs from the Netherlands

events.enhanced_description: Spanish missionaries in Santa Fe de Nuevo México alerted the governor about impending plans for a revolt among the Pueblo Indians. This warning set the stage for the significant Pueblo Revolt that would occur later in the year.

locations.name: Santa Fe, New Mexico, United States

events.name: Spanish Missionaries Warn of Pueblo Revolt

events.enhanced_description: During the Nine Years' War, Dutch forces bombarded the town of Givet, demonstrating the ongoing military engagements between the Dutch Republic and France. This action was part of the broader conflict that characterized the period.
events.name: Dutch Bombardment of Givet

events.enhanced_description: Robert Charnock, convicted for his role in the Jacobite plot to assassinate King William III, was executed at the Tower of London. His execution reflected the harsh measures taken against those perceived as threats to the monarchy.
events.name: Robert Charnock Executed

events.enhanced_description: A devastating fire swept through the Gra Bet (Left Quarter) of Gondar, the capital of Ethiopia, destroying numerous buildings, including significant churches. This incident highlighted the vulnerabilities of urban centers in the region.
events.name: Fire Destroys Gra Bet in Gondar

events.enhanced_description: The second Azov campaign commenced during the Russo-Turkish War, with Russian forces aiming to secure control over the strategic port of Azov. This campaign was part of Peter the Great's broader military ambitions.
events.name: Second Azov Campaign Begins

events.enhanced_description: A partial solar eclipse was visible across western Canada and Greenland, captivating observers and contributing to the scientific understanding of celestial events during the period.
events.name: Partial Solar Eclipse Visible

events.enhanced_description: A total lunar eclipse was observable in western Europe and parts of Africa, providing a spectacular celestial display that was noted by astronomers and the general public alike.
events.name: Total Lunar Eclipse Visible

events.enhanced_description: John Salomonsz was elected as the chief of Sint Eustatius, a significant role in the governance of the Caribbean island. His leadership would influence local politics during a period of colonial competition.
events.name: John Salomonsz Elected Chief of Sint Eustatius

events.enhanced_description: The second Pueblo Revolt erupted in Santa Fe de Nuevo México, with various Pueblo tribes attacking Spanish settlers and priests. This uprising was a response to colonial oppression and marked a significant moment in Native American resistance.

locations.name: Santa Fe, New Mexico, United States

events.name: Second Pueblo Revolt Occurs

events.enhanced_description: The Kangxi Emperor of China led his troops in the Battle of Jao Modo, defeating a significant force of Mongolian troops commanded by Galdan Boshugtu Khan. This victory solidified Qing control over the region and demonstrated the emperor's military prowess.
events.name: Battle of Jao Modo

events.enhanced_description: The death of Jan Sobieski left the throne of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth vacant, leading to a power struggle between Friedrich Augustus, Elector of Saxony, and Prince François Louis of France. This event marked a significant shift in the political landscape of Eastern Europe.
events.name: Death of Jan Sobieski

events.enhanced_description: The Russian fleet successfully occupied Azov at the mouth of the Don River, marking a strategic victory in the ongoing conflict with the Ottoman Empire. This occupation was part of Peter the Great's efforts to expand Russian influence in the Black Sea region.
events.name: Russian Fleet Occupies Azov

events.enhanced_description: William III of Orange was appointed Stadtholder of the Dutch state of Drenthe, further consolidating his power within the Dutch Republic. This role allowed him to influence local governance during a tumultuous period.
events.name: William III Becomes Stadtholder of Drenthe

events.enhanced_description: Forces of the Republic of Venice clashed with the Ottoman Empire near Andros, reflecting the ongoing territorial disputes and military engagements between these two powers during the late 17th century.
events.name: Clash Between Venice and Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1733, the Treaty of Turin was signed in Turin as a secret agreement between King Louis XV of France and King Charles Emmanuel III of Sardinia. This treaty was pivotal in the context of the War of the Polish Succession.
events.name: Treaty of Turin Signed

events.enhanced_description: The Parliament of Scotland passed the Education Act 1696, which mandated the establishment of locally funded, Church-supervised schools in every parish. This act was a significant step towards improving education in Scotland.
events.name: Education Act Passed in Scotland

events.enhanced_description: In a strategic decision during the War of the League of Augsburg, the Royal Navy scuttled the HMS Sapphire to prevent it from falling into French hands after a disastrous battle. This act demonstrated the lengths to which naval commanders would go to protect their assets during wartime.
events.name: Scuttling of HMS Sapphire

events.enhanced_description: The English Navy successfully recaptured York Factory from the French, reclaiming a vital trading post on Hudson Bay that had been renamed Fort Bourbon. This event marked a significant moment in the ongoing struggle for control over North American territories.
events.name: Recapture of York Factory

events.enhanced_description: The Convention of Vigevano was signed, marking a significant ceasefire in Italy and effectively ending the Nine Years' War between France and the Grand Alliance. This agreement highlighted the shifting power dynamics in Europe during the late 17th century.
events.name: Convention of Vigevano

events.enhanced_description: The Imperial Russian Navy was founded under the guidance of Tsar Peter the Great, marking a pivotal moment in Russia's naval history. This establishment was part of Peter's broader efforts to modernize and expand Russia's military capabilities.
events.name: Foundation of the Imperial Russian Navy

events.enhanced_description: The Hand in Hand Fire & Life Insurance Society was established in London, becoming a precursor to modern insurance practices. This organization played a crucial role in the development of risk management and financial security in England.
events.name: Founding of Hand in Hand Fire & Life Insurance Society

events.enhanced_description: John Vanbrugh's play 'The Relapse' premiered in London, showcasing the wit and humor characteristic of Restoration comedy. This performance contributed to the vibrant theatrical culture of the time, reflecting societal norms and issues.
events.name: First Performance of The Relapse

events.enhanced_description: The House of Commons approved a bill of attainder convicting Sir John Fenwick of high treason, reflecting the political tensions of the time. This decision paved the way for his execution, underscoring the severe consequences of political conspiracies.
events.name: Conviction of Sir John Fenwick

events.enhanced_description: French explorer Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville captured and destroyed St. John's, Newfoundland, after a three-day siege. This event was part of the larger conflict between France and England for control over North American territories.
events.name: Capture and Destruction of St. John's

events.enhanced_description: Connecticut Route 108 was laid out to Trumbull, marking an important development in the region's infrastructure. This highway would facilitate trade and travel, contributing to the growth of the area.
events.name: Laying out of Connecticut Route 108

events.enhanced_description: Jean-François Regnard's verse comedy 'Le Joueur' premiered in Paris, adding to the rich tapestry of French theatrical tradition. This work reflected the social dynamics and cultural themes of the time.
events.name: Premiere of Le Joueur

events.enhanced_description: The House of Lords voted to approve the bill of attainder against Sir John Fenwick for high treason, finalizing his conviction. This marked a significant moment in the political landscape of England, reflecting the intense scrutiny of loyalty during this period.
events.name: House of Lords Approves Conviction of Sir John Fenwick

events.enhanced_description: The Inquisition in Portugal executed several Marrano Jews by burning at the stake in Évora, reflecting the religious intolerance of the time. This event underscored the severe consequences faced by those accused of heresy during the Inquisition.
events.name: Inquisition in Évora

events.enhanced_description: The Manchus of the Qing dynasty successfully conquered Outer Mongolia, expanding their empire and solidifying their control over the region. This conquest was part of a broader strategy to consolidate power and influence in East Asia.
events.name: Conquest of Outer Mongolia by the Qing dynasty

events.enhanced_description: The Parliament of England passed the Trade with Africa Act 1697, which ended the Royal African Company's monopoly on English trade with Africa. This act marked a significant shift in colonial trade practices and opened the market to competition.
events.name: Trade with Africa Act 1697

events.enhanced_description: William Dampier's A New Voyage Round the World was published in England, providing detailed accounts of his travels and observations. This work contributed to the growing interest in exploration and the natural world during the Age of Enlightenment.
events.name: Publication of A New Voyage Round the World

events.enhanced_description: Christopher Polhem established Sweden's first technical school, marking a significant advancement in education and vocational training in the country. This initiative laid the groundwork for future developments in engineering and technology in Sweden.
events.name: Establishment of Sweden's first technical school

events.enhanced_description: Heinrich Escher, the Mayor of Zürich, introduced chocolate to Switzerland from Brussels, initiating a cultural and culinary transformation in the country. This event marked the beginning of Switzerland's long-standing reputation as a leader in chocolate production.
events.name: Introduction of chocolate to Switzerland

events.enhanced_description: The use of 'litters', wheelless transports carried by servants, saw an increase in Europe during this period. This mode of transportation reflected the social status and wealth of individuals who could afford such luxury.
events.name: Increase in use of litters in Europe

events.enhanced_description: The 'Seven ill years' of famine in Scotland marked a period of severe food shortages and economic distress. This crisis had lasting effects on the Scottish population and contributed to social upheaval.
events.name: Seven ill years of famine in Scotland

events.enhanced_description: Thomas Aikenhead was hanged outside Edinburgh, becoming the last person in Great Britain to be executed for blasphemy. His execution highlighted the tensions between religious authority and freedom of expression during this period.
events.name: Execution of Thomas Aikenhead

events.enhanced_description: Charles Perrault published 'Histoires ou contes du temps passé', a collection of fairy tales that included beloved stories such as Cinderella and Little Red Riding Hood. This work significantly influenced children's literature and popular culture.
events.name: Release of Histoires ou contes du temps passé

events.enhanced_description: Gerrit de Heere was appointed as the new Governor of Dutch Ceylon, succeeding Thomas van Rhee. His administration would last nearly six years, impacting the colonial governance of the region.
events.name: Gerrit de Heere Becomes Governor of Dutch Ceylon

events.enhanced_description: Conquistador Martín de Ursúa y Arizmendi and his contingent of soldiers arrived at Lake Petén Itzá, initiating the Spanish conquest of Guatemala with an assault on the Itza capital. This marked the beginning of further Spanish incursions into Central America.
events.name: Spanish Conquest of Guatemala

events.enhanced_description: In 1697, Tsar Peter the Great of Russia embarked on the Grand Embassy, a diplomatic mission to Western Europe disguised as an artilleryman named Pjotr Mikhailov. His journey aimed to modernize Russia and establish alliances, significantly influencing Russian foreign policy.
events.name: Grand Embassy of Peter the Great

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1697, the Spanish conquest of the Itza Maya Kingdom culminated in the fall of Nojpetén, the last independent Maya city-state. This event marked the end of significant Maya resistance in the region, leading to Spanish dominance in Central America.
events.name: Fall of Nojpetén

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1697, Charles II of Spain issued a Royal Cedula that granted indigenous nobles in the Spanish colonies the same honors and privileges as the Hidalgos of Castile. This decree aimed to integrate indigenous elites into the colonial administration.
events.name: Royal Cedula by Charles II of Spain

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1697, Safavid troops took control of Basra, marking a significant moment in the ongoing conflict between the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire. This occupation was part of the broader struggle for dominance in the region.
events.name: Safavid occupation of Basra

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1697, Charles XII ascended to the throne of Sweden at the young age of 14 following the death of his father, Charles XI. His reign would lead Sweden into significant military conflicts during the Great Northern War.
events.name: Charles XII becomes king of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1697, Galdan Boshugtu Khan, the last ruler of the Dzungar Khanate, committed suicide as Chinese forces completed their conquest of Mongolia. His death marked the end of significant resistance against the Qing Dynasty's expansion.

image.caption: Map showing wars between the Qing Dynasty and Dzungar Khanate.
image.credit: SY — Own work
image.date_qualification: A map of the broader Qing–Dzungar wars, not a depiction of Galdan Boshugtu Khan’s death. The saved image date is 2018-09-16.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Death of Galdan Boshugtu Khan

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1697, General Bernard Desjean, Baron de Pointis, led a successful attack on the Spanish fort of Cartagena de Indias, utilizing a force of 1,200 soldiers and 650 pirates. The siege lasted 18 days, resulting in significant plunder and subsequent conflicts with the pirates.
events.name: Attack on Cartagena de Indias

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1697, the Tre Kronor castle in Stockholm was destroyed by fire, leading to the loss of a significant portion of the royal library. This event marked a pivotal moment in Swedish history, prompting the construction of a new royal palace.
events.name: Fire at Tre Kronor

events.enhanced_description: On June 2, 1697, Augustus, Elector of Saxony, converted to Roman Catholicism to qualify for the Polish throne. This conversion was a strategic move that allowed him to become Augustus II of Poland, influencing the religious and political landscape of the region.
events.name: Augustus II converts to Roman Catholicism

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1697, the last mass execution for witchcraft in Western Europe occurred when five women, known as the Paisley witches, were hanged and subsequently burned in Scotland. This event marked the decline of witch hunts in the region.
events.name: Execution of the Paisley witches

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1697, Augustus II was elected King of Poland following his conversion to Roman Catholicism. His election marked a significant shift in the political dynamics of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
events.name: Augustus II elected King of Poland

events.enhanced_description: On June 30, 1697, the earliest recorded first-class cricket match took place in Sussex, England. This event is significant in the history of cricket, marking the formalization of the sport.
events.name: First-class cricket match in Sussex

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1697, the Byzantine icon known as the 'Weeping Madonna of Pócs' arrived in Vienna after being forcibly removed from Hungary by order of Holy Roman Emperor Leopold I. The icon has since been housed in St. Stephen's Cathedral, becoming a significant religious artifact.
events.name: Arrival of the Weeping Madonna of Pócs

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1697, a significant naval battle occurred between the Republic of Venice and the Ottoman Empire, with both sides deploying 25 battleships. The Venetian Navy, commanded by Admiral Bartolomeo Contarini, faced heavy casualties, marking a critical moment in the ongoing conflict.
events.name: Naval Battle between Venice and the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1697, Mahmud Shah II became the Sultan of Johor and Pahang following the death of the regent, the Bendahara Paduka Raja. His ascension marked a significant moment in the history of the Johor Sultanate.
events.name: Mahmud Shah II takes power

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1697, the opera 'Vénus et Adonis', composed by Henri Desmarets with a libretto by Jean-Baptiste Rousseau, premiered at the Théâtre du Palais-Royal in Paris. This performance marked an important contribution to the French operatic tradition.
events.name: Premiere of Vénus et Adonis

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1697, the Siege of Barcelona concluded after 52 days, with Louis Joseph, Duke of Vendôme, securing the city's surrender from the Austrian General, Prince George of Hesse-Darmstadt. This event was a significant moment in the War of the Spanish Succession.
events.name: Siege of Barcelona ends

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1697, during the Nine Years' War, the Battle of Hudson's Bay was fought between English and French ships near what is now Manitoba, Canada. The French warship Pélican captured York Factory, a significant trading post of the Hudson's Bay Company.
events.name: Battle of Hudson's Bay

events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1697, the Battle of Zenta took place, where Prince Eugene of Savoy decisively defeated the Ottoman army led by Mustafa II. This battle effectively ended Ottoman ambitions to regain territories in Hungary.
events.name: Battle of Zenta

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1697, Amcazade Köprülüzade Hüseyin Pasha was appointed as the new Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire following the defeat at the Battle of Zenta, replacing Elmas Mehmed Pasha, who was killed by his own troops. This change marked a significant shift in Ottoman leadership.
events.name: New Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1697, the Treaty of Ryswick was signed, concluding the Nine Years' War and King William's War. The treaty recognized William III as King of England and Scotland, and mandated the return of territories captured during the conflict.
events.name: Treaty of Ryswick

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1697, the opera 'Issé', composed by André Cardinal Destouches with a libretto by Antoine Houdar de la Motte, premiered at the Palace of Fontainebleau in France. This event contributed to the flourishing of French opera during this period.
events.name: Premiere of Issé

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1697, King Christian V of Denmark-Norway amended the Norwegian Code to allow for torture of condemned criminals in certain capital offenses. This amendment included provisions for severe punishments, reflecting the harsh legal practices of the time.
events.name: Amendment of the Norwegian Code

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1697, Spanish missionary Juan María de Salvatierra founded Misión Loreto, the first Roman Catholic mission on Mexico's Baja California Peninsula. This mission played a crucial role in the Spanish colonization and evangelization of the region.
events.name: Founding of Misión Loreto

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1697, 'L'Europe galante', the first opéra-ballet, premiered at the Salle du Palais-Royal in Paris. Composed by André Campra and conducted by Marin Marais, this performance marked a significant development in the fusion of opera and ballet.
events.name: First opéra-ballet performance

events.enhanced_description: The Peace of Ryswick marked the end of the Nine Years' War between France and the Grand Alliance, concluding with the signing of treaties in Rijswijk. Key territorial adjustments included the return of the Duchy of Lorraine and other regions to Leopold I of Austria, solidifying the balance of power in Europe.
events.name: Peace of Ryswick

events.enhanced_description: The elaborate burial of King Charles XI of Sweden took place at Riddarholmen Church in Stockholm, more than seven months after his death. This event highlighted the significance of royal funerals in Swedish culture and the enduring legacy of Charles XI's reign.
events.name: Burial of King Charles XI of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: Prince Eugene of Savoy, a prominent military leader in the Holy Roman Empire, purchased a large tract of land in Vienna for the construction of the Belvedere Palace. This palace would later become a significant cultural landmark and a symbol of Baroque architecture.
events.name: Purchase of land for Belvedere Palace

events.enhanced_description: The first service held at St Paul's Cathedral since the commencement of rebuilding work after the Great Fire of London marked a significant moment in the restoration of one of England's most iconic churches. This event symbolized resilience and renewal in the face of disaster.
events.name: First service at St Paul's Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: The marriage of Louis, Duke of Burgundy, and Marie Adélaïde of Savoy took place in the royal chapel at the Palace of Versailles, strengthening political alliances through royal marriage. This union was celebrated with great pomp and was significant in the context of French nobility.

locations.name: Palace of Versailles, Versailles, Île-de-France, France

events.name: Marriage of Louis, Duke of Burgundy, and Marie Adélaïde of Savoy

events.enhanced_description: Tsangyang Gyatso was installed as the 6th Dalai Lama in a ceremony in Lhasa, Tibet, filling a vacancy that had existed since 1682. His tenure would be marked by both spiritual leadership and political challenges in the region.
events.name: Installation of Tsangyang Gyatso as the 6th Dalai Lama

events.enhanced_description: A grand ball was held in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles to celebrate the wedding of Louis, Duke of Burgundy, and Marie Adélaïde of Savoy. This event exemplified the opulence of the French court and the importance of social gatherings in reinforcing royal power.

locations.name: Hall of Mirrors, Palace of Versailles, Versailles, Île-de-France, France

events.name: Ball in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles

events.enhanced_description: The coronation ceremony for King Charles XII of Sweden marked the official beginning of his reign. This event was significant in the context of Swedish history, as Charles XII would lead Sweden through a tumultuous period of military conflict.
events.name: Coronation of King Charles XII of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: The Abenaki tribe and Massachusetts colonists signed a treaty, effectively ending the conflict in New England. This agreement was crucial for establishing peace and facilitating future interactions between Native Americans and European settlers.
events.name: Treaty between Abenaki tribe and Massachusetts colonists

events.enhanced_description: Bishop Jeremy Collier published his pamphlet A Short View of the Immorality and Profaneness of the English Stage, criticizing contemporary playwrights for undermining public morality. This work sparked significant debate about the role of theater in society and its moral implications.

image.caption: Mezzotint portrait of Jeremy Collier by William Faithorne Jr, after Edmond Lilly.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — https://reformedanglicans.blogspot.com/2015/09/23-september-1650-ad-jeremy-collier.html
image.date_qualification: An 18th-century portrait of Jeremy Collier, not a depiction of the pamphlet’s publication.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Publication of Jeremy Collier's pamphlet

events.enhanced_description: Samuel Cranston was appointed as the governor of the Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations, serving multiple terms and playing a significant role in the early governance of the colony.

locations.historical_name: Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations
locations.name: Providence, Rhode Island, United States

events.name: Samuel Cranston becomes the governor of the Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations

events.enhanced_description: King William III granted a charter to the New East India Company, aimed at breaking the monopoly of the existing British East India Company in India, reflecting the competitive nature of colonial trade.
events.name: Charter granted to the New East India Company

events.enhanced_description: The first Eddystone Lighthouse, located off the coast of Plymouth, was illuminated for the first time in January 1698. This lighthouse became an important navigational aid for ships navigating the treacherous waters of the English Channel.
