events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1711, Tuscarora natives captured John Lawson, Christoph von Graffenried, and their expeditionary party, bringing them to Catechna. This event was part of the larger context of conflict between Native Americans and European settlers.
events.name: Capture of Lawson by Tuscarora

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1711, John Lawson was killed by Tuscarora natives after being captured during an expedition. His death marked a significant moment in the Tuscarora War, which was characterized by violent conflicts between Native Americans and European settlers.

image.caption: Possible portrait of John Lawson, attributed to Godfrey Kneller.
image.credit: Godfrey Kneller — https://www.lawsontrek.com/john-lawson.html
image.date_qualification: The supplied image date is 1709-01-01; this is presented as a portrait, not as an image of Lawson’s death in 1711.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Death of John Lawson

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1711, Bishop Bogusław Gosiewski sold the town of Maladzyechna in the Minsk Region of Belarus to the influential Ogiński family. This transaction reflected the shifting power dynamics in the region during this period.
events.name: Sale of Maladzyechna

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1711, the Tuscarora War began when Tuscarora natives, led by Chief Hancock, raided settlements along the south bank of the Pamlico River in North Carolina, resulting in the deaths of around 130 settlers. This conflict would escalate into a prolonged war between the Tuscarora and European settlers.

locations.name: Pamlico River, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Beginning of the Tuscarora War

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1711, HMS Feversham was wrecked on Scaterie Island, Nova Scotia, resulting in the loss of 102 lives. This maritime disaster highlighted the dangers faced by naval vessels during this era.
events.name: Wreck of HMS Feversham

events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1711, a tragic stampede on the Guillottière bridge in Lyon, France, resulted in the deaths of 241 people. The chaos ensued when revelers returning from a festival were blocked from crossing, leading to panic and a deadly crush.
events.name: Guillottière bridge stampede

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1711, Yostos killed Tewoflos, ascending to the throne as Emperor of Ethiopia. His reign marked a significant period in Ethiopian history, characterized by internal strife and external pressures.
events.name: Yostos becomes Emperor of Ethiopia

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1711, the Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts was established in Brussels, Belgium. This institution would play a crucial role in the development of the arts in the region and influence future generations of artists.
events.name: Establishment of Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1711, the southwest spire of Southwell Minster in Nottinghamshire was struck by lightning, causing a fire that spread to the nave and tower, destroying roofs, bells, clock, and organ. This event had a lasting impact on the historic church's architecture.
events.name: Fire at Southwell Minster

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1711, the Dutch East India Company ship Liefde ran aground and sank off Out Skerries in Shetland, resulting in the loss of all but one of her 300 crew members. This maritime disaster underscored the dangers of sea travel during this period.
events.name: Sinking of the Liefde

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1711, the Battle of Wismar took place during the Great Northern War, resulting in a decisive Danish victory over Swedish forces. This battle was part of the larger conflict that reshaped the balance of power in Northern Europe.
events.name: Battle of Wismar

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1711, the Earl of Nottingham successfully proposed the 'No Peace Without Spain' amendment in the Parliament of Great Britain, reflecting the ongoing tensions of the War of the Spanish Succession and the desire to maintain British interests in the region.
events.name: No Peace Without Spain Amendment Proposal

events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1711, the Immaculate Conception Cathedral in Comayagua, Honduras, was inaugurated. This cathedral is one of the oldest in Central America and serves as a significant religious site in the region.
events.name: Inauguration of Immaculate Conception Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1711, a constitution was approved for the Academy of Sciences of the Institute of Bologna, which had been founded in 1690. This institution played a crucial role in the advancement of scientific knowledge in Italy.
events.name: Constitution Approval for Academy of Sciences of Bologna

events.enhanced_description: On December 13, 1711, Wall Street in New York City became the first official slave market for the sale and rental of enslaved Africans and Indians, marking a significant and troubling chapter in American history regarding slavery and commerce.
events.name: Establishment of Slave Market on Wall Street

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1711, the Old Pummerin, a massive bell cast from 208 captured cannons, was consecrated by Bishop Franz Ferdinand Freiherr von Rummel in preparation for its installation in St. Stephen's Cathedral in Vienna.
figures: Bishop Franz Ferdinand Freiherr von Rummel
events.name: Consecration of the Old Pummerin Bell

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1711, the rebuilding of St Paul's Cathedral in London, designed by Sir Christopher Wren, was declared complete by Parliament. The original cathedral had been destroyed in the Great Fire of London in 1666.
events.name: Completion of St Paul's Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: In early March 1712, French Navy captain Jacques Cassard began his expedition, during which he ransacked Santiago in the Cape Verde Islands and pillaged several Caribbean islands, returning to France with loot valued at over nine million francs.
events.name: Start of the Cassard Expedition

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Villmergen occurred in 1712, where the Reformed cantons of Switzerland defeated the Catholic cantons, further entrenching the religious divisions in the region.
events.name: Battle of Villmergen

events.enhanced_description: In 1712, Thomas Newcomen and John Calley built the first known working steam engine in the Black Country of England, marking a pivotal moment in the Industrial Revolution by making practical use of steam power for mechanical work.
events.name: First working Newcomen steam engine built

events.enhanced_description: In 1712, after years of settlement, the Town on Queen Anne's Creek was established as a courthouse for Chowan County, North Carolina, later renamed Edenton in 1720.
events.name: Establishment of Town on Queen Anne's Creek

events.enhanced_description: In 1712, the VOC Zuytdorp was wrecked off the coast of Western Australia, a significant maritime disaster during the Dutch East India Company's trading activities.
events.name: Wreck of the VOC Zuytdorp

events.enhanced_description: In 1712, John Arbuthnot introduced the character of John Bull in his satirical writings, embodying the spirit of Britain as a stout, honest, and somewhat bumbling figure. This character became a national personification of England and has been used in various political cartoons and literature ever since.
events.name: John Arbuthnot creates the character of John Bull to represent Britain

events.enhanced_description: In 1712, John Richardson published a translation of the 1662 Book of Common Prayer into Irish, making the Anglican liturgy accessible to Irish speakers. This translation played a significant role in the religious and cultural life of Ireland, particularly among the Anglican community.
events.name: A translation of the 1662 Book of Common Prayer into Irish is published

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 2017, a total solar eclipse, known as 'The Great American Eclipse', was visible across a band stretching from the Pacific to the Atlantic coasts of the contiguous United States. This astronomical event captivated millions of viewers and was notable for its path of totality.
events.name: Total Solar Eclipse

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1712, the opera Idoménée by André Campra premiered at the Théâtre du Palais-Royal in Paris, marking a significant event in the French operatic tradition.
events.name: Premiere of Idoménée Opera

events.enhanced_description: On January 16, 1712, a military engineering school was established in Moscow, which would later evolve into the A.F. Mozhaysky Military-Space Academy, contributing to military education in Russia.
events.name: Establishment of Military Engineering School

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1712, the Old Pummerin bell, weighing 18,161 kg, was rung for the first time at St. Stephen's Cathedral in Vienna to mark the entry of Charles VI into the city after his coronation as Emperor.
events.name: First Ringing of the Old Pummerin Bell

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1712, the Huilliche people in Chile's Chiloé Archipelago rose up against Spanish encomenderos in a rebellion fueled by grievances over injustices, marking a significant indigenous resistance against colonial rule.
events.name: Huilliche Uprising of 1712

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1712, the Scottish Episcopalians Act 1711 came into effect, leading to the incorporation of the Scottish Episcopal Church, a significant development in the religious landscape of Scotland.
events.name: Scottish Episcopalians Act 1711

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1712, Sweden temporarily adopted the rare February 30 as a day to adjust the Swedish Calendar back to the Julian calendar, a unique occurrence in the history of timekeeping.
events.name: Sweden Adopts February 30

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1712, HMS Dragon, a 38-gun fourth-rate frigate of the British Royal Navy, was wrecked on Les Casquets rocks to the west of Alderney, highlighting the perils faced by naval vessels of the time.
events.name: Wreck of HMS Dragon

events.enhanced_description: On March 30, 1712, Queen Anne of Great Britain administered the Royal touch for the last time, touching 300 scrofulous individuals, including the notable Samuel Johnson, in a ritual believed to cure illness.
events.name: Queen Anne's Last Royal Touch

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1712, the New York Slave Revolt erupted, resulting in the deaths of nine whites and the execution of 21 slaves and other blacks, marking a significant moment in the history of slavery in the American colonies.
events.name: New York Slave Revolt of 1712

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1712, the Battle of Fladstrand took place at sea near Fladstrand, Jutland, between Swedish and Danish forces during the Great Northern War, illustrating the ongoing conflict in the region.
events.name: Battle of Fladstrand

events.enhanced_description: On May 15, 1712, Curuguaty was founded by Juan Gregorio de Bazán y Pedraza on the banks of the Curuguaty River, contributing to the settlement and development of the region in Paraguay.
figures: Juan Gregorio de Bazán y Pedraza
events.name: Founding of Curuguaty

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1712, Peter the Great moved the capital of Russia from Moscow to Saint Petersburg, a strategic decision that aimed to modernize the Russian state and enhance its maritime capabilities.
events.name: Peter the Great Moves Capital

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1712, Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor, was crowned King of Hungary, solidifying his rule and influence in Central Europe during a period of political complexity.
events.name: Charles VI Crowned King of Hungary

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1712, Reus was granted the title of imperial city by Elisabeth Christine, the wife of Archduke Charles, reflecting its importance in the region during the early 18th century.
events.name: Reus is given the title of imperial city

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1712, the Kurtkulağı Caravanserai in Adana Province was restored, and 50 soldiers were appointed to guard it, highlighting the importance of caravanserais as safe havens for travelers and merchants in the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Restoration of Kurtkulağı Caravanserai

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1712, Chatham was officially incorporated as a town in Barnstable County, Massachusetts, marking its development as a significant community in the region.

image.caption: Chatham Light House on Main Street in Chatham, Massachusetts.
image.credit: Bob Linsdell — https://web.archive.org/web/20161031145325/http://www.panoramio.com/photo/99873132
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2 October 2013; the event occurred 11 June 1712.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0; Copyrighted: True

locations.name: Chatham, Barnstable County, Massachusetts, United States

events.name: Incorporation of Chatham as a town

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1712, St Ann's Church in Manchester was consecrated by the Bishop of Chester, symbolizing the growth of the Anglican Church in the rapidly industrializing city.
events.name: Consecration of St Ann's Church

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1712, the British Royal Navy launched the 50-gun ship HMS Advice at Deptford Dockyard, contributing to the naval power of Great Britain during the early 18th century.
events.name: Launch of HMS Advice

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1712, Jesus College, Oxford inherited the extensive library of its Principal, Jonathan Edwards, upon his death, enriching the academic resources of the institution.
events.name: Death of Jonathan Edwards

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1712, during the War of the Spanish Succession, the French forces, led by the Duke of Villars, achieved a decisive victory against a combined Dutch-Austrian army at the Battle of Denain.
events.name: Battle of Denain

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1712, the Stamp Act was passed in the United Kingdom, imposing a tax on publishers, particularly targeting newspapers, which would later contribute to tensions leading to the American Revolution.
events.name: Passage of the Stamp Act 1712

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1712, the Peace of Aarau was signed, concluding the Toggenburg War and establishing Protestant dominance in Switzerland while ensuring the rights of Catholics.
events.name: Signing of the Peace of Aarau

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1712, the British Royal Navy launched the 60-gun ship HMS Rippon at Deptford Dockyard, further enhancing the naval capabilities of Great Britain.
events.name: Launch of HMS Rippon

events.enhanced_description: In September 1712, composer George Frideric Handel relocated to London with the permission of his patron, the future King George I, marking a significant step in his career and influence in English music.
events.name: George Frideric Handel relocates to London

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1712, a severe hurricane struck Bermuda, lasting for eight hours and causing extensive damage to most of the churches on the island.
events.name: Hurricane in Bermuda

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1712, a warrant was issued for the arrest of the notorious outlaw Rob Roy MacGregor by Sir James Stewart, the Lord Advocate of Scotland, reflecting the ongoing tensions between the Scottish clans and the government.
events.name: Warrant for Rob Roy MacGregor's arrest

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1712, King Philip V of Spain established the Biblioteca Nacional de España as the Palace Public Library in Madrid, laying the foundation for one of the most important cultural institutions in the country.
events.name: Establishment of the Biblioteca Nacional de España

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1712, the Bandbox Plot was foiled, which aimed to assassinate British Lord Treasurer Robert Harley, Earl of Oxford, with the intervention of Jonathan Swift, the author of 'Gulliver's Travels'.
events.name: The Bandbox Plot

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1712, the first performance of George Frideric Handel's opera 'Il pastor fido' took place at the Queen's Theatre in the Haymarket, London, marking a significant moment in the history of English opera.
events.name: First performance of Il pastor fido

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1712, the charter for Buchach Monastery, founded by Stefan Aleksander Potocki and his wife Joanna Sieniawska, was signed in Lublin, establishing a significant religious institution in Ukraine.
events.name: Charter of Buchach Monastery signed

events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1712, the Battle of Gadebusch marked Sweden's final significant victory in the Great Northern War, preventing the loss of Stralsund to Danish and Saxon forces.
events.name: Battle of Gadebusch

events.enhanced_description: On December 27, 1712, the opera 'Callirhoé' by André Cardinal Destouches premiered at the Théâtre du Palais-Royal in Paris, showcasing the flourishing French opera scene of the time.
events.name: Premiere of Callirhoé

events.enhanced_description: Ars Conjectandi, a seminal work on probability theory by Jacob Bernoulli, was published posthumously by his nephew Niklaus Bernoulli. This publication laid foundational principles for the field of probability and statistics, influencing future generations of mathematicians.
events.name: Publication of Ars Conjectandi

events.enhanced_description: Basil Matthew II was appointed as the Syriac Orthodox Maphrian of the East, a significant ecclesiastical position within the Syriac Orthodox Church. His leadership played a crucial role in the church's governance and spiritual guidance during a period of religious and political challenges.
events.name: Basil Matthew II becomes Maphrian

events.enhanced_description: San Basilio de Palenque officially became the first free African town in America, marking a significant milestone in the history of African resistance against colonial rule. This community was established by escaped slaves and became a symbol of freedom and cultural identity.

locations.name: San Basilio de Palenque, Bolívar, Colombia

events.name: San Basilio de Palenque becomes free town

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1713, Colonel James Moore led the Carolina militia from Albemarle County in a second offensive against the Tuscarora tribe during the Tuscarora War. Heavy snow forced the troops to take refuge in Fort Reading along the Pamlico River, highlighting the harsh conditions faced by the militia.

locations.name: Albemarle County, North Carolina, United States
Pamlico River, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Tuscarora War: Colonel James Moore leads the Carolina militia out of Albemarle County, North Carolina

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1713, during the Great Northern War, Charles XII of Sweden faced defeat at the Skirmish at Bender against the Ottoman Empire. This battle marked a significant setback for Sweden as it struggled to maintain its influence in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Skirmish at Bender, Moldova: Charles XII of Sweden is defeated by the Ottoman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1713, Colonel James Moore's Carolina militia departed from Fort Reading to continue their campaign against the Tuscarora tribe during the ongoing Tuscarora War. This movement was part of a larger effort to subdue the Native American resistance in the region.

locations.name: Fort Reading, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Tuscarora War: The Carolina militia under Colonel James Moore leaves Fort Reading

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1713, Frederick William I ascended to the throne of Prussia, marking the beginning of his reign. Known as the 'Soldier King,' he focused on military reforms and strengthening the Prussian state.

image.caption: Portrait of Frederick William I of Prussia with August II of Poland, by Louis de Silvestre.
image.credit: Louis de Silvestre — web
image.date_qualification: Undated; stated to be before 1733. The painting is not dated to the 1713 accession.
image.image_date: undated, before 1733 date QS:P571,+1733-00-00T00:00:00Z/7,P1326,+1733-00-00T00:00:00Z/9 (the sitter died that year)
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Frederick William I of Prussia begins his reign

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1713, Colonel James Moore's Carolina militia laid siege to Fort Neoheroka, a stronghold of the Tuscarora tribe. This action was a crucial part of the military campaign aimed at dismantling the Tuscarora's resistance in North Carolina.

locations.name: Fort Neoheroka, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Tuscarora War: Colonel James Moore's Carolina militia lays siege to Fort Neoheroka

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1713, Colonel James Moore's Carolina militia launched a significant offensive against Fort Neoheroka, intensifying the conflict during the Tuscarora War. This assault was part of a broader strategy to eliminate the Tuscarora threat in the region.

locations.name: Fort Neoheroka, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Tuscarora War: Colonel James Moore's Carolina militia launches a major offensive against Fort Neoheroka

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1713, Fort Neoheroka fell to the Carolina militia, effectively ending the military strength of the Tuscarora nation. This victory marked a turning point in the Tuscarora War, although some Tuscaroran allies continued to resist.

locations.name: Fort Neoheroka, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Tuscarora War: Fort Neoheroka falls to the Carolina militia

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1713, the First Treaty of Utrecht was signed, recognizing Philip V as the king of Spain by Great Britain and Austria. This treaty also resulted in Spain ceding Gibraltar and Menorca to Britain, reshaping the balance of power in Europe.
events.name: First Treaty of Utrecht between Great Britain and Spain

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1713, the Second Treaty of Utrecht was signed, officially ending the War of the Spanish Succession. This treaty resulted in France ceding Newfoundland, Acadia, Hudson Bay, and St Kitts to Great Britain, significantly altering colonial territories.

image.caption: A first edition of the Treaty of Utrecht in Spanish beside a copy printed in Latin and English.
image.credit: The_Treaty_of_Utrecht.jpg : Original uploader was RedCoat10 at en.wikipedia derivative work: Angel paez ( talk ) — The_Treaty_of_Utrecht.jpg
image.date_qualification: The image shows treaty editions, not the signing itself. The original image date is 2010-11-13 00:20; this is not the date of the depicted documents.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Second Treaty of Utrecht between Great Britain and France ends the War of the Spanish Succession

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1713, Joseph Addison's play 'Cato, a Tragedy' premiered in London. The play, which championed liberty and republicanism, became influential in both British and American political thought.
events.name: First performance of Joseph Addison's play Cato, a Tragedy in London

events.enhanced_description: On April 19, 1713, Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor, issued the Pragmatic Sanction, which aimed to ensure that one of his daughters would inherit the Habsburg lands. This decree was crucial for the future of the Habsburg dynasty and European politics.
events.name: Charles VI issues the Pragmatic Sanction of 1713

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1713, as part of the Treaty of Utrecht, the Spanish Crown agreed to the Asiento de Negros with Anne, Queen of Great Britain. This agreement granted a subsidiary of the British South Sea Company a 30-year monopoly on the supply of African slaves to colonial Spanish America.
events.name: Asiento de Negros agreement with Anne, Queen of Great Britain

events.enhanced_description: On May 2, 1713, during the Great Northern War, a fleet of the Russian Navy, carrying 12,000 soldiers, set sail from Kronstadt to attack the Swedish Army stationed at Helsinki. This military action was part of Russia's broader strategy to expand its influence in the Baltic region.
events.name: Great Northern War: Russian Navy attacks Swedish Army at Helsinki

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1713, Queen Anne dissolved the Parliament of Ireland, setting the stage for new elections. This action reflected the ongoing tensions and political maneuvering between the British crown and Irish governance.
events.name: The Parliament of Ireland is dissolved by Queen Anne

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1713, King Philip V of Spain issued an auto accordado that altered the order of succession for the Spanish throne, allowing a female descendant within the House of Bourbon to rule. This decision would eventually enable his great-great-granddaughter to ascend the throne as Queen Isabella II in 1833.
events.name: King Philip V of Spain issues an auto accordado changing succession order

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1713, 'Ottone in villa,' the first opera composed by Antonio Vivaldi, premiered at the Teatro delle Grazie in Vicenza. This work marked Vivaldi's entry into the operatic genre and showcased his innovative musical style.
events.name: Ottone in villa, the first opera by Antonio Vivaldi, is performed

events.enhanced_description: On May 21, 1713, during the Great Northern War, the Russian fleet successfully landed a force of 10,000 men at Pernå on the southern coast of Finland. This strategic move was part of Russia's campaign against Sweden.
events.name: Great Northern War: Russian fleet lands troops at Pernå

events.enhanced_description: In June 1713, Colonel James Moore led the Carolina militia into the Pamlico Peninsula to confront the Machapunga and Coree tribes during the Tuscarora War. This campaign aimed to suppress Native American resistance in the region.

locations.name: Pamlico Peninsula, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Tuscarora War: Colonel James Moore leads the Carolina militia into the Pamlico Peninsula

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1713, French residents of Acadia were given one year to declare their allegiance to Great Britain or face expulsion from Nova Scotia. This ultimatum was part of the broader consequences of the Treaty of Utrecht and the shifting political landscape in North America.
events.name: French residents of Acadia are given one year to declare allegiance to Great Britain

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1713, the Junta de Braços, the parliament of the Principality of Catalonia, voted in favor of continuing the War of the Spanish Succession against Philip V of Spain. This decision reflected the ongoing resistance to Bourbon rule in Catalonia.
events.name: The Junta de Braços of Catalonia votes to continue the War of the Spanish Succession

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1713, the Treaty of Portsmouth was signed, officially ending Queen Anne's War. This treaty concluded hostilities between Great Britain and France in North America, reshaping territorial claims in the region.
events.name: The Treaty of Portsmouth brings an end to Queen Anne's War

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1713, the Parliament of Great Britain, the third since the Act of Union, was dissolved. This dissolution set the stage for new elections and reflected the ongoing political changes in Britain following the conclusion of the War of the Spanish Succession.
events.name: The Parliament of Great Britain is dissolved

events.enhanced_description: On August 22, 1713, voting commenced in the British general election, which would continue until November 12. This election was significant in shaping the political landscape of Great Britain following the end of the War of the Spanish Succession.
events.name: Voting begins in the 1713 British general election

events.enhanced_description: The Tuscarora War was a conflict between the Tuscarora Native Americans and European settlers in North Carolina, which saw the Carolina militia, led by Colonel James Moore, return to South Carolina after a campaign against the Machapunga and Coree tribes. The war highlighted the tensions between indigenous peoples and colonial expansion in the early 18th century.
events.name: Tuscarora War

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Schwedt was a significant agreement signed between Russia and Brandenburg-Prussia, where Brandenburg accepted the annexation of Baltic territories by Russia in exchange for the southern part of Pomerania. This treaty was a key outcome of the Great Northern War, reshaping the balance of power in Northern Europe.
events.name: Treaty of Schwedt

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Pälkäne was fought between Russian and Swedish forces during the Great Northern War, where Russian commander Fyodor Arpaskin successfully forced the Finnish troops under Carl Gustaf Armfeldt to withdraw. This battle exemplified the ongoing military struggles between the two empires in the region.
events.name: Battle of Pälkäne

events.enhanced_description: The Dublin election riot erupted during the fiercely contested Irish General Election of 1713, reflecting the intense political divisions and social tensions of the time. This riot underscored the volatile nature of electoral politics in early 18th-century Ireland.
events.name: Dublin election riot

events.enhanced_description: The 1713 British general election concluded with the conservative Tory party winning a significant majority in the House of Commons, securing 358 out of 558 seats. This election marked a pivotal moment in British politics, influencing the direction of government and policy in the years to come.
events.name: 1713 British general election

events.enhanced_description: As part of the agreements made at the Treaty of Utrecht, Great Britain and Spain signed a treaty of commerce and navigation, which aimed to regulate trade relations and facilitate economic exchanges between the two nations. This treaty was a crucial step in stabilizing post-war relations following the War of the Spanish Succession.

image.caption: Image of a first edition of the Treaty of Utrecht in Spanish alongside a Latin and English copy.
image.credit: The_Treaty_of_Utrecht.jpg : Original uploader was RedCoat10 at en.wikipedia derivative work: Angel paez ( talk ) — The_Treaty_of_Utrecht.jpg
image.date_qualification: The image depicts treaty documents, not the signing event; the saved image date is 2010-11-13.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Treaty of Commerce and Navigation

events.enhanced_description: The rebellion of Richard Raworth, Deputy Governor of Fort St. David, against the British East India Company came to an end after two months when forces sent by Governor Edward Harrison negotiated a settlement. This event highlighted the tensions between colonial authorities and local governance in India.

locations.name: Fort St. David, Tamil Nadu, India

events.name: Rebellion of Richard Raworth

events.enhanced_description: Victor Amadeus II, Duke of Savoy, was crowned King of Sicily in a ceremony held in Palermo, alongside his wife Anne Marie as Queen consort. This coronation followed Spain's recognition of Sicilian independence, marking a significant moment in the region's political landscape.
events.name: Coronation of Victor Amadeus

events.enhanced_description: In 1714, Archbishop Thomas Tenison established Archbishop Tenison's School in Croydon, which is recognized as the world's earliest surviving mixed-gender school. This institution played a crucial role in the evolution of education in England.

locations.name: Croydon, Greater London, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Establishment of Archbishop Tenison's School

events.enhanced_description: In 1714, Louis Juchereau de St. Denis established Fort St. Jean Baptiste at the site of present-day Natchitoches, Louisiana. This fort marked the first permanent European settlement in the Louisiana Territory, contributing to the French colonial presence in North America.

image.caption: Photograph of restored Fort Saint Jean Baptiste in Natchitoches, Louisiana.
image.credit: Billy Hathorn — Own work
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2009-08-08; this is not a contemporaneous image of the 1714 establishment.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Establishment of Fort St. Jean Baptiste

events.enhanced_description: In 1714, Worcester College was founded at the University of Oxford, succeeding the earlier Gloucester College, which had been closed during the Dissolution of the Monasteries. This institution continues to be an integral part of Oxford's educational landscape.
events.name: Founding of Worcester College, University of Oxford

events.enhanced_description: In 1714, Stockholm County was officially founded, establishing a key administrative region in Sweden. This development played a significant role in the governance and organization of the area surrounding the capital.

image.caption: Location map showing Stockholm County within Sweden.
image.credit: Erik Frohne — Own work
image.date_qualification: Map created in 2009; it provides geographic context for the county, not a depiction of its foundation in 1714.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Foundation of Stockholm County

events.enhanced_description: In 1714, the Kander River in Switzerland was redirected into Lake Thun, a significant engineering project that altered the local landscape and water management. This project reflects the early efforts in hydraulic engineering in the region.
events.name: Redirection of the Kander River

events.enhanced_description: Prince Azz-ud-din Mirza was blinded on the orders of Emperor Farrukhsiyar after being tricked into deserting a battle against the Mughal Empire by the rebel Sayyid brothers. This event reflects the internal power struggles and brutal political maneuvers characteristic of the Mughal court.
events.name: Blinding of Azz-ud-din Mirza

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Tönning concluded after Danish forces compelled the surrender of the remaining defenders, marking a significant victory in the ongoing conflicts of the Great Northern War. The fortress was subsequently leveled by the Danes, symbolizing their dominance in the region.
events.name: Siege of Tönning

events.enhanced_description: Tsar Peter the Great issued a decree mandating compulsory education in mathematics for children of government officials and nobility, targeting those aged 10 to 15 years. This initiative aimed to modernize Russia and improve the educational standards of its ruling class.
events.name: Decree on Compulsory Education

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Storkyro was fought between Swedish and Russian forces, resulting in heavy casualties for the outnumbered Swedish troops. This battle was part of the larger conflict of the Great Northern War, showcasing the fierce military engagements between the two empires.

image.caption: Carl Gustaf Armfeldt’s sketch map of the Battle of Storkyro, showing the river, road to Vasa, village of Napue, and Swedish troop positions.
image.credit: Carl Gustaf Armfeldt — Johan Henrik Frisenheim - Karolinen som aldrig gav upp
image.date_qualification: Dated 1714 in the supplied image metadata; presented as Armfeldt’s sketch of the battle, not as a photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Storkyro

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Rastatt was signed between Austria and France, concluding the War of the Spanish Succession. This treaty resulted in significant territorial gains for Austria, marking the peak of Habsburg power in Europe.
events.name: Treaty of Rastatt

events.enhanced_description: France signed five separate treaties with various nations, including Great Britain and the Netherlands, to formally end hostilities following the War of the Spanish Succession. This series of agreements marked a significant step towards peace in Europe.
events.name: France signs treaties to end hostilities

events.enhanced_description: Italian Jesuit missionary Niccolò Gianpriamo was dispatched from Portugal on an evangelical mission to Asia, beginning with the Portuguese colony of Goa. His journey highlights the efforts of European missionaries to spread Christianity in Asia during this period.
events.name: Niccolò Gianpriamo's evangelical trip

events.enhanced_description: Queen Anne of Great Britain made the controversial decision to refuse permission for members of the House of Hanover to settle in Britain during her lifetime, reflecting the political tensions and succession issues of the time. This decision had lasting implications for the British monarchy.
events.name: Anne refuses House of Hanover

events.enhanced_description: Johann Sebastian Bach led the first performance of his cantata for Pentecost, Erschallet, ihr Lieder, BWV 172, at the chapel of Schloss Weimar. This event marked an important moment in the development of Bach's musical legacy and the cultural life of Weimar.
events.name: Bach's cantata performance

events.enhanced_description: The city of Kassel inaugurated the summer tradition of the "water stairs" or "great cascades" (Grossen Kaskaden), which empty from the base of the Hercules monument down to the Wilhelmshöhe castle. This event marked the beginning of a cultural and artistic tradition that continues to attract visitors.
events.name: Inauguration of water stairs in Kassel

events.enhanced_description: In France, Bishop Henri-Charles du Cambout de Coislin condemned the papal bull Unigenitus, issued by Pope Clement XI, which inflamed the Jansenist controversy. This condemnation highlighted the ongoing religious tensions within the Catholic Church and the broader society.
events.name: Condemnation of papal bull Unigenitus

events.enhanced_description: Spain and the Netherlands signed a peace treaty to formally end hostilities between the two nations following the War of the Spanish Succession. This treaty was part of the broader efforts to stabilize Europe after years of conflict.
events.name: Peace treaty between Spain and the Netherlands

events.enhanced_description: The Parliament of Great Britain voted to offer a reward for discovering a method to determine a ship's longitude, with escalating prizes for varying degrees of accuracy. This initiative was crucial for maritime navigation and spurred advancements in scientific understanding.
events.name: Longitude prize vote

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Gangut marked the first significant naval victory for the Imperial Russian Navy against the Swedish Navy during the Great Northern War. This victory was pivotal in establishing Russian naval power in the Baltic Sea.
events.name: Battle of Gangut

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1714, Georg Ludwig von Braunschweig-Lüneburg ascended to the throne as King George I of Great Britain and Ireland following the death of Queen Anne. His accession marked the end of the House of Stuart's reign and the beginning of the House of Hanover, as he was the closest Protestant relative to Anne.
events.name: Georg Ludwig von Braunschweig-Lüneburg becomes King George I of Great Britain and Ireland

events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1714, after a prolonged siege, Barcelona fell to the Spanish and French Bourbon armies during the War of the Spanish Succession. This event marked a significant turning point in the conflict, leading to the consolidation of Bourbon rule in Spain.
events.name: Barcelona taken during the War of the Spanish Succession
